ASRS:1829597.n: During initial takeoff roll, at takeoff thrust setting and less than 30 kts, aircraft began uncommanded hard left turn. Initiated slow speed reject, tried to counter with full right rudder and full right nose wheel steering. Tiller was binding, only 10 degrees of travel available as if fighting left tiller inputs. Continued manual braking to a full stop with the aircraft nose close to 45 degrees left of centerline with the aircraft fully blocking taxiway. We informed Tower of the rejected takeoff and that we required a tow back to the ramp. Suspected nose wheel steering malfunction
ASRS:1829597.s: During initial takeoff roll below 30 kts, the aircraft executed an uncommanded hard left turn due to suspected nose wheel steering malfunction. The crew rejected the takeoff, but binding tiller limited steering to 10 degrees, resulting in a full stop blocking the taxiway and requiring a tow back.

ASRS:1829603.n: ATC had just assigned us a descent from our cruise altitude. While in a shallow descent to the newly assigned altitude we received an 'Engine Fire' CAS along with the 'Fire' voice callout. The PM (PIC) immediately identified and reset the master warning. The PM then begun the QRH actions associated with the CAS message as I PF (SIC) suggested lower. The PIC asked for a diversion to [a nearby alternate] from ATC and also asked for a lower altitude. Upon the diversion request ATC asked for the reason why. At this point both crew members agreed this was an [critical] situation and it was declared over the frequency as a possible engine fire. The Controller then asked if we wanted to stay close to the airport and if we could expedite our descent for the ILS. I as PF began an immediate descent to 2,000 feet MSL at around 3,000 feet per minute at full forward speed. In the meantime the PM was donning their oxygen mask while still following the procedures listed in the QRH. As we were about to level off and intercept the localizer our autopilot failed. At this point I was flying the aircraft and setting up the ILS at the same time. Since the autopilot failed I immediately requested the PM to drop the checklist and finish setting up the ILS as I stabilized the aircraft from its descent. It should also be noted that at the time of level off and autopilot failure the Controller issued their first approach clearance to us. Both of us were too busy to properly read it back with everything going on. Once the localizer was set and we were stable we intercepted the glideslope slightly higher than the minimum altitude for the step down fix. I, as PF, kept the speed up and configured with gear first then flaps. I remained at flaps 15 for the landing as I wanted to approach faster to get on the ground quicker. At about 1,200-1,400 feet MSL the red 'Engine Fire' CAS disappeared with the torque decreased to slow the aircraft. I elected to descend below glideslope when the runway was in sight and within glide so we could land as close to the fire trucks as possible that were sitting on the closest adjacent taxiway to the runway. We stopped using full reverse and braking. While the PF was removing their mask I communicated with Tower asking if fire command saw any visible fire. I believe they were on ground frequency while we were on Tower so the response was never heard. After a few seconds I ordered we evacuate the aircraft since we didn't know what the actual situation was. As I was exiting the aircraft the PM (PIC) followed the remainder of the checklist to secure the aircraft for a possible fire. the evacuation was without issue and the remainder of the day was cancelled with the aircraft grounded. While we couldn't confirm a fire existed the degradation of equipment in the aircraft caused enough alarm to assume something could have been seriously wrong. We elected to not shut the fuel off and stop engine as it was still producing power and the surrounding area was IMC with low ceilings. We elected [our preferred alternate] as it provided immediate fire assistance because of their 121 service along with it was directly in front of us. Continuing the flight over water or any longer was not an option as the situation warranted quick action. We were enroute when we encountered the Engine Fire event. The Red CAS ENGINE FIRE illuminated and the aural warning said 'FIRE.' We identified the CAS, cleared the message, noted that the Red CAS ENGINE FIRE stayed illuminated and told ATC we needed to divert. The closest field was [a suitable airport], as we turned towards the field ATC asked our intentions and means for diversion, after quick discussion we agreed we needed to [ask for expedited handling] for the matter at hand. The CAS message came to us as we had descended through 8,000 feet to level off at 5,000 feet per ATC instructions. We had continued our descent and turn towards the field as ATC read us the weather and approach being used. Using our CRM I was running the QRH items and [the Captain] was inputting the ILS into the FMS as we were navigating during the descent. While going through the QRH I was able to put my oxygen mask on and when [the Captain] was going to put his on the autopilot failed and we decided to have him handfly the airplane the rest of the way to the ground and continue without his oxygen mask as we were passing through 3,000 feet and beginning to intercept the localizer for the approach. The full QRH was completed for an ENGINE FIRE red CAS and we evaluated the engine instruments the entire time while on our descent into the field as the CAS had remained on the entire time. We were also looking at the engine cowling and we had not seen any fire or smoke, but we were planning to get the airplane on the ground first before doing any further inspection or analysis. While handling this we were in full IMC and didn't break out of the clouds until passing through 700 feet on the ILS. Upon breaking out of the clouds we were short final for the field and saw emergency vehicles were already standing by for us. We landed safely on the runway, signaled to [ground personnel] we were shutting down the engine on the runway, and then proceeded to evacuate the aircraft. From the first indication of the CAS message to shutting the engine down on the runway was approximately 6 minutes. After shutting down and evacuating the aircraft the fire and EMS teams rushed to make sure we were OK before proceeding to inspect the aircraft. Upon inspection and walk around with the fire crew there was no indication to us on the exterior of the aircraft that we had been on fire at any time. After completing our services with local airport authority, we had the aircraft towed back to the FBO and put in the hangar while I proceeded to talk to [Company] to let them know of our [situation] and the next steps we were doing moving forward to handle the situation. Upon reflection, I wouldn't have changed anything we had done. We deviated from items on the QRH in order to enhance our safety. The last QRH item told us to feather the engine however, while we were in IMC, we would rather use a fully operable engine to get us as close to the field as necessary before shutting it down. [The Captain] and myself had excellent CRM and delegated appropriate tasks accordingly to make sure we got the airplane and ourselves on the ground safely.
ASRS:1829603.s: The crew encountered an Engine Fire CAS and autopilot failure during descent in IMC, prompting a diversion to a nearby alternate for expedited handling. They hand-flew an ILS approach, landed safely, and evacuated the aircraft, though post-landing inspection revealed no visible fire or smoke.

ASRS:1829611.n: Had a near miss with a drone while on final into MSP. On the Date about XA30 we were on final to runway 12L at MSP and I noticed something fly past the left side of the aircraft. I did not see it clearing and asked if anyone else on the flight deck saw that. We had a airline pilot in the jump seat and he stated that he saw it and it was definitely a drone. We were on the visual for 12L at MSP at about 2,800 feet just inside WASHY (the final approach fix), just left (north) of the final approach course. The drone was fairly large and yellow. I did not see the exact configuration as it passed by so quickly. The drone went passed us on the left side of the aircraft from nose to tail. I did complete a post flight walk around to verify we did not hit it and found no indication of any kind of impact on the aircraft.Drone operating at altitude and in airspace not authorized.
ASRS:1829611.s: The flight crew observed a large yellow drone pass the left side of the aircraft during the visual approach to runway 12L at MSP at 2,800 feet. The drone was operating in unauthorized airspace, but a post-flight inspection confirmed no impact occurred.

ASRS:1829612.n: We were cleared for the visual approach 33 and the FO (First Officer) was hand flying. Initiated a descent to 2,700 ft. and a base leg turn. We got an obstacle caution aural on the base leg of the visual approach Runway 33 into SYR at 2,700 ft. Upon getting the obstacle alert, ATC told us MSA was 3,700 ft. and I initiated a climbing right turn to gain obstacle clearance, while keeping the obstacle in sight the entire time. I misread the approach plate for the RNAV33 SYR and thought that we were still clear of obstacles at 2,700 ft. coming from the west outside of the FAF. Be more thorough on briefing an approach, even if the conditions are for a visual approach to an airport you have been to before. Landing Runway 33 in Syracuse. FO (First Officer) was hand flying in visual conditions. We got cleared for the visual 33 and started a descent down to 2,700 ft. and turned toward the final approach course. As we made our base turn we received an obstacle GPWS caution. We did a climbing right turn and had the obstacle in sight. Should have stayed at the MSA until closer to the final approach course, also referencing the approach plate better.
ASRS:1829612.s: The Captain and First Officer received an obstacle caution at 2,700 ft during a visual approach to Runway 33 at SYR. The alert occurred because the Captain misread the approach plate, prompting a climbing right turn to regain the 3,700 ft MSA.

ASRS:1829622.n: ATC given heading for vector for weather and entered cloud with severe turbulence with down draft auto pilot disconnected, and power and pitch up with continued down draft about 1,200 ft. altitude lost and severe turbulence until aircraft was out the cloud, report it to ATC.We were vectored by ATC and we did not see the weather on the radar in IMC. We were getting vectored by ATC to go around weather and on the final vector before the occurrence we got vectored into a cloud that began to produce moderate turbulence. We attempted to get deviations but could not reach the Controller. It was then that we experienced what we described as a severe downward wind shear that made us lose control of the aircraft and the aircraft had an immediate 4000+ ft. per minute drop in altitude. Autopilot disengaged and we found ourselves at 1800 ft. MSL and I began to slow to maneuvering speed to regain control of the aircraft. Once I did I immediately began a climb and we finally had the Controller provide deviation instructions and we exited the cloud and the turbulence subsided.We had nothing on radar and thought the Controller was guiding us away from thunderstorms but he was not seeing it as well.
ASRS:1829622.s: Pilots vectored by ATC into unseen weather lost 1,200 feet due to severe downdraft and wind shear, causing autopilot disengagement and a 4,000 fpm descent to 1,800 feet MSL. The crew regained control after slowing to maneuvering speed and receiving deviation instructions once contact was re-established.

ASRS:1829639.n: On descent in vicinity of sweet intersection, ATC notified of aircraft climbing in front of us in opposite direction. Then immediately gave us a left turn to 070 degrees. Then immediately received a TCAS RA. Complied with RA procedures. Aircraft was less than 500 feet from us. Very close. ATC notified us when aircraft was very close. Our turn and RA happened very quickly.
ASRS:1829639.s: During descent near Sweet intersection, ATC notified the crew of an opposing climbing aircraft and issued a left turn to 070 degrees. A TCAS RA followed immediately, requiring compliance as the other aircraft passed within 500 feet.

ASRS:1829688.n: While in cruise flight, approximately 40NM south of ATL, we were given clearance by Atlanta Center to climb from our present assigned altitude, FL370 to FL380. Within a few seconds of initiating a climb, we received a TCAS alert for 'Traffic'. I immediately noticed an aircraft (a large amber TCAS image on the ND (Navigational Display)) at our same altitude '00', opposite direction. I increased the rate of climb by electing CON (Max Continuous Thrust) on the N1 page of the FMC.Literally seconds later, we received an RA to 'CLIMB'. I immediately disconnected the auto-pilot and manually advanced the power to rapidly climb out of the red displayed warning area on my PFD (Primary Flight Display). At approximately FL380, the TCAS system said to 'Level Off'. At this point I was at 38100 ft. Moments later we received the aural 'Clear of conflict'. Still hand flying, I lowered the nose and descended 100 ft. back to our assigned altitude of FL380. We had just come from an area of weather over Florida and more weather was ahead beyond Atlanta.The radar was on, and I was on a 160 NM scale. In a busy area like ATL, I recalled seeing numerous aircraft on TCAS which was normal and gave no reason for concern. After the event, both of us (Us & Company) advised ATC we received an RA. The Company pilot asked ATC 'what happened back there?'. The controller replied in a broken sounding voice something like: 'I climbed them too late…'. Looking forward, I never saw the oncoming aircraft.My FO (First Officer) said the Company jet passed beneath us from the right side at a slight angle. The last TCAS altitude I recall seeing as we passed was '-02'. Perhaps, I expected that ATC would keep us safely separated at cruise altitude. At the end of the day, TCAS prevented a catastrophic event! No suggestion. I would not have responded any differently than I did. We were flying at FL370 talking to ATL Center approximately 40NM south of ATL VOR at the time of the event. ATL center gave us clearance to climb to FL380. As we got the clearance, we got a TCAS Traffic Advisory. I reached up to zoom in my ND (Navigational Display). I saw the Yellow Square and 00" next to it. During this time, the Captain had set the new altitude, and pushed the ALT intervene button. I said to the captain, 'We are going to get an RA, get ready'. As soon as I said that, we got the RA and instructions to climb. The Captain promptly disconnected the Auto Pilot and pushed the throttles up to comply with the TCAS Climb command. I saw traffic under us under the left wing. AT FL381 we got the TCAS level off command, then a few seconds later Clear of Conflict. We returned to our assigned altitude of FL380. Company later asked ATC what the reason was for getting that TCAS. The ATL controller admitted fault and said they climbed us late. The causal factor was lapse of attention regarding two aircraft nose to nose at same altitude. ATC issued a turn to avoid traffic rather than slow to happen climb instructions. ATC having more awareness in regards to aircraft in their sector that are at the same altitude."
ASRS:1829688.s: Pilots flying a jet at FL370 near Atlanta received a TCAS Resolution Advisory to climb after ATC cleared them to FL380 too late, causing a near-miss with an opposing aircraft. The controller admitted a lapse of attention regarding two nose-to-nose aircraft at the same altitude, but TCAS prevented a collision.

ASRS:1829695.n: This event was in my opinion a near miss. We were at 3,000 feet on a visual approach to runway XXR. Saw on TCAS a target 100 feet below us off left side of Aircraft. ATC said traffic alert turn right 150. Just then we got TCAS RA alert descend, descend now immediately followed by climb climb now. Followed SOP and complied with alert we never visually acquired traffic. After talking with ATC supervisor, he informed me it was Aircraft Y transitioning Class B to ZZZ2. He was at 2,500 feet initially, then for some reason as he approached us he pulled up to 2,800 feet (our TCAS showed him at 2,900 feet, 100 feet below us) once he saw us he descended back down to 2,200 feet and turned west. I do not know if this classifies as a near miss, but it was way too close for my comfort. Aircraft Y never entered Class B, so now [no] rules were broken, but I think the other pilot used questionable judgement being so close to arriving ZZZ traffic and climbing to within 100 to 200 feet of Class B airspace.There must be another area to transition to ZZZ1 from the west that doesn't involve flying so close to ZZZ arriving aircraft. Maybe a 2,000 feet ceiling under the approach corridor for ZZZ?
ASRS:1829695.s: The pilot reported a near miss during a visual approach at 3,000 feet when Aircraft Y climbed to within 100 feet vertically, triggering conflicting TCAS RAs. The reporter attributed the event to Aircraft Y's questionable judgment while transitioning near Class B airspace, noting no rules were technically broken.

ASRS:1829789.n: Smokey day, still decent horizontal visibility but milky white sky. We were on flight following flying east and saw another traffic (not with flight following) on traffic system flying parallel to us on our left, also eastbound. We wanted to turn north, so we decided to make a right 270 degrees to the north in order to pass well behind that traffic. But just as we finished the turn, we realized traffic had turned right and was coming towards us. Out of the haze there appeared to be a Mooney like aircraft. It's bank, color, and convergence angle blended perfectly with the white haze. Even though traffic system said they were 500 feet above, it looked closer than that so I began a rapid descent and was soon clear of conflict. ZZZ was busy and didn't give the traffic alert until just before I saw them out of the haze. Conclusion: Be very careful of traffic during wildfire smoke, especially white aircraft on converging course, expect the unexpected when it comes to movement of other traffic, don't rely on ATC advisories.
ASRS:1829789.s: A pilot flying east in wildfire smoke executed a right turn to avoid parallel traffic but encountered a converging white Mooney obscured by haze. Despite ATC reporting the traffic 500 feet above, the pilot performed a rapid descent to avoid conflict after delayed advisories from a busy controller.

ASRS:1829809.n: I was operating a flight from PHX. I was issued a taxi clearance to Runway 25L. I started the taxi to the runway and advised Ground Control that I would need a few minutes at the end of a run-up, the controller said no problem and advised the tower when you're ready.Tower issued me a takeoff clearance, runway heading. [An A320 NEO] had started the takeoff roll but stayed on the [runway] for about 10 seconds after I started my takeoff roll, and I was about 1000 feet down the runway before [he] took off. After we rotated I was aware of the wake turbulence but was not expecting the Controller to turn me left into his wake turbulence. I was given a left turn into the wake turbulence. It was more than I expected and the passengers were thrown around in the back and both complained about their necks being sore and they seemed to be upset. The Controller gave me a hand off to Departure and I advised him that I hit the wake turbulence. The flight continued as normal and once we landed I was advised that the back of the aircraft took a hard hit and threw open a set of cabin doors and tossed all the secured baggage around. I spoke with the passengers the next morning and they complained of some soreness and mostly shook up from the experience. After a lot of thought, as the PIC, I should have declined the take off clearance and waited a few more minutes. I believe that more separation should be given to the Airbus NEO aircraft.
ASRS:1829809.s: The pilot of a departing aircraft took off behind an Airbus A320 NEO and was vectored left into its wake turbulence by the controller. This caused passenger injuries, cabin door damage, and baggage displacement, leading the pilot to conclude that more separation was needed.

ASRS:1829810.n: Midway through the flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we received 'HYDR #1 PUMP 3' CAS (Crew Alert System) message. The QRH states that system operating times will take longer than expected and that no other action was required. We continued the flight after notifying home base of the situation. Quantity showed 100% on the synoptic page with a pressure stabilized at 3,000 psi.On the arrival to ZZZ1 we were given a level off altitude and 'HYDR #1 PUMP 1' CAS message appeared. Soon after pressure fluctuated between 0 and 3,000 psi. causing CAS messages to appear then extinguish when pressure was high. Due to sequencing into ZZZ1 we had extended vectors for the ILS XX circle to land runway YY. During this time The PIC and I decided we would configure early so I could get a feel of the aircraft and allow extra time for gear extension, flap extension, ect. After being established on a long final for runway XX circle YY, I asked for gear down. We received 3 red down arrows but heard what I would consider normal gear down. We then overflew the airfield so tower could view if the gear was down then executed the missed approach for the ILS XX.The tower reported the gear was down but our indication was three red arrows. After being handed off to ZZZ2 we received delay vectors to trouble shoot the gear issue. At this time hydraulic quantity on system 1 was zero. Because we had a red gear indication, PNF followed the checklist that included pulling the gear T-handle. We still had three red gear indications so we followed the checklist for the gravity free fall. Because the checklist required 190 knots for gravity gear drop I commanded the aircraft to clean wing. This set off additional 'inboard slat fail' CAS message and we added the landing distance penalty required by the checklist.The PNF then followed the checklist for the gravity gear deploy checklist. He pulled the left main gear pull-handle and I applied full left rudder per the checklist, resulting with a left main gear down green indication. As I returned the aircraft to rudder neutral the nose gear indicated down and locked. The PNF then pulled the right main gear pull handle and after applying a slight right rudder the right main gear appeared down and locked. The PNF finished the checklist and we had a three green gear indication.We determined because of the hydraulic/gear issues it was in our best interest to declare an emergency and return to ZZZ and have crews standing by in the event the gear would collapse. Airport conditions were VFR and favored runway XX. We landed the airplane as a non-event and were towed to the FBO due to the loss of nose wheel steering.
ASRS:1829810.s: The crew experienced hydraulic system 1 failures and unreliable landing gear indications during approach to ZZZ1, requiring a missed approach and gravity gear deployment. They declared an emergency, returned to ZZZ, and landed safely with loss of nose wheel steering.

ASRS:1829826.n: On date around XA:25 local time I was entering the traffic pattern at ZZZ airport. I had been making radio calls announcing my intentions to over fly the airport at 6,500 feet and enter left traffic for runway XX. After crossing the airport midfield I announced entering a left downwind pattern for runway XX descending to 6,000 feet while looking for traffic in the area. After passing the numbers I started my approach into ZZZ and about 1.25 away I announced turning left base runway XX while scanning for traffic. Then turning base, I looked for traffic and announced that I was on a 1 mile final for runway XX. About 20 seconds after landing on runway XX I saw Aircraft Y over fly the runway that I just landed on. I cleared the runway and taxied to the ramp area to investigate what happened. During this whole time I didn't hear any announcements from any other traffic in the area. After getting to the ramp I went back through everything to investigate what happened. During which time I noticed that the aircraft wasn't showing up on my ADS-B (Foreflight) until it turned downwind after going around. During the whole time in the pattern I never saw them show up on foreflight. Then I noticed that I was transmitting on 123.7 and not the CTAF frequency 123.0.
ASRS:1829826.s: A pilot entering the traffic pattern at ZZZ airport landed on runway XX without hearing other traffic because they were transmitting on 123.7 MHz instead of the correct CTAF frequency 123.0 MHz. Consequently, the pilot failed to detect Aircraft Y, which overflew the runway shortly after the landing.

ASRS:1829849.n: I was doing take offs and landings at ZZZ using runway XX. I announced departing runway XX and remaining in the pattern. As I was turning downwind a Cessna 182, Aircraft Y announced he was taking off on runway YY. I looked at the runway and he was really departing on runway XX, not YY. I didn't correct him because I was the only one in the pattern and I thought he just miss-spoke. I had him in sight the whole time. After I did several landings I heard Aircraft Y report 9 miles southwest of the airport and he said he was going to land on runway YY. I told him that XX was the runway being used, and he replied that he would enter a downwind for XX.I did another landing and as I reported turning downwind Aircraft Y reported that he would enter the downwind for XX on the 45. I was wondering how he was going to do that if he was southwest of the airport. As I was on the downwind approaching abeam the numbers of XX, I saw Aircraft Y pass in front of me about 100 feet above and 200 feet horizontally. I watched him pass in front of me and then he reported turning downwind for runway XX. I told him he just flew a crosswind for Runway YY and cut across the downwind for XX. I turned base and final for XX and asked Aircraft Y for his location. He reported crosswind for XX, which I was able to confirm. He was no factor for my landing at that point.The guy in Aircraft Y, obviously doesn't know what runway he is using and needs additional training. How does a 182 driver not know which end of the runway is in use? Guys like that are dangerous.
ASRS:1829849.s: A pilot conducting touch-and-goes on Runway XX observed a Cessna 182 depart the active runway while announcing Runway YY. The Cessna subsequently crossed the pilot's downwind leg at 100 feet above and 200 feet horizontally due to the other pilot's confusion regarding the active runway.

ASRS:1829854.n: On the initial climb out of ZZZZ to ZZZ1 we received a DOORS UNLOCKED annunciation light. We were at 700 feet AGL over the bridge. Looked through the cabin to see that the cargo door had opened. At that time the co-pilot went to the cargo hold to secure the door. He was unsuccessful due to no interior handle on the door. After passing the bridge the co-pilot returned to the flight deck and reported that the door had detached and fell into the ocean. There were no adverse effects to the flight characteristics of the aircraft. We continued the visual approach to ZZZZ1. I did not ask for priority handling and landed without further issues.
ASRS:1829854.s: During initial climb from ZZZZ to ZZZ1 at 700 feet AGL, a cargo door opened and detached after the co-pilot failed to secure it due to a missing interior handle. The door fell into the ocean, but the aircraft maintained normal flight characteristics and completed a visual approach to ZZZZ1 without further issues.

ASRS:1829863.n: During preflight fuel was indicated as follows in the 4 tank system in the PA32. L Tip 15 gal, L Main 4 gal, R Main 11 gal, R Tip 17 gal. Through past experience in this aircraft, the gauges had an accuracy of +/- 1 gallon and were considered to be accurate. Fuel was visible in all tanks. I started and taxied on R main tank with the intention of burning fuel from the R main tank to match the L main level. The handbook recommends exhaustion of the main tanks before using the tip tanks. The flight that was going to be conducted was expected to be less than 45 minutes with an expected burn of 12 gallons. Indicated fuel onboard was 47 gallons. Takeoff was accomplished with the fuel selected on R Main tank. At 500 feet as I just started my climbing left-hand turn engine power was suddenly lost. I immediately [advised the tower] and requested Runway XX for an landing. Because I was at such a low altitude I was only focused on airspeed and the best place to land, not restarting the engine. Luckily I had a local flight instructor on board who troubleshot while I flew the airplane. After switching to a tank with fuel (R tip) power was restored almost immediately. I was a bit high and fast for a Runway XX landing and had I continued for runway XX I would have had a significant tailwind. With power restored I elected to land into the wind on Runway XYR because I deemed I was within glide even if power was lost again. I landed on Runway XYR uneventfully. After shutting down it was discovered that R Main tank was completely empty however the gauge was still indicating approximately 11 gallons. Many lessons were learned and I am going to employ the following actions to prevent a reoccurrence. Have fuel gauge for R main inspected and repaired. Heavily scrutinize the level of fuel observed vs the level of fuel indicated on the preflight.
ASRS:1829863.s: A pilot flying a PA32 experienced sudden engine power loss at 500 feet due to an empty right main tank despite the gauge indicating 11 gallons. Power was restored after switching to the right tip tank, allowing a safe landing on Runway XYR.

ASRS:1829864.n: We were taking off from ZZZ and on initial climb out from Runway XX. There had been several prior departures before us that had used the same runway. Approximately 2 miles from the runway we got a traffic alert on our iPads and it was descending into us. The aircraft appeared to be heading into Runway XY and was no making any radio calls. Our eyes immediately went outside the aircraft trying to make contact with the aircraft. We continued to climb as he was descending into us and we made a right turn to avoid head on traffic. Eventually we were able to make visual contact with the airplane and he was approximately 200 feet above us. After we were clear of the aircraft my scan came back inside and I noticed that we were about 100 feet into the ZZZ1 Class Bravo airspace. Immediately a descent was made out of the airspace and the flight continued. We did not hear the other aircraft make any calls on the CTAF throughout their flight/approach.Looking back this all happened very fast, and I would have done a couple things differently. We should have leveled off immediately and made a right hand turn. However, in the moment we were not sure exactly the location of the aircraft. Had we done that we would have remained clear of the other aircraft and remained clear of the Bravo airspace.
ASRS:1829864.s: Pilots departing Runway XX at ZZZ encountered a descending aircraft on an iPad alert and executed a right turn to avoid a head-on collision. The maneuver inadvertently took them 100 feet into Class Bravo airspace, requiring an immediate descent to exit, while the other aircraft made no radio calls.

ASRS:1829903.n: Given RNAV XX approach. Changed to visual approach when near final approach fix. Changed to advisory frequency and called entering downwind leg for Runway XY as wind was now favoring XY. Glider called entering downwind for Runway XX. After doing so, he passed opposite direction to me at same altitude about 100 feet laterally. He then proceeded to land on XX. I continued downwind, base and final for XY and landed while watching for the glider landing on the intersecting runway. I passed the intersection of XY and XX just as he touched down on XX. Due to the stress of the near midair, I did not close my IFR flight plan until after I had parked the aircraft. This delayed a departing business jet on an IFR flight plan. Having fixed wing and gliders using intersecting runways seems dangerous with the amount of jet traffic into ZZZ. I should have closed my IFR flight plan immediately after landing. I do not usually close my IFR flight plan in the air as problems can arise (like a midair!) in the traffic pattern. The glider did not show up on my ADS-B traffic alert nor was it mentioned by ATC. I suspect it had no transponder so it would not show up on TCAS either.
ASRS:1829903.s: A pilot on a visual approach for Runway XY encountered a glider on an intersecting Runway XX at the same altitude, passing 100 feet laterally. The near midair occurred because the glider lacked a transponder and was not seen on ADS-B or TCAS, while the pilot's delayed IFR closure caused a departure delay.

ASRS:1829926.n: While on a descent into ZZZ1 field I inadvertently dipped into ZZZ Class D airspace. Although I am acutely aware of the area airspace and very familiar with ZZZ, a moment of distraction due to very smokey/hazy conditions continued my descent into ZZZ Class D airspace. Upon realizing my mistake I immediately climbed up and clear of their D airspace. My best estimate is 30 seconds inside their airspace.The flight involved 2 passengers whom I invited for a flight and lunch at ZZZ2. It is clear to me that the hazy and smokey conditions contributed to my inattention. However, a much more egregious event occurred upon landing in ZZZ2 and more than anything preoccupied my thoughts. Upon arriving in the pattern at ZZZ2, there were 4 aircraft operating in a left hand pattern using Runway XX. I landed following an aircraft doing touch and goes and pulled off at the intersecting runway. I came face to face with a landing C180 who decided to use the cross runway and very narrowly avoided a collision. In the process of avoiding the landing aircraft I scraped my wingtip on a runway light. In 40 years of flying I have never dented or put a scratch in any airplane and although the damage to my wingtip is minor the event clearly preoccupied my thoughts on the way home and most likely contributed to my inattention to ZZZ's Class D airspace. In most cases when I operate around or especially under the veil our Class B airspace I set my altitude hold thus allowing me to pay more attention to traffic and other tasks. The smokey/hazy condition required hand flying to avoid pockets and areas of lesser visibility. Waiting for a better day would have been a better option.
ASRS:1829926.s: The pilot inadvertently entered ZZZ Class D airspace during descent due to distraction from smokey conditions and a prior near-collision at ZZZ2. While avoiding a landing C180 on a cross runway, the pilot scraped a wingtip on a runway light, which contributed to the subsequent airspace incursion.

ASRS:1829933.n: I was doing drone test flights over water at Soddy Daisy Park in Soddy, TN which is along Lake Chickamauga. Filed a flight plan with Airmap which saw no potential violations of airspace and environment. Flew for approximately .4 hours. While on sight, I checked Google map again and it had the area titled as a bird sanctuary. I shut down the drone and switched to handheld recording.
ASRS:1829933.s: A drone operator conducting test flights over Lake Chickamauga in Soddy, TN, discovered the area was a bird sanctuary via Google Maps. The operator immediately shut down the drone and switched to handheld recording to avoid potential airspace violations.

ASRS:1829935.n: I was on an IFR flight plan from ZZZ to ZZZ1. I began to experience engine surging. I attempted to troubleshoot, but it continued to worsen. I informed Approach that I needed to divert to ZZZ2. That controller asked if I was declaring an emergency, and I said no, but he took my souls on board and fuel remaining. Shortly thereafter he switched me to another frequency. I checked in with that controller and continued to ZZZ2. The condition continued to worsen, so I attempted to contact Approach to let them know I was in an emergency and needed priority into ZZZ2. I attempted to contact Approach multiple times with no response. It sounded as though he was busy on other frequencies. In hindsight I should've squawked 7700, but didn't think of it at the time. I was primarily concentrating on flying the airplane and managing the engine.At this point I was inside ZZZ2's surface area and had reached the last altitude I had been cleared to. I needed to continue my descent to land, so after another failed attempt to contact Approach, I proceeded with my descent and switched to ZZZ2 tower. They were expecting me, and they contacted Approach and informed me I was cleared for the Visual Approach. I landed uneventfully otherwise. Police and fire were waiting for me.I was uncomfortable continuing the descent without being cleared and switching frequencies without being told, but felt both actions were necessary for the safe outcome of my flight. I should have officially declared my emergency when the first controller asked, and squawked 7700. It seems to me the second approach controller forgot about me, or perhaps he was busy making space for me, but either way the lack of communication did add a bit of stress to the situation.
ASRS:1829935.s: A pilot flying an IFR flight experienced worsening engine surging and diverted to ZZZ2 but failed to declare an emergency or squawk 7700 initially. After losing contact with Approach, the pilot descended without clearance and switched to Tower, landing safely with emergency services present.

ASRS:1829943.n: After normal pre-flight, start, taxi, and run up, I pulled up to the hold short line for runway XX at ZZZ. At the time, the frequency had static and it was difficult to hear other aircraft. My radios worked fine on all other frequencies. After following standard procedures and visually clearing for traffic, I announced intentions on the ZZZ CTAF to takeoff from runway XX. I began the takeoff roll with no abnormalities and heard no other aircraft make any radio calls on frequency. I noticed some heat haze/mirage looking down the runway. Around 80 knots, 12 knots below rotation speed, I noticed a single-engine airplane taxiing across runway XX at approximately 4,000 in front of my present position. Based off of computed takeoff, accelerate-stop, and climb performance data, I decided to continue takeoff. I knew that continuing would result in the least amount of runway used and would offer the best deconfliction outcome. I lifted off at 92 knots approximately 3,000 feet away from the traffic crossing the runway. The other aircraft cleared the runway as I was climbing through 200 feet AGL. All subsequent phases of flight were normal. I believe that this event was caused by environmental conditions such as the aforementioned radio static and mirage which prevented the other aircraft from knowing my position/intentions.
ASRS:1829943.s: The pilot of a single-engine aircraft experienced radio static and heat haze while taking off from runway XX at ZZZ, obscuring a crossing aircraft. The pilot continued the takeoff to minimize runway usage, lifting off 3,000 feet from the traffic, attributing the near miss to environmental conditions preventing communication.

ASRS:1829950.n: The spar bumper, in the main wheel well, on the left side of Aircraft X fell off while the aircraft was in the hangar. The aircraft was delivered from the factory 2 years ago and this part was installed incorrectly. Textron considers this a grounding discrepancy because of the chance that the landing gear could hit the main spar in the event of a gear up landing. Other aircraft need to be looked at for proper factory installation.
ASRS:1829950.s: A spar bumper in the left main wheel well of Aircraft X fell off while in the hangar due to incorrect factory installation. Textron classified this as a grounding discrepancy because the landing gear could strike the main spar during a gear-up landing.

ASRS:1829953.n: I was the R-side at Sector 38 during this event. Weather had been impacting Area 6 for the majority of the night, with a solid line from the LNK area up to the FOD area in Area 5. There was a hole that aircraft routed over OVR and LNK points west that aircraft had been deviating through, with some deviating all the way north into Area 5's airspace and then points west. The weather closed in and caused all west bound aircraft to deviate north of Area 6 into Area 5.Shortly after a few of my aircraft entered Sector 30, I was told by the Area 5 supervisor at the time that Sector 30 was overloaded and to try and keep aircraft in my area as long as possible. I had to delay giving aircraft deviations in order to keep them out of 30 as long as I could, and even had to hold 2 aircraft at their present position. Multiple other aircraft were given vectors or were descending several thousand feet to avoid conflicts with other aircraft. Then Area 5 came up with a plan to route all aircraft coming from sector 38 and 43 up over MCW direct FSD and points west. For many aircraft MCW was backtracking and turning them wrong for direction. This was happening near the boundary with 38/30 because information was not passed as to what they wanted from us fast enough. I called for a D-side early on in the stint and it was 100% necessary. Not only was the whole situation very unsafe, it was un-efficient as well. It seemed like TMU wasn't giving us any help with sending re routes out to Chicago and Kansas, so sector 38 and 43 had to re route every single aircraft we talked to during that 1-2 hour period. A plan should have been developed for the weather in case it did close in, which ended up happening, to route all OVR and LNK west bound traffic to the north around the weather. This would have at least pinned them all down to a route instead of having every aircraft asking for deviations at the last minute. Also, I felt unsafe working this stint not only because of deviations, but because we haven't been allowed to work an even remotely busy sector for the last year plus during normal operations. But when events like this happen there is no choice but to work it, so we should be able to work busier stints on a daily basis to prepare for the worst case scenarios as described above.
ASRS:1829953.s: An Air Traffic Controller in Sector 38 managed westbound traffic deviating north into Area 5 due to weather, causing Sector 30 overload and requiring holds and descents. The controller attributed the unsafe and inefficient situation to delayed routing plans, lack of TMU support, and insufficient daily training for high-traffic scenarios.

ASRS:1829963.n: The fire alarm continues to be an issue. The fire alarm started going off, which it has gone off for years now. As I've stated before, it is a huge distraction, the fire alarm is with 10 feet of the radar scopes. I called the airport authority to tell them it was going off, there response was 'Well it's not going off down here.' So me not knowing if it's a real alarm or not, I executed a contingency plan after contacting my manager. This isn't a management issue either, management is doing everything they can to fix this as well. We were somewhat busy with several airplanes inbound and outbound. I don't feel comfortable being watching someone work 10 airplanes while the fire alarm is going off. This needs to be fixed. Fix the fire alarm.
ASRS:1829963.s: An air traffic controller reported a recurring false fire alarm near radar scopes during a busy period with multiple inbound and outbound aircraft. The controller executed a contingency plan after contacting management, citing the alarm as a dangerous distraction that prevents safe monitoring of ten airplanes.

ASRS:1829988.n: Halfway through our flight, our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us. When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley. And, our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell. Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything. No passengers were indicating concern and, we didn't smell anything. I informed the Flight Attendant (FA) if she was medically concerned we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern. All the FAs indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic. They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ2. At that point I told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor. We contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before. Also, to inform Dispatch that they were not comfortable taking the aircraft on our next leg. Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC. We agreed on a patch to medic. During their discussion, Dispatch sent us an ACARS to divert to ZZZ1. The First Officer (FO) notified ATC of our intention to divert. I notified the FAs and passengers of our intent, as well. As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke, Fire, or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke, Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated. Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing, taxi, and at the gate.We kept in constant communication with the A-FA to constantly reassess our situation. On our descent into ZZZ1, medic recommended the two Flight Attendants in question use the portable oxygen. With that information I notified ATC. We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.
ASRS:1829988.s: The flight crew and cabin crew diverted to ZZZ1 after two flight attendants reported a strong cleaning spray odor and respiratory symptoms in the aft galley. Dispatch confirmed the aircraft had been sprayed the previous night, prompting the crew to execute fume checklists and land uneventfully with the affected crew using portable oxygen.

ASRS:1829993.n: We had spoken with Dispatch two hours before the flight about the days weather. We agreed on a new route that would work for all parties and operation needs. The route was filed and clearance gave the route to us. In the departure climbout we got a reroute back into the weather, we looked at it and told them unable. ATC said the almighty TMU needed it. We cited our safety concern and they give us a route that was on the border line of legal, we then had no more options with the weather at hand. TMU had plenty of time to be aware of the route, and gave us the clearance. Why should we even flight plan if we are going to get thrown all these curve balls with no recourse in the air. This is a definite safety concern. TMU is too far overreaching.
ASRS:1829993.s: The flight crew filed a weather-avoidance route approved by Dispatch, but ATC issued a reroute into weather during climbout citing TMU requirements. Despite the crew's safety refusal, ATC provided a borderline legal clearance, which the pilot reported as a safety concern caused by TMU overreach.

ASRS:1830046.n: ILS XXR with circling to Runway XY with tailwind of 10 knots. Briefed the approach for the ILS with the special ops note for the circling approach to Runway XY. Fly the ILS and turn left at 2 miles from Runway XXR threshold to parallel Rwy XY with flap 3 and initially 160 knots till we have the threshold XY at about 45 degrees of shoulder before turning in and going flaps full when somewhat aligned with the landing Runway. We discussed the wind issue. It didn't work out as planned. ATC late speed reduction and clearance, Captain's confusion of 'cleared for the approach' with the 2,500 foot altitude constraints and the resulting delay in descending and speed reduction despite gear down before the FAF kept us higher and faster then ideal. Autopilot was deselected once below the cloud layer while descending to 1,000 feet MSL. I did hand fly the turn to 110 degree before reversing to align myself with the landing Runway. Just before turning in we got the altitude alert. Crew communications could have been better while the Captain wanted full flaps before the turn to align myself with Runway XY. This could have been avoided by a more thorough briefing to the to refresh the procedure. Final Approach to XY was continued safely to an uneventful landing.ATC Issued Low Altitude Warning
ASRS:1830046.s: The crew executed an ILS approach with a circling maneuver to Runway XY in a 10-knot tailwind. ATC issued a low altitude warning due to delayed speed reduction and descent caused by clearance confusion and briefing gaps, though the aircraft landed safely.

ASRS:1830049.n: Upset/wake turbulence event. Approximately five minutes prior to this event First Officer and I had completed our arrival brief and I had given a PA to the passengers that the seat belt sign would be coming on in the next 10 minutes. Ahead of us was a B787 at [our altitude], FL360. [The B787] was directed by ATC to descend and maintain FL340. Within a few minutes we were assigned the same clearance. Shortly after leveling at FL340, our aircraft entered a rapid, shuddering turbulence, followed by a rapid roll to the right. We both immediately put our hands on the controls and recited the upset recovery call outs. We disconnected the autopilot, though the autopilot may have disconnected by itself, and autothrottle. We both fly with our FPV (Flight Path Vector) up so we could see immediately, intuitively that we weren't stalled, but our push was slight, not even half a G, which added to our effective counter roll rate. Prior to our response to the upset, the autopilot had already put in aileron control forces counter to the roll, but the aircraft was still rolling to the right. As we took control, the aircraft reached approximately 40 degrees before the aircraft responded to our control inputs, then rolled left to approximately 20 degrees. Based on the fact we were at FL340 we left the thrust where it was positioned, possibly a slight reduction, as the energy state was good and a large thrust change was not necessary. Our altitude loss was minimal and the descent was very shallow. The recovery point at which we managed our flight path divergence started at approximately FL337, only a 300 FT loss. Rudder may have been used - Indicated by both an overshoot, subsequent bank to the left and a report from the flight attendants that we not only rolled, but yawed. We advised ATC that we had encountered wake turbulence which had caused our descent. They offered us direct HLYWD moving us from the wake of the preceding aircraft. We then checked on the Flight Attendants and passengers to ensure there were no injuries. The seat belt sign had been off and there was a passenger in the lav, but no injuries were reported. The First Officer and I debriefed the event but, because ATC started our descent onto the Arrival, I failed to make a PA to the passengers. After landing, I waited at the flight deck door to thank the passengers. I saw that the event was more impactful than I had realized and a PA would have gone a long way to reassure the passengers and Flight Attendants.
ASRS:1830049.s: The flight crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding B787 while descending to FL340, causing a rapid roll to 40 degrees right. They manually recovered with minimal altitude loss, and no injuries were reported among passengers or crew.

ASRS:1830087.n: I am concerned about the way multiple battery powered devices are being packaged for shipping. It has been observed that Customer Service Representatives who are involved in shipping personal electronic devices with lithium batteries are not following the new procedures regarding packing such items. I am referring to the computer lesson X. Was that effective immediately? It seems that folks did that lesson but then either forgot about it and/or were waiting for an official corporate and/or local management issued directive or bulletin advising Baggage Service agents to do it this way. There are no Hazardous Material Battery labels ordered or specific instructions when packing Personal Electronic Devices (PEDs). I brought it up to my co-workers but it went nowhere.
ASRS:1830087.s: A baggage service agent reported that Customer Service Representatives are failing to follow new packing procedures for lithium battery devices due to a lack of official directives and missing Hazardous Material labels. The reporter noted that despite completing training, staff ignored the requirements, and raising the issue with co-workers yielded no results.

ASRS:1830155.n: Another Airline's Pick up truck on ground vehicle roadway behind parked aircraft, operating at a fast velocity westbound, did not slow down or stop while I was taxing in to gate X. After I stopped the aircraft while in a 90 degree right turn, the driver of the pick up finally looked up and saw us. He then stopped the pick up but too far in to our wing's path for me to continue. Eventually he finally backed up his truck, after other people on the ground had to tell him we couldn't move until he backed up. Had I not stopped, there is a 95%+ probability he would have impacted the aircraft.Most vehicle operators at ZZZ do not comply with the basic rule that aircraft have the right away, PERIOD! This was yet another scenario of many where drivers on the ramp have cut me off and/or almost have impacted our aircraft. At ZZZ, unlike all the other airports I have operated out of over the last 30 years, it is the norm to be cut off and/or almost impacted by every type of ground vehicle, except for the fire and rescue vehicles. Quite frankly, the leaders of airport safety at ZZZ seem to find the blatant disregard for ground vehicle adherence to safety procedures as acceptable. No apologies, after the hundreds of operations I've performed parking at ZZZ gates, it is apparent that there is a serious lack of safety concern on the ramp.Better initial and continuing education and testing for all ramp personnel and ground vehicle operators. Daily observation and audits of random gate parking operations by teams of knowledgeable personnel with the authority to correct the problems. Positive incentives to follow strict safety procedures as well as writing citations to drivers for gross violations. Integrated in to this enforcement it is highly recommended to also audit and enforce strict ramp preparation after aircraft depart and before aircraft arrive to park so that the safe zone is clear of all objects AND personnel. There is no reason cones, air hoses, tow bars, etc should be within the red lines. In addition, all ground personnel should be aware of how Docking Guidance System (DGS) works and know when to pick up the wands and guide us in until the aircraft is parked. Too often, the guideman spend 50% of the time looking at the DGS so when he thinks its ok, to hand us off to the DGS with less than 75 feet to go. We don't know if the DGS is lined up properly or calibrated correctly by this time. Ive had a DGS try to get me to turn off the line in to the jet bridge because it wasn't calibrated properly from the beginning. After 10 years on this aircraft as a captain calling in these problems and writing a few reports and not seeing improvement, I am hoping these last 2 incidents and filing reports will hopefully jumpstart a plan to get ZZZ in compliance. If all the other airports we operate in and out of can comply, I believe ZZZ can do it.
ASRS:1830155.s: A pilot taxiing to gate X stopped to avoid a fast-moving pickup truck that failed to yield on the ramp at ZZZ airport. The driver eventually backed up after ground personnel intervened, preventing a probable wing impact, though the pilot cited a systemic lack of vehicle compliance and safety enforcement at the airport.

ASRS:1830217.n: During push back, the tug driver informed me that the tow bar shear pin had broken. This had occurred in a benign and gentle manner, without any perceivable noise or vibration on the flight deck, or abnormal movement of the aircraft. I set the parking brake and called ZZZ line maintenance. I explained the situation, and asked if this required an inspection or logbook entry (we were on a MAX) and was told 'no' on both counts. My first officer looked up 'tow bar breakage' in the FOM, and read to me the section that states 'an info only write up shall be made and the flight may continue as long as no aircraft damage is suspected'. Unfortunately, that paragraph applies to the 737-NG, but not the MAX. The aircraft should have been inspected, a discrepancy written up in the logbook, and subsequently signed off.Maybe a reminder in the form of a bulletin, for both pilots and mechanics, or a brief mention in the next quarterly CBT (Computer Based Training) to emphasize the difference in policy for the MAX.
ASRS:1830217.s: During pushback of a Boeing 737 MAX, the tug driver reported a broken tow bar shear pin. Line maintenance incorrectly advised no inspection or logbook entry was needed, though the FOM requires these actions for the MAX, unlike the 737-NG.

ASRS:1830234.n: We departed LGB today on a Part 121 passenger flight. Our aircraft was facing north. Our taxi clearance for departure was to taxi to runway 30 via E2 and E taxiway and hold short of J. Our Jeppesen taxiway diagram which is dated 25 June did not have E2 nor E on it. It showed a taxiway closed with X X X on it. We did see the yellow and black taxiway signs of E2 and E. I knew my Jeppesen charts in my iPad were current and up to date with the most recent update. Several hours later and done with my flying, I found the current and up to date taxiway diagram on the FAA NOS website. I downloaded the taxi chart and reviewed it. The NOS FAA chart just like the Jeppesen chart did not show an E2 nor E taxiway. I am confused why a taxiway was commissioned before it was released in charting. I did ask the Tower Controller, who was also controlling Ground, how long the E2 and E taxiway has been commissioned. And if I recall correctly, He said for 2 weeks. I would assume this is adequate time to get updated info to pilots who operate on the field. I also referenced LGB NOTAMS and there was nothing about E2 nor E. Make sure charts are available to pilots that are up to date. When a new taxiway is commissioned it should be charted or NOTAMed.
ASRS:1830234.s: A Part 121 pilot departing LGB found active taxiways E2 and E missing from current Jeppesen and FAA charts despite visible signage. The pilot reported that the new taxiways, commissioned two weeks prior, were not reflected in charts or NOTAMs, creating a discrepancy between ground reality and available documentation.

ASRS:1830355.n: A training flight was conducted to ZZZ. We entered on a 45 to left downwind for runway XX at ZZZ. Heard a call that there was an aircraft 6 mile final just before we entered the downwind. We kept it in mind, but in the process of trying to configure to land, we forgot to look out for him. Upon turning base, we saw him on final directly 12 o clock ahead of us about 150ft above us and about 200ft lateral. We immediately turned right and exited the pattern to come back in for a 45 to a left downwind again. We heard a call that the aircraft on final is going around and offset to the right to rejoin the downwind again. We called and said we were rejoining the pattern again. We ended up rejoining and following traffic on base and came in for a full stop.We did not have traffic alert or traffic displayed because we only had ADS-B out. There was definitely lack of awareness and some complacency on our part. We will be extra vigilant from now on to look out for traffic and keep separation in the pattern.
ASRS:1830355.s: During a training flight at ZZZ, the crew lost situational awareness while configuring for landing and nearly collided with an aircraft on final approach. The pilot attributed the incident to complacency and the lack of ADS-B In traffic display, prompting an immediate pattern exit and re-entry to maintain separation.

ASRS:1830371.n: I was training a primary student. We received clearance from the ground controller to taxi to the runway and contact tower. As we taxied onto the taxiway, Aircraft Y with an elderly gentleman operating single-pilot at the controls was parked facing the taxiway at a perpendicular angle in the run-up area.As we neared this airplane while taxiing down the taxiway toward [Runway] XXR abeam intersection 1, he started moving forward while looking to the left. We got within 20-feet of each other and he never noticed because he failed to clear to his right prior to taxiing onto the taxiway. This other pilot failed to request a taxi on ground from the run-up area as is our local procedure.We slammed on our brakes, coming to an abrupt stop and avoided the collision.
ASRS:1830371.s: A training flight taxiing toward Runway XXR nearly collided with Aircraft Y, operated by a single-pilot student, which entered the taxiway from a run-up area without ground clearance or a right-side check. The training crew avoided impact by braking abruptly after the other pilot failed to follow local taxi procedures.

ASRS:1830394.n: While loading my plane at ZZZ I noticed the wind was favoring runway XX. My daughter noted that the wind sock was also favoring runway XX. As I announced my departure from runway XX I heard a faint XY" on [frequency] XXX.YY. I stopped and asked if anyone was taking off on XY. Then I saw a high wing plane taking off on XY. Then again announced my departure on XY. Note: you cannot see end to end on this runway at ZZZ. Upon taking off I found a low wing plane departing from XY. We were both airborne. Fortunately we both broke to our right at the same time. Wondering if I missed something about wind direction I turned up the volume on YYY.ZZ and found the wind to be still 050 at 3 knots. As to the operation of my radio it worked fine talking to four different ATC facilities on the way home. For ZZZ I would recommend a camera and TV screen at each end so you can see what's at each end. Don't know if you could aim one on the approach for landing plane. Don't know how you would fix downwind takeoffs. Well downwind take offs are not prohibited I think you should put the odds on your side should you have engine failure during the takeoff phase of flight."
ASRS:1830394.s: A pilot at ZZZ airport observed a high-wing aircraft taking off on runway XY while intending to depart on runway XX due to wind conditions. Both aircraft became airborne and avoided collision by breaking right, prompting the pilot to recommend installing cameras at runway ends to improve visibility.

ASRS:1830406.n: Aircraft X departed ZZZ IFR initially assigned 040 heading and 4,000 altitude. Pilot checked on, was identified, handed off and shipped to ZZZ1 Approach having reported established on the airway northbound. Aircraft Y was cleared for the RNAV30 approach at ZZZ and issued direct ZZZ2 (roughly 010) climbing to 4,000 feet on his missed. He was switched to advisory.Aircraft X experienced a total electrical failure. He lost comms and transponder. Pilot elected to return to ZZZ VFR. I was unaware of his intentions and had only a primary only target on his aircraft. When Aircraft Y checked on, I stopped Aircraft Y at 3,000 feet as Aircraft X's last observed altitude was 4,200 feet with an assigned altitude of 4,000 feet. Aircraft X descended into ZZZ and the altitude of Aircraft X as they passed about 2 miles lateral from Aircraft Y and whether or not he was VFR was unknown. The operation was as safe as it could be given the circumstances.
ASRS:1830406.s: An air traffic controller managed Aircraft X, which suffered a total electrical failure and lost comms while returning VFR, and Aircraft Y on an RNAV30 approach. The controller held Aircraft Y at 3,000 feet to avoid conflict with Aircraft X, which passed two miles laterally at an unknown altitude.

ASRS:1830416.n: Just prior to pushing, I was handed a Notice to Crew (NOTAC) for aircraft batteries in compartment D. I signed one and kept it, signed the other and returned it. I didn't look at it closely and didn't realize until cruise that the release was supposed to note it as well.
ASRS:1830416.s: The pilot received a Notice to Crew regarding aircraft batteries in compartment D just prior to pushback but failed to note the release on the document. The oversight was not realized until the cruise phase of flight.

ASRS:1830523.n: Radioactive material loaded in 2L. In accordance with Flight Operations Manual should have been position 3 and aft. Hazmat cargo incorrectly loaded by ramp. I failed to catch error. [Captain suggest company] develop software that will not allow paperwork to print if Hazardous Goods are incorrectly loaded. The ramp agent loaded radioactive II 0.1 T.I in position 2l. The crew did not catch it.
ASRS:1830523.s: Ramp agents incorrectly loaded radioactive material in position 2L instead of the required position 3 and aft. The flight crew failed to detect the error, prompting the captain to suggest software preventing flight document printing for incorrect hazardous goods loading.

ASRS:1830581.n: Upon push back from the gate in ZZZ, a putrid/rancid smell filled the aft galley and was detectable by myself, the D flight attendant, the A flight attendant and at least 2 passengers causing eye irritation, headache and nausea for me, and a headache for the D. The Captain was notified immediately. Having experienced this leaving ZZZZ on the prior leg flown by this aircraft, the decision was made to return to the gate and have Maintenance look at the aircraft. The A, B, and C flight attendants all agreed that we didn't feel safe in an environment where we and our passengers were potentially breathing toxic fumes. A 21 point inspection was run at the gate and it was determined that the plane had no mechanical issues. I tried (as did the Captain) to mention that it was likely the odor was not reproduce-able at idle. It was only evident under power. It was deemed a safe aircraft, so we re-boarded the flight, only to experience the odor, eye burning, headache, and nausea after push back. A second gate return occurred and passenger and crew deplaned.
ASRS:1830581.s: Crew and passengers experienced toxic fumes causing illness during pushback from ZZZ, prompting two returns to the gate. Although a 21-point inspection found no mechanical issues at idle, the odor persisted under power, forcing a second deplaning.

ASRS:1830641.n: Initial descent into ZZZ, engine roughness and loss of power (300-400 RPM). Applied carb heat, engine continued to lose power, requested priority with tower, squawked 7700, maintained altitude and airspeed until landing at airport was assured. Landed plane without incident and taxied to FBO. Initial descent from 3,500 feet MSL engine roughness drop of 300+ RPM. Was pilot not flying. Pic pulled carb heat. I requested priority, squawked 7700. Engine made partial power until landing.
ASRS:1830641.s: The pilot reported engine roughness and a 300-400 RPM power loss during initial descent from 3,500 feet MSL into ZZZ. After applying carburetor heat and squawking 7700, the aircraft landed safely with partial power.

ASRS:1830724.n: Flight was deviating off the ZZZZZ arrival due to thunderstorm activity. Subsequently cleared direct ZZZZZ and told to descend to 5,000 feet. While it is possible both the Captain and FO (First Officer) heard the wrong altitude, the FO read back 5,000 feet. Even though the published altitude is 6,000 feet, this did not seem unusual to us as we were flying below storm overhangs and had barely flown any of the arrival up to this point. After reaching 5,000, the controller asked why we were at 5,000. We informed him that was our cleared altitude. He informed us 6,000 was the minimum vectoring altitude. On arriving into ZZZ, we were taken off the ZZZZZ4 arrival due to thunderstorms in the terminal area. Upon contact with Terminal Radar Control we were issued radar vectors. The Air Traffic Controller stated that we would rejoin the arrival at ZZZZZ. We were told to fly heading 090 and cleared to descend from 9,000 to 6,000. The clearance was read back and confirmed by both of us. Shortly thereafter the controller gave us a further descent down to 5,000. The clearance was read back and confirmed by both of us. After the clearance was read back, ATC never intervened on the altitude that we read back. ATC then told us to fly direct to ZZZZZ. Whilst we were level at ZZZZZ at 5,000, ATC stated that [the next fix] had an altitude of 6,000 ft. I stated that we were cleared by him down to 5,000. There were no traffic conflicts.
ASRS:1830724.s: The flight crew descended to 5,000 feet on ATC clearance while deviating from the ZZZZZ arrival due to thunderstorms, despite the published minimum vectoring altitude being 6,000 feet. The controller later questioned the altitude, but no traffic conflicts occurred.

ASRS:1830811.n: We brought the aircraft in from ZZZ1 arriving at gate in ZZZ at XA:34 local. The flight from ZZZ1 was uneventful. Arriving at gate ramp personnel hooked up ground electric as well as ground air. The APU was shut down after both were connected. Approximately 15 minutes to departure I turned the APU back on. Once on line and available I deselected ground electric. Once the ground crew disconnected both ground electric and air I selected the APU bleed on. Within 30 secs of the APU bleed being selected on I noticed the odor of dirty socks indicating the presence of neurotoxic tricresyl phosphates emanating from the ventilation system. I quickly turned off the APU bleed and asked the First Officer if he noticed the smell as well, however he was unsure. I then proceeded to turn the bleed on one more time to confirm we smelled it and immediately after turning the APU bleed on the odor was back. Again I then selected the APU bleed off. We then asked operations for ground air and electric to be placed back on the aircraft while we called Maintenance Control. We also had the passengers deplane. Maintenance Control had contract maintenance come out and after conferring with Maintenance Control, Airbus Fleet Management, and [name] in the Chief Pilots Office we performed an engine run-up with contract maintenance onboard. We used a ground air cart to perform ground air start, bypassing the APU. Once the pack systems were turned on using the engine bleeds the odor was back, however at a much lighter presence. The bleeds and packs were quickly selected off and we began to shutdown and secure the aircraft. The airplane was taken out of service. Company Maintenance came in from ZZZ2 overnight and confirmed a significant oil leak from the APU. [The cause was an] APU oil leak.
ASRS:1830811.s: The flight crew detected a neurotoxic odor from the APU bleed system at the gate, prompting passenger deplaning and an engine run-up that confirmed the smell persisted with engine bleeds. Maintenance confirmed a significant APU oil leak, causing the aircraft to be taken out of service.

ASRS:1830820.n: On climbout received level 1 CABIN CLIMB alert followed by level 3 CABIN ALTITUDE alert. We stopped our climb at 12,000 feet then coordinated with ATC for descent to 10,000 feet. Completed checklist, consulted [company], decided to continue to ZZZ1. Passing through FL320 on subsequent climb we received a level 3 CABIN ALTITUDE alert again. We [advised ATC] and initiated emergency descent to 10,000 feet, then completed checklist again. We consulted with [the company] and decided to divert back to ZZZ. Normal approach and landing in to ZZZ with no further issues.Equipment failure of pressurization system, yet to be determined. During climb out we got a Cabin rate indication followed by Cabin Altitude warning passing approximately 12,000 feet. We descended to 10,000 feet to accomplish QRH procedures. Cabin pressurization control returned to normal. After consulting with [company maintenance], we proceeded enroute to ZZZ1. During climb through approximately 32,000 feet the same alerts reoccurred and [we advised ATC], and emergency descent to 10,000 was accomplished. QRH procedures were again accomplished followed by return to ZZZ. Cabin pressure controller malfunction. (Probable cause at this writing).
ASRS:1830820.s: The flight crew experienced repeated cabin altitude alerts during climbout and at FL320 due to a pressurization system malfunction. They performed emergency descents to 10,000 feet, completed checklists, and diverted back to ZZZ for a safe landing.

ASRS:1830831.n: After a long duty day because of weather delays we finished our four day trip by taxiing into our gate in ZZZ. The ground crew guided us in to the spot and shut down the engines. When the gate agent tried to pull the bridge up to the aircraft she realized the aircraft had been stopped at the wrong spot. We were told we needed to move the aircraft a few inches forward. I made a PA and told passengers that we would have to move forward but missed mentioning to take a seat. We were told by the ground crew to release the brakes so the tug could capture the nose gear. Because of the confusion between ground crews, gate agent driving the bridge, and us we did not realized the bridge was very close to the aircraft. At the same time the ground crew had not securely captured the aircraft and the aircraft rolled forward about two feet. We were taken by surprise as we were not expecting to move forward. As the aircraft moved forward and immediately set the parking brake but the aircraft had moved about two feet while being close to the bridge and while still having some passengers standing on the aisle. After setting the parking brake the aircraft stopped and flight attendants proceeded to make sure everyone was safely seated. The ground crew then guided the gate agent to move the bridge away from the aircraft and capture the aircraft to then move it back the correct parking spot. The bridge was reconnected and everyone deplaned without any more issues. No one was hurt and there were no damages to the aircraft. The ramp supervisor apologized and explained the ground crew was new to the job.Miscommunication between ground crew, gate agent and flight crew. Inexperience and new to the job by ground crew. Fatigue and long duty day were also factors for the flight crew. Rushing to get everyone off the aircraft. Better communication and verification by flight crews when dealing with ground crews. Understanding and self assessment of alertness and fatigue conditions. Using others to coordinate better and cross check for missed items. Take the time think and assess the situation.
ASRS:1830831.s: Flight crew, fatigued after a long duty day, inadvertently rolled the aircraft two feet forward at the gate due to miscommunication with inexperienced ground crew and a gate agent. The movement occurred while passengers were standing and the bridge was close, but no injuries or damage resulted after the parking brake was set.

ASRS:1830855.n: Departing ZZZ, received a No. 2 engine bleed leak message on pneumatic panel, with EICAS message. Deselected engine bleed source per QRH procedure. Continued flight after considering air return to ZZZ as bleed leak warning went out shortly after deselecting right engine bleed. Later in flight at FL250, suddenly noticed acrid strong odor. Captain called flight attendant on interphone and confirmed some smoke and strong odor present in cabin. Decided to perform 'smoke in cockpit' memory items. During this procedure apparently Captain's mask interphone failed and he was unable to communicate with O2 mask on. Pilot Flying assumed flying and ATC communication responsibilities and coordinating descent and weather deviation with ATC. [Requested ATC priority handling]. During descent eventually Pack 1 overheat EICAS message annunciation. Smoke and odor dissipated so O2 masks removed and normal crew communication resumed. Continued to destination as no longer producing smoke and no odor detected in cockpit and confirmed by flight attendant in cabin. Landed uneventfully in ZZZ1 with good priority handling by ATC and some weather deviation due to local rain showers. [I] understand that the left air conditioning pack failed, causing smoke and odor noted. At FL250 with right pack and bleed deselected, began to get smoke throughout aircraft. Donned masks and [requested priority handling] with ZZZ ATC. We received clearance direct to ZZZ1 from about 80 miles out and descended to 10,000'. After about 2-3 minutes, smoke dissipated and did not reappear. Uneventful landing.
ASRS:1830855.s: The flight crew experienced a No. 2 engine bleed leak and subsequent smoke and odor at FL250, likely caused by a left air conditioning pack failure. After donning oxygen masks and requesting priority handling, they descended to 10,000 feet, where the smoke dissipated, allowing for an uneventful landing at ZZZ1.

ASRS:1830905.n: I was departing runway XX at ZZZ. Noise abatement procedure calls for no turns below 1,000 feet. I was climbing out at 80 Mph when a warning flashed on my ADSB in software on my tablet. I was nose high and did not see the traffic approaching me from the NW and below my altitude. When I looked left, I saw a twin engine aircraft climb through my altitude and fly past me on a southeast heading. I was just starting my crosswind turn when I first saw the aircraft. They were not on the CTAF frequency even though they were flying through the pattern for ZZZ. After I was sure the plane was clear, I resumed my turn to downwind for runway XX and then checked the ADSB in information on the target to be sure I had seen the correct N number as it flew by. The N number I wrote down was the same N number that showed up for that target on ADSB-in. It was disconcerting to have a plane fly under me and so close laterally while I was in the pattern.
ASRS:1830905.s: A pilot departing runway XX at ZZZ experienced a close call with a twin-engine aircraft climbing through their altitude while executing a noise abatement climb. The intruder was not on the CTAF frequency, causing a near collision that was detected via ADSB-in software before the pilot resumed the pattern.

ASRS:1830923.n: The [SQL] ATIS recording is almost always very hard to understand. Many times it cuts in and out when it is recorded. This means that pilots may not be able to clearly hear critical information such as the altimeter setting or the wind. This has been reported to the tower controllers but the situation hasn't been improved. Pilots often times have to report they don't have the WX and ask the Controller to read it. This defeats the purpose of having an ATIS. The recording sounds like the person is not always speaking into the microphone.
ASRS:1830923.s: Pilots reported that the [SQL] ATIS recording is frequently unintelligible due to audio cutting in and out, preventing clear reception of critical data like altimeter settings and wind. Despite reports to tower controllers, the issue persists, forcing pilots to request weather information directly and defeating the purpose of the ATIS.

ASRS:1830930.n: I departed my home base airport on a VFR flight for the purpose of gaining experience using the VNAV (Vertical Navigation) function of recently installed GPS Navigators and an autopilot in the aircraft.
