As I was intending on changing altitudes throughout the flight to test out the VNAV I decided to not request flight following and instead on my Comm 2 radio I monitored 121.5. The conditions were VFR with about 10 miles visibility, but there was significant haze. To best test out the VNAV functions I created a flight plan with a final fix (another airport) located approximately 79 miles from the departure airport. My initial intent was to test out the VNAV functionality throughout that path on a few different occasions and with different step downs, then turn around at the final fix, without landing, and return to my home base airport. While descending to 3,500 feet about 45 miles from the final fix, I flew about 2 miles north of a non-towered airport and about 5 miles north of a city. When flying in that area, I looked at my IPad which has Foreflight and I did not notice any Parachute Jump Area (PJA) rings over that airport and expecting to see those rings in the relevant areas I did not notice the parachute symbol by the airport that appears on the VFR Sectional on the IPad. Having successfully completed one test of the VNAV about 45 miles before arriving at the final fix, and predominately due to the haze, I decided to discontinue flying towards the final fix and to begin heading back to my home base earlier than originally anticipated. Looking again at the IPad I did not notice any PJA rings or the parachute symbol by the airport near the city and I decided to use that airport as part of my route towards my home base airport and turned toward that airport. Within a couple of minutes I overflew that airport eastbound at 3,500 feet MSL (approximately 2,300 AGL) while using the autopilot and noticed a small aircraft landing southbound on the airport's runway. I then looked up about 45 degrees from the horizon and saw one open canopy parachutist about 300 feet above the airplane and another at about the 2 o'clock position 500 feet laterally and 300 feet above the plane. It was immediately clear from their rate of descent that I would be past both of them before they would reach my altitude. I quickly scanned for other parachutist and put my thumb over the autopilot disconnect switch, but not having any idea how many parachutists were out there and not seeing others except for the two with which I recognized I was not in a collision course, I thought that maintaining heading and altitude would make me as predictable as possible and it would give any other parachutist that could see or hear me the best opportunity to avoid me. Thus, I covered the controls to use them to override the autopilot if needed but did not disengage the autopilot or perform any evasive maneuvers. Upon landing, I immediately checked my iPad again to see if there were any PJAs over the airport, and none were present over that airport, and I then noticed there were no PJAs depicted anywhere over any airports. When looking at the IPad on the ground I did identify the Sectional's parachute symbol near the airport. I then compared my IPad's Foreflight map display with that on my IPhone and saw that the IPhone displayed the PJA rings. The next day I contacted Foreflight as I could not identify the difference in the settings that was causing the IPhone to display PJA rings and not on the IPad. They very quickly pointed me to a setting for Airspace that I had not enabled on the IPad and as soon as I enabled it, the PJAs showed up on the IPad. I believe my over reliance on Foreflight's PJA rings caused me to not inspect the map closely enough to identify the parachute symbol by the airfield near the area that I was not originally intending to use as a turn around point. Verifying that this setting is enabled is now a checklist item for me;and when there are changes to a plan that will cause me to fly near an airport, regardless of the altitude over the pattern, I will more closely inspect for the parachute symbols even if there is no ring depicted on Foreflight. Also, even when engaged in local flights that require maneuvering and changes in altitude and that may place me near multiple airports, I intend to request flight following.
ASRS:1830930.s: A pilot flying VFR in haze overflew a non-towered airport at 3,500 feet MSL and encountered two parachutists above the aircraft. The incident resulted from the pilot's over-reliance on Foreflight, which failed to display Parachute Jump Area rings due to an unselected airspace setting, causing the pilot to miss the parachute symbol on the sectional chart.

ASRS:1830935.n: Engine failure just after lift off. Attempted feather of inoperative engine, but got partial recovery of power in the process, was unable to climb and landed in a field.
ASRS:1830935.s: The pilot reported an engine failure just after lift-off. After attempting to feather the inoperative engine and experiencing partial power recovery, the aircraft was unable to climb and landed in a field.

ASRS:1830939.n: Moderate turbulence at 43,000 feet, right engine flame out, requested priority handling immediately at ZZZ.
ASRS:1830939.s: The crew experienced moderate turbulence at 43,000 feet, causing a right engine flame out. They immediately requested priority handling at ZZZ.

ASRS:1830946.n: I was in cruise and on autopilot for the past few hours. I was handed off to another controller with ZZZ center. He was so busy I could not break in to establish contact. After a few minutes of trying I pressed IDENT so he would know I was with him. I finally got through and was switched to another controller.Checking my instruments my airspeed was very slow, 70 knots. I checked my RPMs and it was at 2,500. I assumed my pitot static tube was blocked. I checked to make sure my pitot heat was on. Next, I checked my engine analyzer. All cylinders were cold. I switched tanks and turned on the boost pump and ALT air. Note: Mooney Ovation has an automatic alt air system that opens with any blockage.There were never any signs of icing. This aircraft is certified for Known Ice (FIKI).All within seconds I was in an unusual attitude and in IMC. With no power, in IMC, and in an unusual attitude, I requested assistance. I have been flying for more than 20 years and never had required immediate assistance. I was focused 110% on flying the plane. The Autopilot was off. I pushed forward to gain airspeed in case I was in a spin, then leveled the wings and asked for vectors to the nearest airport. ZZZ was 10 miles behind me. The controller was switched to another frequency. He was fantastic. I was on best glide speed direct to ZZZ. I notice I was getting some power and shortly my engine was running normally. Even though everything was operating normally, I flew a VFR approach to ZZZ1 for a precautionary landing. I wanted to have it looked at by an A&P mechanic.The mechanic took off the cowling with my help. He felt everything looked normal and operational. He noted that the engine had good compression. His recommendation was to go to a test area and run up the engine to full power a few times. All appeared normal. I fuel up with fuel and continued my flight the following day. It flight was uneventful, but I stayed in VFR conditions as a precaution.
ASRS:1830946.s: A pilot in a Mooney Ovation experienced an engine power loss and unusual attitude in IMC during cruise, likely due to a blocked pitot tube causing erroneous airspeed indications. After recovering control and landing at ZZZ for inspection, the mechanic found no faults, and the pilot resumed flight the next day.

ASRS:1830953.n: While replacing a radar transceiver, the pitot line to the Captain's ADM (Air Data Module) was removed to help make room for transceiver removal. After installation the line was not reinstalled. The root cause was not attaching a red streamer to the line to remind myself to hook line back up after the installation and troubleshooting of the radar.
ASRS:1830953.s: A mechanic removed the Captain's pitot line to the Air Data Module while replacing a radar transceiver but failed to reinstall it. The cause was the mechanic's failure to attach a red streamer to the line as a reminder to reconnect it after the work.

ASRS:1830956.n: Aircraft X had been on radar vectors for the ILS RWY XX approach at ZZZ1. They were on H [Heading]180, and then I turned them left H080, maintain at or above 5,000 feet until established on the localizer, and cleared ILS RWY XX approach. I watched Aircraft X turn towards the localizer, he had a good read back, and was descending out of 067. Shortly after I saw them through the localizer still on H080 and at 052. I advised them they flew through the localizer, and turned them first H030, then H020 to join but quickly realized that they would not turn before the entered an adjacent 060 MVA [Minimum Vectoring Altitude]. I issued a low altitude alert and advised they climb to 060 immediately. When they got to the MVA I vectored them back to the localizer. I asked if the pilot had received the localizer, and he responded affirmative. On the next attempt, I kept them at 060 and asked to report established. They flew through the localizer again, and said they were not receiving it and requested the RNAV RWY XX. I vectored them to final for the RNAV RWY XX, and they were able to establish on final and I cleared them for the approach.Leading up to this event, our facility had just finished working our cargo arrival rush, and traffic had slowed significantly. I was on West Radar, but then got the East Radar controller off position and worked them combined. After a period of about 30 minutes, traffic had built up to moderate levels and moderate-high complexity. This was due to wildfire smoke in the area, and nearly all aircraft being IFR. Our visual separation LOA with ZZZ2 was turned off, and I was staggering approaches between ZZZ2 and ZZZ, and also had a 3 aircraft sequence into the ZZZ1 airport, which has a temporary fire tower in operation. This caused multiple inbound calls via landline for the 3 arrivals. I had a high workload with multiple shout line coordination's from ZZZ3, ZZZ ATCT, and ZZZ2. The FLM was helping with my strips, and another controller came in and after the traffic had slowed a little we split the positions again. It was during this cool down period that the MVA violation happened. The 2 aircraft ahead of Aircraft X both flew the ILS [Runway] XX without issue. When I turned and cleared Aircraft X for the approach, he was in a good position to join final and was descending well, and I remember I was not concerned about them intercepting the localizer.I had been watching my strips print out, and realized it was going to get a little busy but wouldn't be a big deal. However, a military aircraft departed ZZZ2 into the radar pattern, and we got a divert from ZZZ4 to ZZZ1, and some of the coordination's that happened were unforeseen. I just didn't recognize how busy I would become in time to ask for help before traffic became difficult. Of course I will be more diligent in my scan and also recognizing overload situations and ask for help sooner. I think just having Hand-off staffed would have alleviated the overload, and my scan would likely have been better without such a high peak of workload followed by the lull of less traffic. I will also consider vectoring to a longer final and having aircraft join at 060 instead of 050.
ASRS:1830956.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X for an ILS approach at ZZZ1, but the pilot flew through the localizer twice and descended below the 6,000-foot MVA. The controller attributed the incident to high workload from wildfire smoke, multiple coordination calls, and a sudden traffic surge that impaired situational awareness.

ASRS:1830963.n: SWAP night at ZZZ (Severe Weather Avoidance Plan). I had just arrived at work for the mid and taken over the two local positions from the outgoing controller. I settled in and started working the traffic and Aircraft X was one of the first few aircraft I cleared to land after taking over the position. It was VFR conditions after weather that had impacted the airport earlier had moved well out of the area. Everything seemed routine except it was busier than usual due to the weather delays as traffic was landing and departing on parallel runways. Ground Control was open and working the outbound departures to runway XXL. At ZZZ, traffic must cross runway XYR in order to access runway XXL because the runways are staggered. Ground control was taxiing Aircraft Y on taxiway 1 and I learned afterward that the aircraft was instructed to hold short of runway XYR. As Aircraft X was approaching runway XYR (our arrival runway) I noticed the taxi light on Aircraft Y was still illuminated and the aircraft seemed to still be in motion. I quickly scanned the ASDE-X (Airport Surface Detection Equipment) and as I looked up, Aircraft Y's data tag started to flash. I issued a go around clearance to Aircraft X as soon as I saw that Aircraft Y was not going to hold short. The ASDE-X did issue a go-around alert, but I had already been issuing the go-around clearance. I climbed Aircraft X to 3,000 feet on runway heading. As Aircraft X was starting into a stable climb, I issued a turn to a 300 heading away from the traffic departing runway XXL that had been cleared on a 245 heading prior to the go around and was already on departure roll. Aircraft X was then switched back to approach control for resequencing and landed about 10 minutes later without incident. Aircraft Y was then issued a runway crossing clearance by Ground Control and instructed to contact the Supervisor in the TRACON once the aircraft was parked on a taxiway.No recommendations. In a telephone interview with the flight crew by the Supervisor, it was learned that the crew was confused by the lights (ZZZ has wigwags at all the hold short lines and it is unmistakable where to stop for the runway) and failed to stop at the hold short line on taxiway 1.
ASRS:1830963.s: An air traffic controller issued a go-around to Aircraft X after Aircraft Y failed to hold short of runway XYR due to crew confusion over hold short lights. The controller used ASDE-X alerts to intervene, climbing Aircraft X to 3,000 feet and rerouting it for a safe landing ten minutes later.

ASRS:1830970.n: Aircraft X arrival to ZZZ1 and Aircraft Y ZZZ departure were in direct conflict. An IFR release was received from ZZZ2 approach for Aircraft Y and after Aircraft Y was airborne Aircraft X's data tag was in view on the edge on my radar screen. I advised ZZZ tower on the situation immediately then passed traffic to Aircraft Y. As the collision advisory appeared a traffic alert was issued where the pilot immediately got the traffic in sight and asked what direction to go. Aircraft was on an IFR departure climb below the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) so I advised the pilot left or right turn at pilot's discretion. Aircraft Y turned to avoid.I don't know the current visual aids used by approach for release availability to each facility but I'd advise that their visual aids should be made more effective. A radar software update to where ZZZ1's instrument final turns red if someone has been cleared for the approach would give ZZZ [Tower] better situational awareness and be a home run in terms of ensuring this doesn't happen again. ZZZ controllers standard radar setting does not allow for view of ZZZ1 instrument arrivals much farther out then 10 mile final but we can always see the final and a change in its color would be noticed.
ASRS:1830970.s: A ZZZ controller managed a conflict between an arriving Aircraft X and departing Aircraft Y below Minimum Vectoring Altitude, issuing a traffic alert that prompted Aircraft Y to turn and avoid. The controller attributed the incident to limited radar situational awareness and recommended software updates to improve visual aids for approach clearances.

ASRS:1831010.n: During approach into ZZZ while receiving vectors was cleared to 9,500 feet MSL and told cleared for the ILS XX and to maintain 9,500 feet until established. Selected APP and aircraft captured GS and LOC and was descending on the app with GS and LOC locked on. Got a call from approach at 8,100 feet letting us know we were low and to climb up to 8,600 feet I immediately disconnected the auto pilot and initiated a climb while maintaining LOC. After crossing ZZZZZ I then recommenced my descent and flew visually using the PAPI as my guidance. Landed the aircraft within the touch down range and stopped on the runway. CA taxied aircraft to gate. During taxi we were informed by approach that the GS had issues and they thought it had been fixed. We initially intercepted the GS and LOC approximately 20 miles out. At approximately 2 miles out the GS was back in line with the PAPI. We were doing the ILS Z Runway XX into ZZZ. Night time, good visibility, no clouds. ATC had us at 9,500 feet, turned us to intercept final outside of ZZZZZ and cleared us for the approach. Autopilot was on. We were flaps 1 about 190 knots at the time and about 22 miles on final. We intercepted the localizer and the glide slope at about the same time. At which point we were busy setting touch down zone, putting flaps down and gear. A moment later ATC gives us an altitude low warning, climb immediately to 8,600 feet. The flying pilot ( first officer) immediately disconnected auto pilot and initiated climb. We were around 8,100 feet, on the glide slope, auto pilot on when this was initiated from what we could tell. We had just passed ZZZZZ (FAF, but 17 miles out). The controller mentioned they had some glide slope problems just a week or two prior, and asked us if we were ok to proceed visually. Still being over 10 miles out, runway and PAPI in site, and glide slope still showing slightly below us, we proceeded visually with reference to PAPI and GS. The problem may have been from the auto pilot intercepting the LOC and GS at the same time and possibly overshooting the GS as it sometimes does when far out and possibly exasperated by configuration changes. This all happened about 15 to 20 miles from touchdown. Or it could have been from a faulty GS signal that they have had problems with previously.
ASRS:1831010.s: During an ILS approach at night, the crew received an ATC low altitude warning at 8,100 feet and climbed to 8,600 feet after disconnecting the autopilot. The deviation was attributed to either a faulty glide slope signal or an autopilot overshoot during simultaneous localizer and glide slope capture.

ASRS:1831011.n: Fix CI051 came up when approach ILS 05R Z entered into FMGC. Fix is not on that approach, nor any approach into MMMX. Fix MX901 which is on the approach was not in the FMGC. This is not noted on NOTAMs. If pilots are not careful and neglect to delete CI051 and add MX901 with an altitude constraint prior to being cleared the approach they would not comply with a clearance and potentially 'jam' themselves on this approach.
ASRS:1831011.s: Pilots reported that the FMGC incorrectly loaded fix CI051 instead of MX901 for the ILS 05R approach at MMMX, a discrepancy not noted on NOTAMs. Failure to manually correct this could cause non-compliance with clearances or jam the aircraft on the approach.

ASRS:1831038.n: On receipt of a Dangerous Goods message (Dry Ice), we discussed it and the need for the final dangerous good message before push. Per that conversation, I folded that message and hung it from a switch on the Mode Control Panel. The objective was to have that page visible and reminder not to push without final notification. When all of the usual items and checklists were complete, I called for the 'before pushback checklist' which was completed, and we called for push. During the pushback procedure I noticed that we had not yet received the required final dangerous goods message. That message was requested and received before we disconnected from the pushback tug.
ASRS:1831038.s: The flight crew hung a Dry Ice message on the Mode Control Panel as a reminder during pushback but realized the final Dangerous Goods message was missing. They requested and received the required message before disconnecting from the pushback tug.

ASRS:1831057.n: When we arrived in ZZZ to start our trip we meet with the inbound crew to discuss the inbound leg and aircraft. There was no mention from them about any odors or problems with the aircraft. When we boarded the aircraft we were over come by a strong smell throughout the plane. Looking back it was strange the previous crew didn't mention this. It was similar to a strong carpet cleaner smell or an odor like when you clean an oven. There was no indication of fire or smoke much less any indications of a malfunction. We discussed the issue with the crew and found no reasons not to continue safely. As we boarded the aircraft several passengers started to complain especially in the rear cabin about the odor. We discussed what the cause of the smell could be and determined that it was not a safety of flight issue since we could not isolate any problems. All systems operated normally. We agreed to continue on the short flight to ZZZ1 hoping that at altitude the fresh air would dispute any smell. We felt that since there was smoke all around the area from west coast wild fires that could possibly be the cause. At cruise the smell seemed to disappear in the cockpit but as we got closer to our destination the FA'S informed us that it remained in the cabin. There was no smoke or any indications of a malfunction. They then stated that many passengers complained that they were starting to get headaches and feel bad. We asked if there any immediate concerns and were informed there were none. Inbound we decided to inform maintenance control that there was an odor which seemed to be coming from the gasper vents via an MRM entry so that on arrival they could trouble shoot and see if they could remove it. After landing we started the APU and received a low oil level indication. Not sure if this contributed to the problem or not as we accepted the aircraft in ZZZ with the APU operating and had no indications of any problems at that time. Arriving at the gate we noticed that the smell in the cockpit remained but the cabin was stronger. We had an hour on the ground before our next flight so felt that the problem could be resolved. After block in we meet with maintenance and he noticed the smell as well. His feeling is it smelled like burning oil. We had no indications at any time of an overheat or fire on any system. I then received a call from Name our Chief Pilot to contact Name 1 in Maintenance Control for some questions. I was asked generic questions about the entire flight to help trouble shoot the problem. As I stated everything went great expect for the strong smell. They removed the aircraft from service and we continued our trip with another aircraft. The entire crew handled the situation professionally and with merit. I applaud how we worked together to assist passengers needs and answer any questions or concerns they may have had. The flight was concluded safely and professional with our [company] principles.
ASRS:1831057.s: The flight crew encountered a strong odor resembling burning oil or carpet cleaner during the ZZZ to ZZZ1 flight, which caused passenger discomfort but no system malfunctions. Maintenance identified the smell upon arrival, removed the aircraft from service for troubleshooting, and the crew completed the trip on a replacement aircraft.

ASRS:1831059.n: Once again the PAPIs at PTKK are inoperative. There should be a Company response to lack of electronic/ visual glidepath for night operations.
ASRS:1831059.s: A pilot reported that the PAPIs at PTKK were inoperative, leaving no electronic or visual glidepath for night operations. The reporter requested a company response to address this lack of visual aids.

ASRS:1831089.n: This event occurred during preflight at the gate. The aircraft arrived at ZZZ gate XX from the maintenance hanger eight minutes before boarding time. After review of the AML, I confirmed the aircraft had a couple of MEL items including a #2 engine thrust reverser inoperative. We contacted maintenance for three additional items, including excessively high wheel brake temperatures on wheels three and four. Those temperatures were 340 degrees C and 270 degrees C, respectively. When the mechanic arrived at the aircraft, I asked him for the reason the brakes were so hot after a tow or taxi delivery from the hanger. He inspected the brakes and found them to be 'very warm.' He also ran a few diagnostic tests. Unfortunately the mechanic could not give an adequate explanation for the high wheel brake temperatures, nor could he verify the proper functioning of the wheel brakes on the right main gear. I refused the aircraft on the basis of safety-of-flight because I felt the aircraft was unsafe to operate with an unknown wheel brake issue coupled with an inoperative thrust reverser.The primary causal factor for refusing the aircraft was the unknown reason for the hot brakes. This issue was not resolved to my satisfaction. The risk of operating the aircraft with both a brake issue and inoperative reverser was too high to warrant continuation of the flight.Maintenance personnel should resolve obvious aircraft issues before releasing the aircraft to the flight crew.
ASRS:1831089.s: The pilot refused the aircraft at the gate due to unexplained high wheel brake temperatures and an inoperative #2 thrust reverser. Maintenance could not verify brake function or explain the heat, leading the pilot to deem the aircraft unsafe for flight.

ASRS:1831106.n: After pushing back on the ZZZ ramp, we went to start the engines. During the start, the Blue Hydraulic pressure gauge came up low, just to the yellow line. Note that the Blue Hydraulic system had been serviced in ZZZ by Maintenance while we hub turned. In consultation with ZZZ Maintenance, we shut down in position and they went to service the Blue Hydraulic. After some time the Blue Hydraulic was back in the Top Hat. Cleared off Maintenance, and restarted engines. After start, When the bleed air transferred over to the packs, we immediately started getting smoke in the cockpit. I initially smelled it. Then with the rising sun coming in my side window, you could clearly see the smoke (vaporized Skydrol?) coming out of my air vent starting to fill the cockpit. The intensity of smoke increased with time. We opened the windows for fresh air and shut off the packs. Approximate about 3 - 4 minutes of chemical exposure. We wound up taxiing back to the gate and eventually shut down the engines. I felt a little light head, a scratchy throat, and was beginning to cough. Captain had some similar issues. After speaking with Chief Pilot, and self-evaluating our symptoms, we were driven to the local ER to get checked out. At the hospital, poison control was contacted, X-ray's were taken and a breathing treatment administered before being released. Exact cause for this issue is still unknown to me...but it clearly has to do with the servicing of the Blue Hydraulic system and possible failure of aircraft parts.
ASRS:1831106.s: The flight crew experienced cockpit smoke and chemical exposure after restarting engines following Blue Hydraulic system servicing. They taxied back to the gate, shut down, and sought medical attention for symptoms attributed to the recent maintenance and potential part failure.

ASRS:1831114.n: After landing on Runway XXL at ZZZ, we cleared off the runway at Taxiway 1 and was instructed to hold short of Runway XYL. Tower subsequently cleared us to cross Runway XXL and hold short of Runway XYR. We proceeded to taxi to satisfy the clearance. In an attempt to try to clear Runway XYL and also hold short of Runway XYR we encroached on Runway XYR causing a go-around of an aircraft attempting to land on Runway XYR. I believe this event was caused by an impossible clearance in combination with an attempt to comply with it. In hindsight, we should have recognized earlier that the clearance was not possible to comply with and should have communicated that to Tower. Flight was uneventful through departure, enroute, ILS Runway XXL, landing and rollout on Runway XXL, ZZZ. Weather was VMC. Told to clear right on Taxiway 1 and hold short of Runway XYL. Executed uneventfully. We were then quickly given clearance to 'Cross Runway XYL on Taxiway 1 and hold short of Runway XYR.' The Captain executed that clearance to the absolute best of his ability, set the parking brake, and turned off the taxi light short of Runway XYR. The Captain pulled up very close to Runway XYR, in order to no longer obstruct Runway XXL. In his estimation, the nose wheel was short of the Runway XYR hold short line, and the aircraft was only on Taxiway 1, not at all on Runway XYR, but he was trying to fit a 209 foot long B777 in a very small space.In hindsight we should have said 'Unable' to the impossible clearance, but we did not see that the space available on Taxiway 1 between the runways was insufficient until we were committed to cross Runway XYL. The aircraft was short of Runway XYR, and to the best of his estimation was clear of Runway XYL. At this point I realized we were crossed the hold short line and saw the landing aircraft on final. I spoke up and said I think we are on the active runway for the landing traffic. Seconds after I brought that up to everyone's attention, the tower then directed the small aircraft (I believe a PC-12) on extended final to Runway XYR to go around. All crew members had taxi charts open. Solid procedures were used. Everyone understood the clearance. There was no confusion at all, until we crossed Runway XYL on Taxiway 1, then I noticed we had crossed Runway XYR hold short line and saw the traffic on final. Debriefed that we should not have accepted the clearance and should have said 'Unable' to attempting to fit a B777 on Taxiway 1 between Runway XYL and Runway XYR.Attempting to do the impossible, to meet a clearance to fully cross Runway XYL and hold short of Runway XYR, to fit a B777 on Taxiway1 between Runway XYL and Runway XYR at ZZZ. Also, a misunderstanding of the controllers expectation (due to local knowledge). We should have transmitted one of two things. Best choice would have been to transmit 'unable' to the clearance and hold our original position short of Runway XYL, even though cleared to cross. Second, once committed to cross Runway XYL, and in observance that the task was impossible to transmit, 'We are holding short of Runway XYR, but still obstructing active Runway XYL.' We should have done this and left more room between the nose of the aircraft and Runway XYR. Clearly, we could have been more directive in the situation. One suggestion would be to have Tower change the comm to transmit, 'Cleared on to Runway XYL, but hold short of Runway XYR.' That would convey the point that they understand Runway XYL will remain obstructed. In that case, we would have not been concerned with obstructing Runway XYL and left more room between the nose and Runway XYR. Better still, have Tower wait until such a time as they can clear a B777 across both runways at once.
ASRS:1831114.s: A B777 crew at ZZZ encroached on Runway XYR while attempting to comply with an impossible clearance to cross Runway XYL and hold short of XYR on Taxiway 1. This caused a PC-12 on final to execute a go-around, which the crew attributed to accepting an unfeasible instruction without declaring "unable."

ASRS:1831141.n: After landing and taxiing towards our parking spot the we got indications of an APU fire. The APU was running and supplying electrical power to the aircraft. Almost simultaneously with the fire warning ground control called and said [they] could see smoke coming from the tail of the aircraft. The Captain stopped the aircraft set the brakes and called for the APU FIRE QRC. We ran the items and the fire was immediately extinguished. We then called for fire department support and was happy to see them already at the aircraft as the Ground Control called them for us. After confirming the fire was out, we taxied into our spot and shut down the aircraft. It was great to see how fast the Ground Controller was there to confirm our fire suspicions and to call local fire rescue for us. [Other personnel] were on the scene so fast that if an evacuation would have been necessary, they would have been a great help to us. On taxi to freight facility after landing got a APU fire warning closely followed by ZZZ Ground informing us that there was smoke coming from the tail area of the aircraft. Stopped the jet, asked ATC to roll the fire equipment and completed the APU FIRE QRC followed by the QRH. We discharged one fire retardant bottle. The fire warning went away and ground personnel indicated there was no further evidence of fire. We taxied to parking spot and shut down. Did not [request priority] as we were already on the ground and required no priority handling. We did call immediately for fire trucks to come to our location.Simulator training works well and prepared us for the event. Cannot overstate the great help available from the ground controller and fire department.
ASRS:1831141.s: The flight crew received an APU fire warning and smoke report from Ground Control while taxiing after landing. They stopped the aircraft, executed the APU fire checklist, discharged one bottle to extinguish the fire, and taxied to the parking spot with fire department support.

ASRS:1831146.n: When cruising at FL350 and deviating right of course for thunderstorm avoidance on a heading of 075 we began to encounter blow off and overhangs from other cells in the area reducing visibility to IMC. ATC was overwhelmed and could not give us requested higher altitude and due to high traffic in the area we did not initiate a further deviation right of course until we could ask ATC. Our radar was operating and being manipulated by the Captain showing no cells along our route of flight. We did not realize our radar had failed (no cockpit indications) and suddenly we were in a extreme thunderstorm cell. Our altitude deviated considerably 1,500 feet up and 700 feet down from FL350. We encountered light hail extreme precipitation and severe turbulence. Upon exiting the cell we immediately flew towards clear air and made the decision to divert to ZZZ. Suspecting possible negative G limits had been exceeded and concerned about possible aircraft damage. ATC was able to immediately accommodate our diversion and I landed on runway XX at ZZZ without further issue. The radar and possible turbulence damage was written up in the maintenance log and the company notified according to SOPs and Op Specs. Ensure all radars are operational and checked regularly by Maintenance. Also release this incident to the entire pilot group so that they are aware of this possible issue when operating near thunderstorms.
ASRS:1831146.s: The crew encountered severe turbulence and hail while deviating for thunderstorms at FL350 due to an undetected weather radar failure. They diverted to ZZZ after significant altitude deviations, suspecting possible negative G limits and aircraft damage.

ASRS:1831150.n: Aircraft X departed ZZZ with its planned destination of ZZZ1. The aircraft taxied for runway XXR and departed on an IFR clearance. By all indications the takeoff was normal and nothing unusual occurred. At approximately 200 feet the Garmin autopilot Self - Engaged and put the airplane into a steep descent. I immediately pushed the Auto-Pilot (AP) disconnect switch, which (briefly) disconnected the AP before it re-engaged. This occurred two or three times consecutively as I tried to troubleshoot the issue. I then pushed and held the AP disconnect switch for 5-6 seconds with no success. (All the while the airplane continued to make attempts at descents.) Additionally, I tried the CWS (Control Wheel Steering) button to attempt to regain control over the autopilot. The current weather in ZZZ was IMC, with ceilings of 600 feet and 6 miles visibility with mist. I was on an IFR flight plan, and made the decision to request priority handling with ZZZ tower. I remained below the weather to return to the field and land runway XXR. To regain control over the autopilot, I turned off the avionics, and landed without incident. The cause of the event is unknown at this time while maintenance is troubleshooting the issue. At this time it is unknown (from a pilot's perspective) as to what could have prevented the malfunction of the autopilot, and cause it to self-engage.
ASRS:1831150.s: The pilot of Aircraft X experienced an uncommanded autopilot engagement and steep descent at 200 feet after takeoff in IMC. After failing to disconnect the system manually, the pilot turned off the avionics, returned to the airport, and landed safely while the cause remains unknown.

ASRS:1831174.n: Shortly after pushing back from the a strange odor, like rotten eggs or sulfur, filled the back galley. The B and I, as well as the jumpseater all mentioned it. It grew stronger, so we investigated where we thought it was coming from and called the Captain. While I was speaking with the pilots, the smell dissipated and grew weaker. They asked if it returned we [should] call them.A couple minutes later as we continued to taxi, the smell returned. We had [name], a non revenue Flight Attendant in seat X and we asked if she noticed any odors. She noticed the odor and it seemed to stop around row R or so. We called back the pilots and returned to the gate.
ASRS:1831174.s: Cabin crew and a jumpseater detected a sulfur odor in the back galley shortly after pushback, which intensified during taxi. The flight returned to the gate after the smell reappeared and was traced to the area around row R.

ASRS:1831179.n: The flight crew was concerned about an deferral used for a flight deck door peep hole. [Maintenance] was notified and determined that the flight deck door peep hole can not be placed on MEL or NEF. [Maintenance] created an [work order] to repair the door.
ASRS:1831179.s: The flight crew reported a concern regarding a deferred flight deck door peep hole. Maintenance determined the item could not be deferred per MEL or NEF and issued a work order to repair the door.

ASRS:1831191.n: Company is applying flight time restrictions wrongly to exceed the flight time of their crews who fly to the U.S. As example, a flight ZZZZ to ZZZ is around 14 hours block time, 4 crew flights. They don't compute the time in the rest (bunk) towards the total flight time, so they only log 7 hrs each way. Crews are flying more than 130 hrs a month and logging less than 100 hours, all this with the consent of the Foreign Civil Aviation Authority. With more than 100 flights to U.S. each week this is a huge safety threat to all. On top of that the rest are they getting in some U.S. destinations after these long flights is less than 24 hrs in the rest facility (hotel). For obvious reasons this cannot be raised to Company or Foreign Civil Aviation Authority.
ASRS:1831191.s: A crew member reported that the company incorrectly calculates flight time for 14-hour U.S. flights by excluding bunk time, causing crews to fly over 130 hours monthly while logging under 100. This practice, approved by the Foreign Civil Aviation Authority and involving less than 24-hour rest, is described as a significant safety threat.

ASRS:1831199.n: Called on the telephone, #1 for takeoff RWY 28 DLZ. Released, climb 3,000 Direct TRAKK. We took off. Called departure. Cleared to 10,000 ft. Was told about traffic 12:00. Given Altimeter setting. I said on radio 'We have traffic on TCAS...' (could not see the airplane but had him on the computer screen). I wish I had just said traffic not in sight. I told the PF (Pilot Flying), the CA (Captain), I did not see traffic. To me the TCAS showed traffic on our screen about in the 11:30 position. So I advised the CA to turn right. We continued to merge. My eyes were outside, no traffic. We were about his altitude, 1 mi. We got RA to climb and the CA pulled back hard, full power. I told center we had an RA. Never saw traffic. I'm not happy about the event. Wished CA had stopped climb when we were still below. Wished center had left us below.
ASRS:1831199.s: The crew of a departing aircraft received a TCAS Resolution Advisory to climb after merging with unseen traffic at 10,000 feet. The Captain executed a full-power climb, but the First Officer reported never seeing the traffic and criticized the decision to climb rather than remaining below the other aircraft.

ASRS:1831203.n: In cruise heading north on flight following with Travis Air Force Base RAPCON at 5,500 feet at 167 KTAS. Travis called out a descending C17 on approach into Travis with a caution for wake turbulence. Assumed I was above their trailing wake but flew into the turbulence and experience rough turbulence as we crossed the wake. Hit my head on the ceiling and the contents of the cockpit got tossed up in the air. Lesson learned: Don't try to gauge the altitude of wake turbulence. It's too hard to pinpoint where the risk is. Either climb well above it or turn around go the other way. I could have easily turned away and climbed to avoid it completely. I misjudged the location of the wake turbulence. Appreciate Travis RAPCON calling it out. I just didn't adjust enough.
ASRS:1831203.s: The pilot flying a light aircraft in cruise at 5,500 feet encountered severe wake turbulence from a descending C-17 despite a caution from Travis RAPCON. The pilot misjudged the wake's location, resulting in rough turbulence that caused head injury and unsecured cockpit items to become airborne.

ASRS:1831215.n: During the approach to landing at ZZZ on runway XX, the TIS traffic warning on the GPS came on. I was at 500 ft and descending to the runway. I believed it to be an 'echo' of my transponder, which sometimes happens, so I reset it and continued with the approach and landed (The conflicting traffic was showing +200 ft). An observer on the ground came into the terminal office and asked to see the pilot of the flight that had just landed. I introduced myself and he asked me if I had seen the helicopter over the airport. I explained that I could not see them as they were in the cloud layer and could not hear them, of course. I had made three position reports during my approach to the airport, but none were made by the military helicopter, which is not unusual. It is my estimation that the crew of the helicopter turned on their transponder to let me know of their presence as they saw me on their traffic awareness system. While it is not a common practice for the military to have their transponders on during operations, it would be invaluable for them to do so while on training missions that would get them close to civilian aircraft and airports.
ASRS:1831215.s: During approach to ZZZ, a pilot received a TIS traffic warning at 500 ft from a military helicopter in clouds, which the pilot initially dismissed as a transponder echo. The helicopter crew reportedly activated their transponder to alert the pilot, highlighting the value of military transponder use during training near civilian airports.

ASRS:1831234.n: I was working as TRACON Data for West in position of R1. I did not notice my Controller drop the tag for Aircraft X. About 5 minutes later, I coordinated a point out with Lone Rock sector control on Aircraft Y at 8,000 who would just clip our NW airspace. My Controller, being busy and trying to clean up his scope for a position transfer to me, was dropping tags on several aircraft above our airspace. He mistakenly dropped Aircraft X.A few minutes later, I was relieved of position and busy taking the position brief for R2 control position. The new R1 TRACON Data Controller took a call from Lone Rock and was asked if he talking to Aircraft X. He, of course did not know who they were talking about since the aircraft was a splat with no information. The R1 Controller asked me if I knew who that was, and I not hearing with the noise in the TRACON, said something like, 'Of course not, that was a point out, I was thinking they were talking about the point out I took on Aircraft Y. Shortly after, the R2 controller figured out the splat was one of our aircraft and took corrective action to avoid the two aircraft getting any closer.The NOTAM that was produced for departing aircraft from OSH during EAA Experimental Aircraft Association contributed to this. Expecting dozens of aircraft to pick up IFR flight over DLL VOR at the same point at the same time is inviting loss of separation. Many aircraft filed incorrectly, leading to much frequency congestion. One pilot in particular, during my following 30 minutes on the R2 scope wanted to argue with me that he filed correctly, when he didn't. Several aircraft were in Lone Rock and Dubuque sectors looking to pick up their IFR, requiring further point outs and coordination. Several aircraft required 6/10 [Flight Plan] amendments in order to gain their flight plans. Most aircraft were at same altitudes and required valuable frequency time for separation, to ensure they were at correct altitudes and separated from other IFR aircraft. In short, the EAA Air Adventure is a set up for controllers at my facility. The loss of IFR separation is almost inevitable given the volume, complexity and inherent confusion at certain heavy periods. There is probably no recommendation I can give other than tell a certain number of aircraft to pick up IFR at different points, or just have them fly VFR."
ASRS:1831234.s: A TRACON Data controller failed to notice a supervisor dropping the tag for Aircraft X, causing a loss of radar identification during a point-out coordination. The incident was attributed to high traffic volume and flight plan errors during the EAA Air Adventure, which created frequency congestion and separation risks.

ASRS:1831246.n: Aircraft X was 12 miles Northwest of ZZZ on a base heading 220 at 3,000 feet being vectored to the ILS Runway XXR at ZZZ airport. I observed an unidentified VFR target depart ZZZ1 airport climbing out of 1,700 feet southbound. At first the the target was flying away from Aircraft X but then I observed the target start a a turn to the east. I then assigned Aircraft X heading 250 anticipating the VFR target would make a turn to the north east to avoid the immediate incursion into the ZZZ Class C airspace. This caused Aircraft X to go through the final for Runway XXR and I climbed Aircraft X to 3,100 feet because the new projected flight path would be into a higher Minimum Vectoring Altitude. I then anticipated the VFR target would turn east bound once it got north of the Class C. So I took Aircraft Y off the arrival who was 10 miles north west of the airport on the downwind. I stopped his descent at 5,000 feet when I would normally descend aircraft at this phase of flight to 3,000 feet. It then became apparent the altitude adjustment wasn't going to be enough so I turned Aircraft Y to a 220 heading. The VFR target did make a turn to the east once north of the Class C climbing opposite direction into our arrival corridor at ZZZ. The VFR target did eventually contact another controller for an IFR pickup in my airspace.This event only had a positive outcome because this happens so frequently I have become overly cautious and I guessed correctly what the non participating aircraft was going to do every step of the way. I could have easily guessed wrong and could have had a dangerous situation develop into a crash. I recommend an airspace change that would extend controlled airspace over ZZZ1.
ASRS:1831246.s: An air traffic controller vectored Aircraft X and diverted Aircraft Y to avoid an unidentified VFR aircraft departing ZZZ1 that climbed into the ZZZ arrival corridor. The controller attributed the safe outcome to anticipating the VFR pilot's turns and recommended extending controlled airspace over ZZZ1 to prevent future incursions.

ASRS:1831256.n: Air return due to pirep telling us we had a 6 foot flame coming out of engine 2 on takeoff.Mid-way down the runway for takeoff, a regional aircraft 'other carrier flagged', stated 'using the afterburners, huh?' Since we were empty (no Passengers, and not much fuel), we were accelerating quickly, and thus his comments made sense. Upon rotation, the Tower asked the regional aircraft, 'what was that you said'. To which he responded, 'looks like (Company) is using afterburners, a six-foot flame was coming out of the back of the #2 engine'. Upon reaching clean up altitude, we ran all the appropriate checklists, and returned back to ZZZ. The fire trucks were called by ATC, and they performed an inspection upon taxiing clear of the runway. We were cleared to taxi to the gate, and the event was entered in the logbook, and Maintenance and Dispatch, and the Chief Pilots were notified.The regional aircraft could have been more clear in his comments, and we could have aborted the takeoff at low speed.
ASRS:1831256.s: A pilot reported a six-foot flame from engine 2 on takeoff, noted by a regional aircraft as afterburner use. The crew returned to ZZZ, where fire trucks inspected the aircraft; the pilot noted the regional's unclear call prevented an early abort.

ASRS:1831286.n: Halfway through our flight our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us. When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley. Additionally, our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and having a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell. Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything. No Passengers were indicating concern and we didn't smell anything. The Captain asked the Flight Attendant (F/A) if she was medically concerned, and if so, we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern. All the F/As indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic. They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ. At that point the Captain told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor. We also contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before. Additionally, we informed Dispatch that the F/As were not comfortable taking the aircraft on our next leg. Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC to get F/As, operations and medic on the line for a conference call. During their discussion, Dispatch sent us an ACARS message to divert to ZZZ1. As a result, we notified ATC of our intention to divert. The Captain notified the F/As and Passengers of our intent, as well.As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke, Fire, or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke, Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated. Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before with antimicrobial spray. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing, taxi, and at the gate. We kept in constant communication with the A F/A to constantly reassess our situation. On our descent into ZZZ1 medic recommended the two Flight Attendants having issues breathing use the portable oxygen. With that information, we [advised] ATC to have Medical Personnel standing by. We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.The anti-microbial spray the night before was a bit much. That needs to be more regulated. I think the call to divert was a good call, but happened very fast. Our Crew day also ended up being super long with this diversion on our first leg. We were OK to continue after the diversion, but that kind of day, with what we went through, is probably not completely safe.
ASRS:1831286.s: The crew diverted to ZZZ1 due to a strong antimicrobial spray odor in the aft galley that caused two flight attendants breathing difficulties. Dispatch confirmed the aircraft was sprayed the night before, prompting the diversion and medical standby, though the crew landed uneventfully after following fume checklists.

ASRS:1831299.n: Ramp cleared us to push for spot 1XX on ramp short of taxiway 1. Upon completion of the After Start Checklist, ATC clearance instructed us to taxi to runway XXR via Taxiway 2 short of taxiway 3. After reading back the taxi instructions, Captain cleared the left side of the aircraft's path as I cleared the right side. As he powered up to make our way out of the ramp area before reaching taxiway 1, I noticed a grey airport operations vehicle approaching from right to left on the service road at a high speed. I immediately told Captain to watch out for the car as it did not appear to be slowing down. He did not hear me the first call, so I said it again and instructed him to stop for the high speed car now about to pass directly in front of us. Captain immediately got on the brakes to stop the aircraft as the port car finally noticed we were taxiing out and slammed on his brakes swerving to the right to avoid a collision. I then told ground control of the car cutting us off informing him of the cars color and identification number. He then told us that they will take care of it and gave us taxi instructions once again for the departure runway. After completing the after start checklist and beginning our taxi, FO warned me a car was approaching quickly and was not stopping. The car swerved to avoid us hitting him and I abruptly applied the brakes. After bringing the airplane to a stop, I called the flight attendants to see if there were any injuries. I was told there were none. After telling the ground controller what had happened, we continued our taxi. I made a pa at cruise altitude informing the passengers what had occurred. About three hours into the flight, I was informed that a Flight Attendant injured herself when she fell into the galley divider from the hard braking. I then informed dispatch and they called med link on my behalf. After arriving in ZZZ1, I contacted the duty manager. The car was a gray airport operations vehicle.
ASRS:1831299.s: During taxi after pushback, a First Officer warned the Captain of a high-speed grey airport operations vehicle approaching on a service road. The Captain applied brakes to avoid a collision, but the hard stop caused a Flight Attendant to fall and injure herself in the galley.

ASRS:1831345.n: During takeoff roll, FO (First Officer) seat became unlatched horizontally, causing FO to slide aft. As pilot monitoring, I assumed control of the aircraft and steered us back to runway center line until FO was ready to assume control again. Seat not properly locked horizontally. Latching mechanism possibly in need of adjustment. Double-checking seat lock with a good 'shove' prior to departure. Also closer maintenance inspection of seat latches may be warranted.
ASRS:1831345.s: During takeoff roll, the First Officer's seat unlatched horizontally, causing the pilot to slide aft and requiring the pilot monitoring to assume control. The reporter attributed the incident to a seat not properly locked and suggested maintenance inspection of the latching mechanism.

ASRS:1831349.n: Immediately after takeoff, the horizontal trim failed. Neither pilot could activate the electric trim. The manual trim wheels were used to keep the aircraft in a trimmed condition, though with a significant amount of difficulty possibly due to the trim motor clutching against the manual inputs. The Stabilizer Trim Inoperative QRH procedures were followed. [We advised ATC] and the flight returned to ZZZ for an uneventful flaps 15 landing.I don't know why the electric horizontal trim failed. I do know that the manual trim was significantly more difficult to operate during this event than it had been in previous instances where I've had to use the manual trim wheels. The aircraft was never too far out of trimmed condition, but a strong binding was felt as we rotated the trim wheels. It was suggested to me after the event that this binding sensation was in fact the trim motor 'clutching' against the manual inputs. I'm not a strongman, but I worry that two smaller, weaker pilots might have found themselves in extremis.Figure out why the manual trim wheels felt as if they were binding, and correct that design condition. Everything that occurred prior to the time we became aware of the Stab trim failure was normal and uneventful. Shortly after Takeoff, the Captain said his stab trim didn't seem to be working and asked me to check mine. My stab trim was also inoperative. There were no other secondary issues. We continued with the departure while reviewing/going through the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative procedure. Once we had gone through the QRH procedure, we [advised ATC] and returned uneventfully to ZZZ where we wrote up the problem. We were given a new airplane about an hour later and continued our trip to ZZZ1. Cause, unknown maintenance issue.
ASRS:1831349.s: Pilots experienced an inoperative electric horizontal trim shortly after takeoff, requiring difficult manual trim operation likely caused by motor clutching. The crew followed QRH procedures, returned to ZZZ for a safe landing, and attributed the failure to an unknown maintenance issue.

ASRS:1831420.n: We were climbing out of DEN on the EEONS 8. Crossed HIDEF at 10,000 feet and started the climb again. We started to pick up wake turbulence from the 777 in front of us through about 11,000 feet. We received a call from ATC for traffic northeast of us as we were coming through 11,500 feet. We started looking for the traffic and when I looked back inside we were going through 12,000 feet about 1-2 miles prior to SHOBO. We began correcting back to 12,000 feet. Max altitude was about 12,300 feet. No call or mention of the deviation from ATC. While climbing out on flight from DEN via EEONS8 departure from 34L, we were given a traffic call from ATC as we neared SHOBO. At the same time, we encountered wake turbulence from a heavy aircraft on the same departure. As Pilot Monitoring, I was looking north for traffic as the aircraft was responding to the turbulence and controlling the aircraft. Simultaneously, we neared SHOBO, which has a no higher than 12,000 feet restriction. PIC called altitude at approx 250 feet above the restriction, and smoothly leveled, then began descent to maintain 12,000 feet until passing SHOBO, then resumed climb. No ATC comm was received during this time.
ASRS:1831420.s: The crew climbing from DEN on the EEONS 8 departure encountered wake turbulence from a preceding 777 and received a traffic call near SHOBO. This distraction caused an unintentional climb to 12,300 feet, exceeding the 12,000-foot restriction, which the pilots corrected without ATC notification.

ASRS:1831462.n: Aircraft X had maintenance after block out for right pack failed. Crew and I identified MEL that could be applied as part of the process, but one of the provisions of the MEL was that there could be no dry ice carried on the aircraft. Aircraft X was carrying over 500kg of dry ice, so no option but to return to the gate to have the dry ice taken off. Maintenance problem with the aircraft.
ASRS:1831462.s: Aircraft X experienced a right pack failure after block out. The crew returned to the gate to remove over 500kg of dry ice because the applicable MEL prohibited carrying it with the inoperative pack.

ASRS:1831529.n: I set up for the visual to Runway XX backed up with the ILS into ZZZ. The approach met stable approach criteria and landed at approximately 85 knots. Upon landing with all three gear down, the left gear began shaking. I assumed I had a flat tire as we started to drift left slightly. I applied brakes and right rudder, neither of which rectified the situation. The aircraft then continued to roll off to the left of the runway. We hit the grass and the gear caught and we spun around 180 degrees. I notified ATC and shut down the engines. I then called company to inform them that I was off the runway and needed the FBO to bring their passenger van. I asked the passengers if they were okay and explained I thought we had a flat tire. A passenger then informed me my left tire was on the runway about 500 feet further down. I helped the passengers get off the aircraft and told them to stay behind the wing. They all said they were uninjured and were brought to the Gate XX where our agents met them. I stayed with the aircraft and got in contact with Maintenance. When I returned to the terminal I wrote up the aircraft for the tire coming off and the aircraft departing paved surface. I was asked to go back and take more photos of the tire. FBO mechanics came awhile later and were able to get a spare tire on. They said half of the rim was missing so operations and fire went back to the landing spot where they found part of the rim and a handful of pieces of the landing gear all over the runway. The aircraft was towed to the hangar and I left the pieces with the log book with operations in ZZZ.
ASRS:1831529.s: The pilot landed an aircraft on Runway XX when the left main gear tire separated, causing the aircraft to veer off the runway, strike grass, and spin 180 degrees. No injuries occurred, but the gear rim and components were scattered on the runway, requiring the aircraft to be towed to a hangar for repairs.

ASRS:1831546.n: At cruise, I adjusted my lap belt and the left hand portion of the belt came loose from the seat pan. I was able to locate the nut and washer that had completely detached from the bolt, and I reattached the belt assembly by hand. I entered this discrepancy in the aircraft logbook, advising that the assembly was only hand tightened. I felt this was a safety issue, as I could have been injured if we had performed a rejected takeoff, or if we had encountered severe turbulence. FAA regulations state I need to wear my lap belt at all times while in my seat. I reattached the lap belt by hand so that I would have some degree of safety and protection. I don't know how this nut backed off the bolt holding my lap belt to the seat. Other A321 aircraft in our fleet should probably be inspected. Other A321 aircraft in our fleet should be inspected for lap belt security. It looked like a lock nut type fastener that obviously failed during service. I will be giving my lap belts a firm pull to check security from now on.
ASRS:1831546.s: A pilot reported that during cruise on an A321, the left lap belt detached from the seat pan due to a failed lock nut fastener. The pilot manually reattached the assembly, logged the discrepancy, and recommended fleet inspections for similar belt security issues.

ASRS:1831566.n: ADS B OUT L and loss of GPS position. [Caused by] GPS jamming.
ASRS:1831566.s: The crew experienced a loss of ADS-B OUT L and GPS position due to GPS jamming.

ASRS:1831572.n: After an uneventful departure from ZZZ runway XX we followed the departure instructions and were told to contact approach. Once in contact with approach for approximately 1 minute we received an audio and visual message indicating 'trim in motion'. FO (First Officer) in the right seat was flying, and I reached down to engage the trim interrupt button. The audio and visual messages went away as I was hovering over the button, so FO attempted to manually re-trim. The trim motor didn't seem to move on his command, and about 5 seconds later it continued to trim nose up. After initial indications that it was trimming up again I engaged the trim interrupt, and ran the QRH as FO kept positive control of the aircraft. The trim was about halfway up on the indicator, and FO indicated he was not having issue in controlling the aircraft. The QRH led us to disable the main trim motor, and we were able to use the alternate stab trim. After completion of the QRH vectors back to landing was uneventful. We advised ATC of the issue about 1 minute after it occurred, and there was no delay in them vectoring us back to ZZZ.
ASRS:1831572.s: The crew experienced an uncommanded nose-up trim event shortly after departure from ZZZ. They engaged the trim interrupt, followed the QRH to disable the main motor, and used alternate trim to return for an uneventful landing.

ASRS:1831587.n: Master Warning illuminated with CAB ALT annunciation came on through 14,000 feet.
ASRS:1831587.s: The crew reported a Master Warning and CAB ALT annunciation illuminating while the aircraft was below 14,000 feet. The narrative does not specify the cause or outcome of this event.

ASRS:1831588.n: I touched down at ZZZ and just like always, pushed my flap lever up to zero and reached over and pulled the condition lever to low idle. I was rolling on the runway and getting ready to turn around and back-taxi, but needed some momentum for the turn, so I reached down while looking outside and pushed the condition lever to high idle. When I did that, I heard it click through the gate. I looked down and noticed it was in low idle and the annunciator panel was lit up with several warning lights. At that point I realized that I had just pushed the condition lever from cut-off to low idle. I immediately pulled it back to cut-off, but the ITT temp was already up at the 1090 red line. Black smoke started rolling out of the exhaust. I then shifted my focus to getting passengers off the airplane. I turned around and announced that we had to get out of the airplane. There was a woman with children aboard. She started unbuckling the children. I grabbed the fire extinguisher and ran around to open the air stair door. I got the passengers off the airplane and to the side of the runway. I then went back to the airplane with the fire extinguisher, but by that time the black smoke had stopped rolling out of the exhaust. No flames were ever evident. I did not discharge the fire extinguisher. After making sure nothing was on fire, I retrieved the passengers' coats from the airplane. The agent arrived on his four-wheeler, along with a man in a pickup. The passengers got into the pickup while I contacted center to let them know there was a disabled airplane on the runway. With the help of the agent and the man in the pickup, we towed the airplane off the runway and on to the ramp. Once on the ramp, we unloaded the passengers' bags and the mail. The agent took charge of the mail. After a brief discussion with the agent about how best to secure the airplane, I started making phone calls to all the appropriate people (dispatch, maintenance, maintenance control, center to let them know the runway was clear). While talking with maintenance they had me try a dry motor of the engine. I could hear the starter motor attempting to turn and see a voltage drop, but the engine did not turn (Ng stayed at zero). When the [airport worker] showed up, he told me there were tie-downs behind the building at the end of the ramp. He had an aviation band radio in his truck, and we kept in constant contact on the CTAF frequency while he was towing me. He helped me tow the airplane to that end of the ramp. The tie-downs were very close to the airport fence, so I made sure he stopped well clear of the fence in a position from which we could push the plane back into the tie-down spot. It took us about 10 minutes of pushing and resting, but we got the airplane into the tie-down spot. As I was securing the airplane, maintenance control called. I told them I would give them a call back as soon as I had the plane secured. I secured it to the tie-downs with cargo straps. I installed the tail-stand, pitot covers, prop-tie, chocks, rudder lock, and cowl plugs, then closed the inertial separator. Dispatch diverted a pilot to come pick me up and once he arrived, I took the chocks from his airplane to chock the co-pilot side wheels as well. After securing the airplane I called maintenance control back. After briefing them about what happened on the runway and telling them about the results of the attempt at motoring the engine, they concluded they would initiate a plan to replace the engine. I took photos of the secured airplane and of the interior of the engine compartment on both sides. I saw no immediate evidence of fire or fire damage.
ASRS:1831588.s: The pilot inadvertently moved the condition lever from cut-off to low idle during the landing roll at ZZZ, causing an engine overheat and black smoke. Passengers were evacuated, the aircraft was towed to the ramp, and maintenance determined the engine required replacement.

ASRS:1831614.n: We had just started boarding when the Captain called to the back of the aircraft and asked if we smelled anything unusual. I could smell an oil/chemical smell. We then deplaned the pax that had boarded and we got off the aircraft.
ASRS:1831614.s: Cabin crew and the Captain detected an oil/chemical smell during boarding. The crew deplaned passengers and evacuated the aircraft.

ASRS:1831646.n: Recently FDK completed its Runway 5/23 extension from 5,219 ft to 5,819 feet. The next chart cycle date reflected the runway/taxiway markings. As of cycle 2108, all of the FDK airport diagram and approach charts now show the runway 5/23 at 5,219 ft again. The reasoning from the airport manager was the FAA approach plate 'people' said that since they have not done an approach assessment (to be performed in March of 2022), that they would not allow the runway to be shown as extended, and the group unilaterally changed all airport/approach charts to show the runway shortened, but with a 600 feet relocated threshold and a taxiway leading up to the new unmarked runway threshold in cycle 2108. Cycle 2107, the previous cycle, properly showed the runway's extension. Also to note, the RNAV approach that services Runway 5 has been NOTAMed NA since the completion of the runway extension. Fun to note, that the RNAV approach was allowed when the runway was shortened by about 500 feet to 4,700 feet during runway extension construction without a NOTAM showing un-coincidental glideslope/PAPI relationship. This is no longer an issue, although it was brought up by local based charter pilots as being unsafe and improper.The following instances may occur. An aircraft landing Runway 23 at night, may rightfully assume they have 600 feet past the Runway 5 threshold markings to exit at Taxiway A1, when in fact, there is no pavement past the Runway 5 threshold. This can cause a runway excursion by confusion of the actual markings and the chart diagram. Aircraft may proceed onto Runway 5 from Taxiway A1 to pull up to the 600 foot relocated threshold, causing a runway incursion. May cause pilot confusion or disorientation when a pilot lands or departs runway 5/23. Changing a diagram that does not depict the actual markings without a proper NOTAM or notification by the Tower is extremely reckless behavior and should not be tolerated as standard practice.Requested Fix: NOTAM the runway length to 5,819 feet, NOTAM to disregard the relocated threshold and revert the airport diagram and all approach charts to the Cycle 2107 depiction of the airport diagram/layout. Do not allow the FAA Approach Office to unilaterally change the airport diagram's of airports without concurrence of all related parties, and if the FAA Approach office does not have the concurrence, the office should perform a good faith effort to mitigate all safety issues.
ASRS:1831646.s: A reporter reported that FAA Approach Office personnel unilaterally reverted FDK Runway 5/23 charts to a shortened length in Cycle 2108 despite a physical extension to 5,819 feet. This discrepancy between charts and actual markings creates risks of runway excursions and incursions due to pilot confusion regarding the relocated threshold.

ASRS:1831655.n: Upon landing at home base (ZZZ) oil was noted on the cowling of the number 1 engine. I elected to stay running and send the crew to tell the mechanic to come look at the leak. The crew returned and informed me that the mechanic was aware of the leak and that it was in limits.My concern was raised as I wondered how can he determine from inside the hangar that this is the same leak, or at the same rate without a visual inspection.I shut down the aircraft and approached the mechanic with those concerns, he stated he was to busy to look into it any further. I wrote the leak up and informed him of such, he stated 'I'll just sign that off'20 minutes later, without having me run the aircraft up, the mechanic handed me the logbook with the write up signed off with appropriate references that state that the aircraft was run up and the mechanic performed a visual inspection in accordance with the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM). As I was the only pilot on duty, and I did not run up the aircraft, it is my opinion that my logbook was falsified in order to maintain an in service rate. I informed management of this and they said there is nothing they could do.
ASRS:1831655.s: The pilot reported an oil leak on a rotorcraft's number 1 engine after landing, but the mechanic allegedly falsified the logbook by signing off a required run-up and visual inspection without performing them. Management refused to act on the pilot's report of the falsified maintenance record.

ASRS:1831656.n: [Priority handling was requested] with ZZZ Center on an IFR flight plan. [This] was requested because of a total loss of electrical power in the cockpit. I maintained radio contact with center for a few minutes and advised them that I was deviating to ZZZ (the nearest airport) I gave them my personal information and canceled my flight plan once on the ground. There was no destruction of property or injuries to report.
ASRS:1831656.s: The pilot experienced a total loss of cockpit electrical power while on an IFR flight plan with ZZZ Center. The pilot diverted to the nearest airport, ZZZ, and canceled the flight plan upon landing with no injuries or property damage.

ASRS:1831657.n: I'm a new CFI with 475 hours total time and 6 hours instructing. I was approached by another CFI that teaches at a local flight school to see if I was interested in doing part time instruction. He instructs in a Piper PA-28-161. We scheduled to meet. Two days prior I sent the CFI a message asking what I could do to prepare for the flight and if there was a specific lesson I should be prepared to teach. He called me the day prior to the flight and said there was nothing to prepare for, 'we're just going flying'. He then asked if I could instruct a student that day. I said no based on not having any experience in their aircraft, personal insurance in their aircraft, or proof of employment. On the day of the flight, I arrived as scheduled. The CFI/Pilot in Command was already at the airplane with a 'new' student. This was to be the students 'intro' flight. They had already preflighted the airplane. I sat in the back seat. The CFI/Pilot in Command took off with window and top of door not latched. I reminded him while we were taking the active runway but he said there was a law on this aircraft that they could takeoff with the door all the way open. Once we took off he gave his student the flight controls. The CFI/Pilot in Command asked his student if he had ever touched a cloud. The student said no, and the CFI/Pilot in Command took the controls. He immediately flew next to a cloud and had the student stick his hand out the window. We were flying in a broken layer. He then asked the student to fly directly between two clouds, which had a very narrow gap, definitely not within legal cloud clearances. At this point I asked if there was any traffic awareness and found out there was no traffic advisory or ADSB on the aircraft. After approximately 20 minutes, we full stop landed at ZZZ and the CFI/Pilot in Command asked me to move to the front seat. I asked, 'left or right'? He said, 'actually get used to the right seat please.' I asked if I could sit left for the first time since this was a different model Piper than I have previously flown with somewhat different avionics. He said 'no, sit in the right. This isn't an evaluation, I'm flying.' The student sat in the back seat. The CFI/Pilot in Command performed the takeoff and then gave me the flight controls at 300 feet. During our climb to 7000 feet I noticed that the Alternator Amps read 0. I alerted the CFI/Pilot in Command who pulled out the checklist and asked me what that meant if the alternator failed. I said, 'that means we have roughly 30 minutes of battery life left and we should head back to the airport.' He told me the alternator failed last night on a long cross-country trip and their maintenance technician didn't have time to come inspect it today, but not to worry because they had a second battery besides the main. He also showed me how he cycled the on/off switch and that power was restored. He went on to say that they bought and installed 'crappy overhauled alternator' which was likely the issue. We stayed within 15 miles of ZZZ and the CFI/Pilot in Command asked me to demonstrate stalls. He then took a map from the backseat and covered the entire instrument panel, restricting my view to standby instruments or even the tachometer. I said 'I'm not going to do a stall without being able to see my rudder.' He told me it was an outside maneuver and I didn't need any instruments to do it. I stated again, 'I'm not kidding, I'm not doing it without my instruments. I've never done that before and I do not want to get into a spin.' He reluctantly took the map down. I demonstrated a stall and then he did multiple falling leaf stalls on his own to show how I didn't need my instruments. At this point he asked me to demonstrate a falling leaf and when the power was pulled I heard the engine choke slightly. At this point we were getting very far over the ocean and I said I was done with stalls and wanted to go back toward shore and ZZZ. He took the controls at thispoint.He then asked the student (now in the back seat), 'do you think (my name) ever played the toilet paper game?' I asked what it was and he told me I was about to find out. He then flew out over the water and dropped two rolls of toilet paper out the window. He then pulled the power and in a nose-diving turn aimed right between the two falling rolls. The goal he said was to hit the toilet paper on the wing. He gave me controls at one point, but I told him my fear of the toilet paper getting in the cowling and he said it wasn't an issue. He got down to 2500 feet and I told him I didn't want to go any lower over the ocean. He said we were taking it down to 1500 feet. Then we flew back to ZZZ and he told the tower he wanted to do a go around. He told the student that we were going to float over the runway at 6 inches. We did this until we got to the 1,000-foot bars on the departure end of the runway when I told him to add power and start going around. He flew it all the way to the numbers and then finally pulled up. I thought we were going to crash as this was so last minute.He then asked me if I wanted the controls and I said yes. We stayed in the pattern. When he asked tower for another go-around, I called them back saying it was going to be a full stop. He questioned my decision and I told him I wanted to end the flight. After we landed, I noticed there was zero fuel indicated in our right tank and the left was reading full. This had to be incorrect as I visually checked the tank prior to flight and it was half full. As the flight progressed I felt more and more unsafe. By the end of the flight I was sure that mine and the students safety were in jeopardy and I can't help feeling that I should have done more to stop it.
