ASRS:1831657.s: A new CFI observed a Piper PA-28-161 flight where the instructor operated with an unlatched door, no traffic awareness, and a known alternator failure while performing unsafe maneuvers like cloud penetration and dropping objects. The reporter terminated the flight due to escalating safety risks, including low-altitude ocean flying and a near-miss go-around, citing the instructor's disregard for regulations and equipment status.

ASRS:1831663.n: During the second leg of our day on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 sudden turbulence was encountered. Approximately 3.5 hours into the flight while descending through an estimated 27,000 feet, we felt a bump which we both agreed was likely Clear Air Turbulence. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. The aircraft was not adversely or noticeably affected in its ability to fly and no buffet or shudder was noted in the flight controls. After landing and unloading the line crew notified me that the right engine cowling was missing. Upon further inspection it was noted that the right engine cowling was in fact missing and the horizontal stabilizer had likely been struck at the time the engine cowling separated from the aircraft. The flight was from ZZZ to ZZZ1. After preflight inspection, we had an uneventful takeoff out of ZZZ. At an altitude between 35,000 feet and 25,000 feet during the descent we hit momentarily clear air turbulence. We both agreed that it was turbulence. We continued our descent into ZZZ1 as briefed. After a normal approach and landing we parked the aircraft then assisted the passengers with their bags and they went on the way. On post flight walk around we discovered the right engine cowling was missing and a small dent in the leading edge of the tail of the aircraft. That is when we suspected that the clear air turbulence was caused by the right engine cowl departing the aircraft. ZZZ Tower, our company operations manager, and the FAA were then notified.
ASRS:1831663.s: Pilots reported that during descent through 27,000 feet on a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, sudden turbulence occurred. Post-flight inspection revealed the right engine cowling was missing and had likely struck the horizontal stabilizer, causing the turbulence.

ASRS:1831665.n: I departed ZZZ shortly after XA00 from runway XX, heading west. Shortly after I put my gear up at approximately 100 knots airspeed and a couple hundred feet of altitude the engine started to run rough and appeared to be losing power. I made an immediate left turn to return to the runway. I was planning to land on runway XX however, the engine appeared to be losing power and airspeed. I lowered the nose to maintain airspeed and decided to attempt to make it to runway 6 with the runway lights visible. I felt that I was too low to make the runway and raised the nose to gain some attitude and give up some airspeed. At which time i heard a felt a loud bang and immediate vibration. After that point I pointed the aircraft towards the runway lights, dropped the landing gear. Although this all happened very quickly, I think a couple of minutes or so it felt as though the engine was intermittently losing and gaining power.After I landed about mid field, I was able to brake and maintain control. The vibration was mild and the engine continued to run. I stopped on the taxi way just off the runway and checked the engine gauges, verifying good oil pressure and temperature and fuel flow, was normal. I taxied to my hanger.Inspection revealed some dents in the left wing, engine cowling and damage to the 3 propeller blades. I called [an FBO] and explained the incident. He brought a replacement prop and installed it. Shortly after this I started the engine and did a run up which was all normal and smooth. I then flew the plane a couple of miles to [the FBO]. Further inspection revealed some vegetation in and around the wing gap seals. Although I did not see what I hit. I suspect it was a tree top somewhere off the airport property.
ASRS:1831665.s: The pilot experienced engine roughness and power loss shortly after takeoff, followed by a loud bang and vibration while attempting to return to the airport. Post-flight inspection revealed propeller and wing damage caused by suspected impact with a tree top, though the engine ran normally after repairs.

ASRS:1831672.n: I was traveling eastbound over the south end of ZZZ 4800 feet under broken cumulus clouds at 6500 feet. I was monitoring the ZZZ1 glider CTAF flying with Mode S transponder squawking 1202. I monitor Fore-flight to provide TFR's and NOTAMs. No TFR's or NOTAMs were noted. A falling skydiver appeared at 11 o'clock out of the cloud deck. I attempted to turn right and another appeared at 3 o'clock. Then it appeared a half dozen or so were falling around and past me out of the clouds. I continued east to leave the area and then saw skydivers under canopy headed north toward the airport ahead of me. They had fallen in the blue sky area south of the airport. I may have passed one closer than 500 feet but can't say for sure. Next I saw the Drop plane headed north to the airport in front of me wag his wings acknowledging he had seen me. I could not see the jump aircraft before the jumpers exited the aircraft at 12000 feet or so, because they were above the cloud I was flying under. Many of the jumpers fell through the cloud and I did not see them until they fell clear 1500 ft above me.ZZZ TRACON was probably monitoring the operation however failed to see my transponder or provide alerts to traffic in the area not listening to approach control. It is impossible to see and avoid jumpers falling through clouds. It is impossible to see the jump aircraft above the clouds.Jump operations should not be allowed in uncontrolled airspace with clouds when see and avoid rules are to be followed.
ASRS:1831672.s: A pilot flying eastbound at 6,500 feet encountered multiple skydivers falling from 12,000 feet through clouds, potentially passing within 500 feet. The reporter attributed the near-miss to the inability to see jumpers or the drop aircraft through clouds and criticized ZZZ TRACON for failing to alert traffic in uncontrolled airspace.

ASRS:1831683.n: We were at TPA (Traffic Pattern Altitude) (1000 ft.) and had entered a direct downwind Runway XXL as instructed by ZZZ Tower. Aircraft departing XXL, Aircraft X, did not comply with their departure instructions and began a crosswind departure in our direction. Tower called 'Aircraft X, fly runway heading, you were instructed to turn left at the river. Traffic 12 o clock, one thousand.' The aircraft responded 'We were cleared for a left standard departure' and Aircraft Y continued their climbing turn straight at us approaching our same altitude. TCAS alerted traffic. I had to take controls and immediately descended to the right away from the aircraft down to 700 ft. as they climbed above us. As Aircraft Y passed over they called Tower 'Below traffic in sight'.
ASRS:1831683.s: The pilot at 1,000 ft. TPA on downwind for Runway XXL descended to 700 ft. after Aircraft X ignored left-turn instructions and climbed straight toward them. The conflict, caused by Aircraft X's non-compliance with departure clearance, triggered a TCAS alert and required immediate evasive action.

ASRS:1831686.n: Left gear collapsed upon landing. A part failed and allowed the gear to go up. I lowered the gear on downwind, all indicators showed gear down and locked. Upon touchdown, I slowly veered off the runway to the left. I immediately communicated my situation on the radio, still all indicators showed gear down and locked.
ASRS:1831686.s: The pilot reported that the left landing gear collapsed upon landing due to a part failure that allowed the gear to retract, despite indicators showing it down and locked. The aircraft veered off the runway to the left after touchdown, and the pilot immediately communicated the situation while indicators remained unchanged.

ASRS:1831720.n: I was doing a training flight with my student. Our first four touch and goes went fairly smooth. The fourth touch and go we landed, cleaned up our flaps, visually checked our left flap was up, and added power. I was taught to visually check our flaps to make sure the motor works. I checked my left one and the motor was working. Previous flight instructors never stressed the importance of checking both flaps before taking off in case of a rod failure. I am not sure when our right flap rod broke. Our take off and landing appeared normal. After climbing 50 feet, we rolled to the left. I added right rudder to counter the roll and regain aircraft control. We made a much smaller pattern to get back to the runway we took off from. Our climb performance was poor. I made sure to keep airspeed up knowing if we stalled we would spin with the asymmetrical flaps. We safely landed without any damage to ourselves or airplane. Maintenance on the field replaced the rod on the same day and deemed the rod failure was metal fatigue. There were no signs of over-sped flaps. Although some POHs allow the first notch of flaps above the white arc, I stress to my students to never put in flaps if above the white arc. It is very easy to add too much flaps. Other instructors at the school do not teach it the same way as I do. Although not confirmed, I personally believe this could have caused the metal fatigue and the rod finally decided to give up during our flight.
ASRS:1831720.s: A flight instructor and student experienced a left roll after takeoff due to a right flap rod failure caused by metal fatigue. The pilot maintained control with rudder input and executed a safe landing with no damage, suspecting excessive flap usage above the white arc contributed to the failure.

ASRS:1831723.n: Departed ZZZ VFR. Our destination airport was ZZZ1. Standard FAA Telephone Weather Briefing was conducted by co-pilot. That information [was] High Pressure, No Significant Weather, Winds Aloft at planned Altitude - 7 knots. NOTAMS/TFRs Checked. Flight Planned distance was 440 miles. Altitude was 6,500 feet. Engine was Leaned as per Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH). Aircraft Fuel Gauges were Operational. At 15 miles from ZZZ1 the Engine began to Sputter. I positioned the Mixture Control to Full Rich, Turned On Aux pump (A) and switched fuel tanks. The Engine Came Back Alive.3 Minutes Later, the engine began to sputter again. I switched to AUX Pump 2. The engine came back alive momentarily, then quit. At this point, I was descending at L/D Max Whilst Looking for a suitable landing site. A country highway was selected, and used. The off airport landing was uneventful. No Injuries or damage to equipment or property occurred.I telephoned the FAA right-away, and advised them of the situation. After FAA Approval, we put fuel in airplane, [officials] blocked [the] road, and I took off (solo) Flying the airplane to ZZZ1. At ZZZ1 an FAA Field Inspector met me, and I gave him a written statement of the events. The airplane has 'Engine Blow-BY'. The oil turns black in 15 hours of operation. The manual (1979 Aircraft X) 'Book Performance Values' are not accurate. The Engine was Consuming 11.1 Gallons per hour, that should not be. I should have stopped for fuel sooner! Do not believe older owner airplane manuals/POHs. If fuel guages read low to empty - believe them!!
ASRS:1831723.s: The pilot of a 1979 Aircraft X experienced engine sputtering and failure at 15 miles from destination due to excessive fuel consumption and inaccurate POH data. The pilot executed an uneventful off-airport landing on a highway with no injuries or damage.

ASRS:1831728.n: I was preparing to conduct a Part 91 IFR flight from OAK. My clearance was Runway 30, CNDEL4 Departure EBAYE AVE EHF and to climb via the SID. Upon reaching Runway 30, I was holding on Taxiway Whiskey behind an A321. After the A321 started its takeoff roll, I watched and noted the point at which it lifted off. At the same time I was instructed to 'Line up and wait'. After what I thought to be a very short time, less than a minute from lining up, I was cleared for takeoff with a caution warning for wake turbulence. Upon reaching Vr and prior to the A321's rotation point, I rotated and began my initial climb. I had 1900 ft set in my Altitude Select as I was to cross LECHE at or below 2,000 ft, on a heading of 296 degrees which I had set on my DG's bug. At approximately 600 ft I engaged the autopilot. Almost immediately after entering IMC conditions at approximately 700 ft, I entered very heavy turbulence. I disengaged the autopilot at which time the plane entered an un-commanded roll to the left. I tried to recover but the plane was shaking very violently and kept wanting to violently roll to the left between 35 to 40 degrees of bank angle. The plane was really not responding to my control inputs, at least not according to my flight director. I really had no idea what was happening at the time and was very startled. At first I thought I might have a control surface failure. Then I realized that I must have flown through and was now within the A321 wake vortices. I had a very hard time controlling the aircraft. I was worried if I could not keep the plane out of an upset condition, I was way too low for a successful recovery. I could also hear that my passengers were very uncomfortable. At this point, I just reverted to flying 101, aviate, navigate, communicate. I hit my Takeoff/Go-Around switch which also disengaged the yaw damper and put my command bars at a 10 degree nose up and wings level command. At that point I was just trying to concentrate on putting the airplane symbol into the command bars and just keep wings level. All the while keeping my eye on my TCAS for any aircraft near or around me. (I never got one traffic warning or alert during this whole event). At some point a controller came on and began giving me vectors. I had not yet talked to the controllers or advised them of my situation as I had not gotten to the communicate" part yet. I was also told to squawk my assigned transponder code. I had selected the code prior to taxi but failed to enter it. At approximately 1800 feet I began to try to level the airplane but was having a hard time doing so. I did not want to push down too hard and put the plane in an excessive negative G situation. I think I passed the max altitude by 150 ft but, immediately corrected to 1800 ft. When I was switched to the next frequency I was still attempting to regain my composure and just follow the controller's instructions. The turbulence completely disappeared out of about 2,500 feet. Out of 10,000 feet, I cancelled IFR and continued VFR with flight following. The rest of the flight was uneventful until I was advised by NorCal of a possible pilot deviation and was given a phone number to call upon landing. How the problem arose: Inadvertent flight into wake turbulence. Contributing Factors: Too early release behind a heavy aircraft. IMC Conditions. Failure to ask for a possible short delay to my takeoff clearance due to wake turbulence. How it was discovered: Difficulty in controlling the aircraft due to violent and uncommanded aircraft attitudes. Corrective Actions: Maintain wings level attitude. Follow ATC Instructions. Perceptions: Fear of possible loss of control in IMC conditions and very low altitude for recovery. Judgements: Just fly the plane. Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. Decisions: Do whatever it takes to keep wings level attitude. Factors affecting the quality of human performance: The startle effect. Actions or Inactions: Have hand written, 'Enter Squawk Code';in my Pre-Taxi Checklist. Just did what I could to fly my plane out of an inadvertent but bad situation."
ASRS:1831728.s: A Part 91 pilot departing OAK on Runway 30 encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding A321 shortly after takeoff in IMC conditions. The pilot experienced violent uncommanded rolls and control difficulties at low altitude but recovered by maintaining wings level and following ATC vectors, resulting in a reported pilot deviation.

ASRS:1831731.n: Wake turbulence caused aircraft to lose 500-700 feet altitude abruptly. Maintained control of aircraft. NY Center reached out why we are descending. We advised it was from moderate/heavy wake turbulence. We were in trail of heavy aircraft landing IAD. We were cleared down to FL180 and the remainder of flight was normal.
ASRS:1831731.s: The pilot reported that wake turbulence from a heavy aircraft landing at IAD caused an abrupt 500-700 foot altitude loss while cleared to FL180. Control was maintained, NY Center was advised of the cause, and the remainder of the flight was normal.

ASRS:1831743.n: On 45 degree in bound to left downwind for Rwy 34 at 7S5 (Independence, OR), getting close to downwind turn. I was at 1,200 feet MSL which is pattern altitude. Made radio call noting distance and intent to turn downwind. A [light aircraft] took off on Rwy 34, turned crosswind, well below pattern altitude, and then started turning downwind right underneath me, still climbing as I was about to turn downwind. I took evasive [action] and turned left to miss him. He continued into the downwind, then base/final for a full stop. I left the pattern northbound and returned back to home base.
ASRS:1831743.s: A pilot on left downwind for Runway 34 at 7S5 at 1,200 feet MSL encountered a light aircraft climbing below pattern altitude directly underneath. The pilot executed a left evasive turn to avoid a collision and subsequently exited the pattern to return to home base.

ASRS:1831756.n: As my student and I where approaching ZZZ airport Aircraft Y passed behind us possibly closer than 500 feet separation.They were approaching from the right and were descending. However, they adjusted course to pass behind us.We were on 6 mile final for ZZZ and at a lower altitude in communication with Tower. Aircraft Y was on a different frequency, most likely with Approach.I do not believe safety was compromised but am filling out a report because separation was close enough that is could be borderline for the regulations.
ASRS:1831756.s: A pilot and student on 6-mile final to ZZZ reported Aircraft Y passing behind them at less than 500 feet separation while descending from the right. The reporter noted Aircraft Y was on a different frequency but believed safety was not compromised, though the separation was borderline for regulations.

ASRS:1831758.n: Loss of power in flight, precautionary landing in open field.Plane was purchased and a condition inspection was completed. A program letter was provided to FSDO and receipt was confirmed. Plane was run for an extended period of time and was being flown from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Engine operated normally for 1.5 hrs prior to issue. Engine started to lose power and small amounts of smoke were produced. The plane is a STOL plane and I elected to land in an open field instead of attempting to fly over a populated area toward the airport. There was no damage to the plane, and a normal landing was made. We requested priority handling with tower when we elected to land in grass. We were a flight of two. I was lead pilot/plane in a flight of two from ZZZ to ZZZ1.I was in contact with approach as a flight of two. The other plane referred to as 'plane 2' in the flight had engine trouble and partial loss of power. I requested priority handling for the aircraft in distress. They elected to land in an open field with no damage to plane and no injuries.The [plane] that landed in the field is a short take off and landing aircraft and equipped to land in grass. A normal landing was made.I in 'plane 1' circled over head as requested by ATC to ensure the pilot evacuated the plane safely and to report location to ATC to relay to police/emergency response.ATC was contacted via telephone by the pilot in 'plane 2' after precautionary landing
ASRS:1831758.s: A flight of two STOL aircraft experienced partial engine power loss and smoke during cruise from ZZZ to ZZZ1. The lead pilot requested priority handling, allowing the distressed aircraft to make a safe precautionary landing in an open field with no damage or injuries.

ASRS:1831771.n: Normal approach and landing at ZZZ. Normal touchdown. Shortly after the nose wheel touched down the nose gear collapsed into the wheel well. The prop contacted the runway and we slid to a stop on the runway surface. There were no injuries, no leaking fluids. damage appears confined to prop and engine.
ASRS:1831771.s: The pilot reported a nose gear collapse shortly after touchdown during a normal landing at ZZZ. The propeller contacted the runway, causing the aircraft to slide to a stop with damage confined to the prop and engine, but no injuries or fluid leaks occurred.

ASRS:1831775.n: I was holding short of runway XX on taxiway 1, and there was a light aircraft that was landing and a jet holding short of runway XX on taxiway 2. The jet was cleared for takeoff on runway XX and I radioed tower that I was ready for departure XX. The tower controller started to tell me to hold short runway XX, then gave me clearance to cross runway XX and cleared me for takeoff runway YY. When I took runway YY, I noticed what appeared to be a large vehicle past the departure end of the runway. I believed it to be on a road or parked beyond the runway. Due to the curvature of the runway, I couldn't even see the lower portion of the vehicle. Midway through my takeoff roll, I then noticed the van closer and possibly just off the end of runway YY. After I rotated, I noticed the large yellow vehicle, a utility van, was on the runway! I immediately sidestepped the runway and overflew the yellow utility van. When I looked down at it, I noticed it parked south of the runway ZZ numbers and that there was a person 15 feet south of the van looking up at me flying over. The tower never radioed me about the incident and failed to provide me any information about vehicles and personnel on the runway. The tower may have even been unaware of the situation.
ASRS:1831775.s: The pilot reported a runway incursion while taking off from runway YY, where a utility van and a person were found on the active surface. The pilot sidestepped to avoid the vehicle, noting that the tower failed to provide information about the obstruction or the incident.

ASRS:1831782.n: During cruise at 7,500 feet MSL with a properly leaned engine and (nearly) full fuel, the engine on the aircraft suddenly lost power. The engine struggled to maintain idle speed at full power. I [requested priority handling] when the fuel controls (mixture and throttle) were checked and the problem persisted. When enroute to the closest landing location it was found that the engine could be coaxed to approx 2/3 power by pumping the throttle in and out. Upon landing, a mechanic looked over the fuel system (to include sumps and fuel strainer) but found no issues. During a subsequent run-up, the engine performed as expected without issue. When the in-air engine issue occurred the outside air temperature was noted to be approximately 45 degrees. Based upon the lack of issues found with the fuel system, the subsequent successful run-up and the noted temperature, it is believed that the aircraft experienced carb-icing which caused the issue. After review with the mechanic, the aircraft was returned to service. No damage or injury was experienced as a result of this issue. Approach was notified via the approach frequency when the aircraft successfully landed and no subsequent actions/communication was requested.
ASRS:1831782.s: During cruise at 7,500 feet, the pilot reported sudden engine power loss attributed to suspected carb-icing in 45-degree temperatures. The aircraft landed safely with no damage or injury after the engine was temporarily restored by pumping the throttle, and a mechanic found no fuel system faults.

ASRS:1831783.n: The aircraft was parked and unpowered. This incident occurred during the early stages of the pre-flight. I set the parking brake thinking that accumulator was charged. Then I exited the aircraft and removed the chocks. The aircraft started to roll and impacted a vehicle parked on the ramp about 20 feet away. The way to avoid any occurrence like this is to turn on the battery and allow the hydraulic pump to charge the brake system.
ASRS:1831783.s: During pre-flight on an unpowered aircraft, the pilot removed chocks after setting the parking brake, assuming the accumulator was charged. The aircraft rolled and struck a vehicle 20 feet away because the hydraulic pump had not been activated to charge the brake system.

ASRS:1831827.n: Brand new RNAV SID has very confusing altitude constraint text, says 'top altitude assigned by ATC'. The CPDLC top altitude assigned was 7000 feet, the same as the BLOSM waypoint of 7000 feet or below on the SID. Just prior to BLOSM, ATC cleared us to 'climb via except maintain 10,000 feet.' Again very confusing clearance wording and a total setup for miscommunication. Wording should be 'after BLOSM climb and maintain 10,000 feet.'
ASRS:1831827.s: The pilot reported confusion during departure on a new RNAV SID due to conflicting altitude constraints and a poorly worded ATC clearance to "climb via except maintain 10,000 feet." The reporter stated this wording created a setup for miscommunication and recommended clearer phrasing.

ASRS:1831872.n: Issued a HAZMAT NOTAC with regard to one package containing a Fire Extinguisher Class 2.2 HAZMAT. Paperwork was completed and a verbal brief was conducted by the Pilot and Ramp. Operations Agent was issued the paperwork with applicable signatures. I made the mistake of not contacting Dispatch to have HAZMAT added to the Release. I was contacted by Dispatch via ACARS regarding the infraction and we pen/inked the addition at time XA27Z and prior to takeoff.Attention to detail on all parties regarding paperwork and added HAZMAT. During a late departure taxi out in ZZZ to ZZZ1 we realized the NOTAC wasn't noted on the Release. While we were waiting for our departure sequence, the Captain called and pen/inked it with Dispatch while I monitored Ground Control. We were late and tired from multiple ground stops and airborne holding and diversion planning while trying to get out before we timed out.
ASRS:1831872.s: The Pilot and Operations Agent failed to add a HAZMAT NOTAC for a Fire Extinguisher to the Release before taxiing for departure. Dispatch contacted the crew via ACARS, and the Captain corrected the paperwork prior to takeoff after fatigue and delays caused the initial oversight.

ASRS:1831901.n: I began this trip with my flying First Officer (FO) starting leg 3 of his transition operating experience from the Airbus, one International Relief Officer (IRO) relatively new to the fleet and still not yet consolidated, while the other IRO was a seasoned FO on the 777 fleet.We pushed back from gate. After the left engine start was complete we noticed a strange and unfamiliar odor that wasn't readily identifiable. A brief discussion took place on the flight deck about the possibilities of the odor origin and all agreed it was not an electrical smell so we continued with the right engine start procedure. Within seconds of the right engine start completion, smoke was noticeable in the cockpit along with a very strong and identifiable electrical burning odor. We noticed flashing switch lighting on the overhead panel, specifically the window heat switches but no EICAS warnings had appeared. Thoughts of Swiss Air flight 111 many years ago instantly entered my mind and rather than execute a lengthy non-normal procedure, I made the decision based on being on the ground that we would be better off in the long run to remove power immediately from the aircraft. I elected to shutdown both engines at that point and have one of my IROs open the door and check in the back with the purser and check if the cabin had smoke as we were assessing whether to initiate an evacuation or not at this point. There was a lot of ground traffic around us in all directions, both automotive and aircraft, and I was wanting information as to just how bad things were in the cabin before committing to an evacuation. XXXXXX reacted above and beyond any expectations I had and promptly reported back with the following information:Door 1R Flight Attendant (FA) had seen smoke coming from the floor area around the jumpseat as well as the seat 1L floor area. The customer in seat X was relocated away from the smoke area. I was told there was some smoke in the galley and forward seats but that was it and that it appeared to cease escalating and that the floor was not hot. XXXXXX had also opened up the electronics (EE) compartment door and performed a visual inspection that revealed a scorched panel with no visible fire. He mentioned, that while the scorched panel was warm, it was not hot and felt certain that whatever had precipitated the event had stabilized and all we had was smoke at this point with electrical odor. With that firsthand information and no further comments from the FAs, I made a PA informing the customers and inflight crew of the situation, realizing there probably were flashing lights along with some smoke in the cabin we were certain there was no further reason to suspect a fire and that we would be returning by tow back into the gate. I would later find out from the FA and Passengers through sharing of information in the boarding lounge that it was the initial PA that was responsible for de-escalating anxiety and growing concern that would later facilitate a timely and orderly deplaning of the aircraft at the gate as well as all but 2 of our original customers re-boarding the new jet. It was XXXXXX's 'eyes on' first hand assessment along with the purser and 1R door FA assessment that the smoke had ceased to proliferate that led to de-escalating my thoughts of evacuation onto a busy tarmac and into that of a tow back to the gate and expedited deplaning.We contacted ramp and explained our situation... 'XXX on taxiway has smoke in the cockpit with all engines shut down and requested that they facilitate a tow back to the gate right away'. The ramp agent working the frequency appeared agitated with us and told us we would need to contact Maintenance to coordinate. I repeated with urgency, our situation as unable to taxi and needing their help with coordination... I received no answer. XXXXXX, my other IRO assumed the responsibilities of communicating with ramp trying to facilitate help and continued to receive a comment that 'if wecould just taxi back it sure would make things a lot easier'. I continued to make PA to let folks know our progress and what the plan was when we got to the gate. We had shut down all fans and other electrical items such as cabin services and entertainment. Later we would discover that the APU had actually auto-shutdown and we were on battery only. The smoke had gotten pretty thick in the cockpit but was now beginning to subside while we were being towed back to gate. We requested Airport Rescue Firefighting (ARFF) be standing by should things deteriorate and instructed operations to let Ramp know that we did not want any cargo doors open for fear of possibly fueling a bad situation with large amounts of fresh air. Once at the gate, we coordinated with airport personnel that we had no electrical power to enter a log writeup and subsequently completed the additional paperwork for Maintenance with regard to smoke. I was able to inspect the cabin and had noticed quite a bit of smoke during the deplaning. I would later find out from the flight attendants, that the smoke did not actually start appearing in the aft sections of the cabin until the door was opened and passengers started deplaning. Once off the jet, I debriefed my crew using company CRM skills, spoke with and briefed Chief Pilot as well as submitted the required incident report before making my way to the next aircraft. I met with our inflight crew at the new aircraft and spoke with each of them to thank them for their calm and professional approach to what had potential to have been a very different outcome. Everyone assured me that [they] were fit and ready to continue with our new jet into ZZZZ. I did speak with one FA who waited for me outside the flight planning room. She wanted to tell me she had experienced a headache and was removing herself from the trip. I made a PA in the boarding lounge thanking everyone for remaining calm and following their crew member instructions and proceeded to offer a very high level explanation of the event while praising the highly experienced crew I had to work with who were quick to identify and de-escalate the situation allowing us to deplane orderly and continue to ZZZZ with this new jet. We were fortunate that this happened on the ground and that we had the option of simply and quickly removing the power from the aircraft. We all felt certain that after seeing the pictures, that had this happened in flight, we would have never had time to run a multi-page procedure hoping to isolate before something unrecoverable may have occurred within the electrical system ultimately affecting a successful outcome.A few things to note after our cockpit crew debrief:Of interest is that we elected to open the cockpit windows to vent the smoke. I suspect that because we were on the ground, no one ever mentioned the memory item of donning the O2 mask or the thought that we might exacerbate the problem by opening the windows. We did however consider this idea as it pertained to opening the cargo doors as we were being towed back. We train 'smoke in the cockpit/cabin' in the simulator and it can become somewhat of a spring loaded evacuation solution as we don't have any outside cues from which to assess. In real time with real visual feedback in the moment, one gets an overwhelming reality check as to just how dangerous an evacuation of 250+ people can be on a busy tarmac if there are other options. It may pay dividends to assess the risks and current information prior to committing to an evacuation. In retrospect, after seeing the scorched panel, it is believed that the initial odor was that of burnt dust and paint before the onset of obvious electrical smoldering. It may also be worth a precautionary discontinuance of starting with any odor that is not readily identifiable. With both engines shut down, we were surprised to later discover the APU had also auto-shutdown contributing to some confusion as we were on battery only. Moving forward, I will now add to my before pushback ritual, the review of a telephone number for operations as we all felt strongly that we spent precious minutes trying to solicit help on the radio from ramp when we could have probably made a phone call directly to Ops to help coordinate all of the services.
ASRS:1831901.s: The Captain and crew of a Boeing 777 experienced smoke and electrical odors during engine start on the ground, prompting an immediate shutdown of both engines and the APU. A visual inspection revealed a scorched panel in the electronics compartment, leading to a decision to tow the aircraft back to the gate for orderly deplaning rather than evacuate on the busy tarmac.

ASRS:1831916.n: Crew departed late due to brake accumulator issues on previous aircraft, and a potential one on this aircraft.Ground Ops were completely normal and the FO (First Officer) had no problems deploying the flaps to 3 for takeoff.Takeoff was normal and as we were turning to an assigned heading, we reached the cleanup altitude. I called for flaps 1 and noticed that the FO had some what I felt was minor difficulty bringing the flaps up to 1. This is not unusual, a hand slips, or the lever used to move the flap handle out of the detects isn't gripped correctly for easy retraction. I thought little of it.When I called for flaps UP, the raising was again delayed, and I noticed my FO reaching around with his right hand to put both hands on the flap lever to get it up. We talked about him having trouble getting them up, and I flew the aircraft only to ensure that I did not over speed the flaps. Eventually he was able to get them up which I saw on the speed tape on the PFD and I verified on the display, and flap handle position.We discussed what had happened a bit but decided to focus on safely exiting the terminal area and getting to altitude since the aircraft was now in the safe, and proper configuration. We made a plan to contact Maintenance Control at cruise and notify them of the problem and get advice about continuing the flight.After reaching altitude, the FO told me what he had encountered and explained how difficult it was to move the lever that released the flap handle from the detent to raise the flaps.A phone patch was initiated with dispatch and Maintenance Control and we discovered that our radio 2 wasn't able to receive over long distances. We ended up substituting radio 3 for radio 2 and temporarily disabling ACARS to complete the phone patch. Maintenance Control was very helpful on the phone patch and felt like he knew what the problem was. Maintenance Control was asked if he felt the aircraft should continue to ZZZZ, and he wanted it to go to a maintenance hub. As a Captain, I agreed with that thought process and asked the Dispatcher to bring in the Ops Manager so that we could all agree on a plan of action. We could have landed the aircraft at ZZZZ if there had been a flap malfunction, but the aircraft would have been stuck there quite a while.Eventually after consideration of landing lengths, the close to overweight landing weight of the aircraft, and the potential for wet runways in ZZZ1, that the best and safest place to divert the aircraft would be ZZZ1 in case the flaps would not deploy normally. Consideration was based on the worst case, flaps up scenario.Destination was changed with ATC once the plan was agreed upon by all parties and the phone patch was terminated and ACARS restored.Maintenance Control was asked via ACARS if we should leave the flaps down after landing and they asked them to retract them as much as we could.Fortunately, the landing in ZZZ1 was uneventful. The flaps deployed normally. Upon taxi-in. The flaps were retraced to position 1, where the handle binding began to be very difficult to overcome.Upon arrival at the gate, after shutdown, I tried to move the lever that releases the flap handle from the detent and found that it was impossible to move with just one hand. We were doing a flaps 3 takeoff from [Runway] XXL. After the acceleration altitude, and above flap retraction speed, the pilot flying called for flaps to 1. I noticed, while moving the lever from 3 to 1, that the flap lever was nowhere near as smooth and free moving as it usually is, rather, it was quite difficult to move. As we accelerated through flap 1 retraction speed, it took considerable effort to get the lever out of the detent. I mentioned it to the captain who quickly made sure to raise the nose and not over speed the flaps as I used both hands to get the flap lever compressed and moved to the up position. The flaps moved as expected, with no issues, the flight control page showed normal, and the hydraulic page showed normal. We continued the climb out of ZZZ, and when reaching a safe altitude, I took the controls and radios with ATC, while the captain initiated an incredibly detailed conversation with dispatch and Maintenance Control. After exhausting every bit of information we could give, and every insight Maintenance Control had, the decision was made with dispatch and everyone in planning that they were talking to, to divert to ZZZ1 instead of potentially having a flight control issue on landing in ZZZZ, on a shorter runway, at an international station, and then leaving the plane there. We didn't [request priority] but asked approach to slow down early to get the flaps out and make sure they extended. We had planned every contingency for having to go around and then [request priority] if they didn't, and were ready to run whichever QRH abnormal procedure would have applied based on where the flaps ended up. On the approach, the flaps came down just fine and a normal landing was made. After landing, we planned, with maintenance approval, to attempt to retract the flaps but to stop if they locked again and not force anything. The lever was much less stiff from flaps full to flaps 1 than earlier, but again locked at the detent there. We left the flaps at 1 into the gate, let ramp know to tell anyone they could, and had maintenance meet us there. Sounded like they were going to replace the entire flap lever section.
ASRS:1831916.s: The crew experienced significant difficulty retracting the flap lever from detents during climb after a Flaps 3 takeoff, requiring two hands to operate. They diverted to ZZZ1 for safety, landed normally with flaps extending correctly, and found the lever locked at position 1 upon taxi-in.

ASRS:1831969.n: After takeoff from ZZZ climbing through approximately FL220 in night IMC, we got an ALT DISAGREE EICAS message, followed shortly afterwards with a IAS DISAGREE EICAS message. During the climb the Captain's and FO's altimeters disagreed by several hundred feet, and the airspeed indicators by up to 15 knots. We leveled off at FL310 to evaluate the situation. At FL310, the airspeed disagree EICAS went away, but the alt disagree EICAS remained. At FL310, we recorded Capt/FO/Standby altitude as 31000/31350/31900 and IAS as 280/285/295 knots. We completed the appropriate non normal checklists. After conferring with dispatch via SATCOM, we determined that the safest course of action was to divert to ZZZ1. We coordinated the diversion with ATC, and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1. We felt it was unnecessary to declare an emergency, as the IAS disagree EICAS had gone away. The flight attendants were briefed for a normal landing.
ASRS:1831969.s: The crew experienced ALT and IAS DISAGREE EICAS messages while climbing through FL220 in night IMC, with altimeters differing by hundreds of feet and airspeeds by up to 15 knots. After leveling at FL310 and consulting dispatch, they diverted and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1 without declaring an emergency.

ASRS:1831997.n: A [ramp employee] driving a cargo loader cut in front of a 787 marshaling in at gate XX at XA20 on Date, the right wing walker did have his stop signal but the aircraft could not stopped. The [ramp employee] barely made it to the right side of aircraft with out any incidents.
ASRS:1831997.s: A ramp employee driving a cargo loader cut in front of a 787 marshaling at gate XX at XA20. Although the right wing walker displayed a stop signal, the aircraft could not stop, but the loader cleared the right side without incident.

ASRS:1832035.n: This event was a near midair collision in ZZZZ. On Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZZ. Weather at ZZZZ was not a factor even though there was a significant storm cell over the final approach fix to Runway XX. ZZZZ was reporting 10 miles visibility. While making approach into ZZZZ we were told to go around due to previous aircraft reporting a pothole with gravel on approach end to Runway XX. Tower immediately closed the runway. We then went around and did published missed procedure. We entered holding at 8,000 feet at ZZZZZ per instructions. After we exited holding (now at 6,000 feet) the controller gave us instructions to go direct to ZZZZZ1 fix and begin RNP approach into Runway YY. We loaded the approach to the opposite Runway YY since the pothole was on the approach end of the Runway XX and proceeded to ZZZZZ1 on about a 200 heading. Then unexpectedly, the controller gave us a vector of 090. In hind sight, we think this vector was meant for another aircraft. The new heading of 090 ended up sending us directly for another aircraft at same altitude. TCAS began with a TA then an RA. At same time controller frantically gave us a new vector. After properly executing the resolution advisory, we narrowly missed the conflict aircraft and proceeded back to ZZZZZ1 and did the RNP to Runway YY for normal landing. We never saw the conflict aircraft however they did have us in sight, and I don't recall who the conflict aircraft was. There were two jets in holding. We think the controller got our call sign confused with someone else for the 090 vector. English as a second language may have been a factor in this event. Both the F/O (First Officer) and myself remember hearing our call sign in the 090 vector. In the end it was TCAS that saved the day.
ASRS:1832035.s: Pilots of Aircraft X experienced a near midair collision while holding at 6,000 feet after receiving an erroneous 090 vector intended for another aircraft. The conflict was resolved by executing a TCAS resolution advisory, likely caused by controller call sign confusion and English language barriers.

ASRS:1832042.n: During pre-flight programming of the MCDU, Takeoff Performance page, I noticed the loaded EOAA (Engine out Acceleration Altitude) was too low by 520 feet. The EOAA that was downloaded vis ACARS was 3,180, but the EOAA for Runway XXR was 3,700 feet for Flaps 1, which we were using. Most of the time the ACARS-loaded EOAA value is normally within 30 feet, but this one was 520 feet too low! I have also noticed in a past flight from ZZZ1 Runway XY, that the EOAA was over 700 feet too low with reference to company data.In accordance with the Ops Manual, crews are to verify the accuracy of the EOAA when programming the MCDU for flight. However, if this is missed, the potential for a near mishap is significant. I lack the technical knowledge in this matter to make a specific recommendation. The requirement here is to ensure the EOAA value found in performance data is the same as the EOAA value that gets downloaded via ACARS in the MCDU.
ASRS:1832042.s: During pre-flight MCDU programming, the pilot discovered the ACARS-downloaded Engine Out Acceleration Altitude was 520 feet too low for the specific runway and flap setting. The reporter noted this significant discrepancy could lead to a near mishap if crews fail to verify the value against company performance data.

ASRS:1832044.n: Holding short Runway XXR [at] ZZZ we received an ECAM 'ENG 1 FADEC A FAULT.' Upon informing tower of the need to examine a fault, tower cleared us to cross [Runway] XXR and hold short of XXR on the eastern side. Coordinating with Maintenance Control a circuit breaker reset failed to resolve the ECAM. Maintenance informed me this was a 'no-go' ECAM. We informed tower we needed to return to a gate, tower then cleared us to taxi onto XXR and exit taxiway 1. We subsequently taxied to gate XX.This was an unfortunate mechanical failure. This item was a repeat item and had been examined by maintenance technicians, cleared and 'signed-off' as recently as the previous flight.This was an unfortunate mechanical failure but as a repeat item the only suggestion is possibly more scrutiny on previous occasions.
ASRS:1832044.s: The flight crew received an ENG 1 FADEC A fault ECAM while holding short of Runway XXR at ZZZ. After a failed circuit breaker reset, maintenance declared it a no-go, forcing a return to the gate for this repeat mechanical failure previously signed off.

ASRS:1832046.n: Suspected #4 Hydraulic Leak Divert to ZZZZ1Departed ZZZ enroute to ZZZZ. Several hours enroute we noticed #4 hydraulic system indicated abnormally low quantity at approximately .45.We continued to monitor and noticed a .01 decrease per approx every 30 to 45 minutes. Over [geographic area 1] as we neared [geographic area 2] we became concerned that we did indeed have a slow hydraulic leak as we were now indicating .39.We preempted the 'hyd quantity low 4' QRH procedure in hopes that depressurizing system 4 pumps would slow or prevent our suspected leak given we still had nearly 6 hours to destination. If the current trend continued we would have faced a possible loss of system 4 resulting in degraded flight controls and manual gear extension at destination.After depressurizing system 4 the downward trend in hydraulic quantity continued. Shortly after our coast out point of ZZZZZ I made the decision to advise company operations and ATC of our situation and made arrangements for us to divert to our planned enroute alternate of ZZZZ1.We repressurized system 4 prior to landing as per the QRH and landed without further incident at ZZZZ1.Plan more ground time to address trending maintenance items on a more regular schedule to strike a balance with the demanding flight schedule as hydraulic issues are appearing more regularly and have been documented in recent logbook discrepancies with this particular aircraft.
ASRS:1832046.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZZ1 due to a suspected slow leak in the #4 hydraulic system, which showed a decreasing quantity trend despite depressurizing the pumps. The crew recommends more frequent ground maintenance to address recurring hydraulic issues documented in the aircraft's logbook.

ASRS:1832095.n: During cruise at around XA:20 the B Flight Attendant and I were sitting on the aft galley jump seat on the right side of the aircraft and the B Flight Attendant said 'do you smell that'. I lowered my mask and said yes. The B Flight Attendant, I, and the C Flight Attendant smelt a burning smell that smelt electrical. The B Flight Attendant called the A Flight Attendant to notify her and to tell the Captain. For the safety of flight all flight attendants began to search for the location of the burning smell, and used the backs of our hands to locate any heat. The Captain called and suggested that two flight attendants return up front then return to the back to see if the smell was still apparent. The A and the C went back up front and then the A only came back. The B noticed the vent closest to the aft galley service door was warm and the odor of something burning was coming from that vent. I got down on my knees to smell the vent and did notice and odor and the vent was very warm on aircraft right. The A called the Captain to relay our information. Time was now XA:30 and Captain said to clean up the cabin, we would be diverting to ZZZ. At XA:40 cabin was cleaned and Captain called to say we were landing in 15 minutes. The cabin lights were all off and we asked the Captain if it was him, and now the vent was cool to the touch. We landed in ZZZ and passengers remained seated.
ASRS:1832095.s: Flight attendants detected an electrical burning smell from a warm vent near the aft galley during cruise. The Captain diverted to ZZZ, where the vent cooled and the odor ceased before landing.

ASRS:1832168.n: I was doing pattern work with my student. Once we turned crosswind, we noticed an aircraft pass underneath us approximately 50 ft. Aircraft Y made no radio calls and did not enter the pattern on a 45-degree entry. I took controls from the student and made the decision to go right over the lake to avoid further conflict. I made a call asking if there was 'anyone else on midfield left downwind Runway XX.' They did not respond. I made the decision to leave the pattern to the south after I noticed my aircraft was faster and going to overtake Aircraft Y. After I announced that I was leaving the pattern, the aircraft in question made a call that he was turning left base Runway XX. Shortly after Tower opened XA:00 and the aircraft departed the pattern to the north. Aircraft had capability to make the calls and chose not to, leading to a potential midair collision.
ASRS:1832168.s: A pilot and student conducting pattern work observed Aircraft Y pass 50 feet below without radio calls or a proper 45-degree entry. The pilot diverted over a lake to avoid conflict, attributing the potential midair collision to Aircraft Y's failure to communicate despite having radio capability.

ASRS:1832170.n: Departed ZZZ on Runway XX at XA01. Engine ran smoothly on run-up and during takeoff roll, all cylinder temperatures normal. Assigned climb to 5,000 ft. via radar vector 200 heading by ZZZ Tower. After departure, handed off to ZZZ1 Approach. Checked in with ZZZ1 Approach at approximately 2,200 ft. MSL, after which the engine started to run very roughly and cylinder head temperatures started to rise above normal levels. [Requested priority handling] with ZZZ1 Approach and stated that I needed to return immediately to ZZZ. ZZZ1 Approach asked if we needed assistance, to which I replied negative. Switched back to ZZZ Tower, requested priority handling with them again, and stated that we would be returning to the airport and landing on Runway XY.ZZZ Tower cleared out other traffic and cleared us to land on Runway XX, in response to which I restated that [we] would be landing on Runway XY. This back-and-forth transmission was repeated a couple of times, but eventually [we] were cleared to land on Runway XY by ZZZ Tower. Completed 270-degree turn, extended landing gear, and landed on Runway XY without further incident. [We] were able to taxi back to ramp with no further issue. Problem hasn't been verified, but suspect water contaminated fuel that sloshed to fuel pickup on rotation. Will analyze engine logs to check for proper fuel flow.
ASRS:1832170.s: The pilot experienced rough engine operation and high cylinder temperatures shortly after departing ZZZ on Runway XX. Suspecting water-contaminated fuel, the pilot returned and landed safely on Runway XY after resolving a clearance discrepancy with Tower.

ASRS:1832206.n: The flight was conducted by an experienced ATP-AMEL owner as PIC and training Captain and an experienced commercial AMEL pilot as Trainee. No passengers were on board. The purpose of the flight was a training mission from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and back to ZZZ and for aircraft familiarization and to run an errand in ZZZ3. The flight landed ZZZ1 uneventfully after about 2.0 hours and estimated 28 gallons of fuel burn. Fuel on board at departure from ZZZ was 70 gallons of 84 gallons maximum usable and flight on only the main tanks (48 gal avail, 28 required) was planned. The two pilots parked at the FBO and requested fuel to be topped then proceeded to take the crew car to town for a couple hours to take care of some business in town and get lunch.Upon return to the FBO line service had already serviced the aircraft and a receipt for 26 gallons of fuel was provided. The pilots performed the pre-flight on the aircraft. The ATP checked the fuel quantity visually on the left side and the commercial pilot checked fuel visually on the right side. By verbal agreement the fuel was observed full in all 4 tanks left and right. The receipt for fuel purchase showed approximately the expected amount of 26 gallons burned on the previous flight.Approximately halfway back to ZZZ from ZZZ1, at about 1.3 hours flight time, the right engine failed. The ATP took over controlling the aircraft and completed all of the memorized and checklist emergency procedures and diverted to ZZZ2 in visual conditions. The landing was uneventful with no damage to the aircraft, no injury to the pilots and no passengers nor ground personnel were involved.Upon inspection of the aircraft the problem was determined to be the right main fuel tank was empty. This should not have been the case because it held 27 gallons usable and the 1.3 hour flight should've only burned 8-9 gallons on the right side, flown entirely on the main tanks. The aircraft was fueled at ZZZ2 and the left main took 8.5 gallons commensurate with fuel burn estimates. The fuel selector valves and fuel strainers were tested repeatedly and found to be in working condition. There were no evidences of fuel leakage and the tanks all held fuel properly after refuel. The inescapable conclusion is that the FBO failed to fuel the right main tank. One can account for the volume of fuel added at ZZZ1 prior to departure because auxiliary tanks and main tanks were not full at original departure. This made the quantity placed on board commensurate with the quantity used yet it is inexplicable why the Fueler would have not fueled the right main tank. The right main tank would have had 10 gallons in it. This is commensurate with the one 1.3 hour flight to the point of failure. The pilot in training who checked the right main tank either saw what he expected or saw a glare but didn't properly check fuel quantity on the right main tank. Corrective actions for the future: The PIC should always supervise the personnel during fueling to alleviate any confusion about where the fuel is to be placed. Secondly, the PIC should always check fuel tanks visually himself never trust even another experienced pilot to do that for you. Also, while fuel gauges are properly never to be trusted as a reliable fuel assessment or fuel planning tool and many pilots properly rely on visual checks of fuel and fuel burn calculations, a gauge that show a grossly different from what was visually checked should indicate that a visual recheck is required. Also, stay current on emergency procedures. In this case being absolutely current on engine failure procedures and knowing where VMC alternate were made for an uneventful approach and landing.
ASRS:1832206.s: Two pilots conducting a training flight in an AMEL experienced a right engine failure due to an empty right main tank caused by FBO fueling error and inadequate visual verification. The PIC executed emergency procedures to divert and land safely with no injuries or damage.

ASRS:1832210.n: Flying at 31,000 ft. and the pressurization audible alarm sounded, and we noticed that the cabin pressure was climbing. It was at 9,800 ft. normally, but had risen to 12,500 ft. I donned my oxygen mask as the cabin pressure over the next 1-2 minutes rose to a maximum of 15,500 ft. At 15,000 ft. we began an emergency descent. As we were setting up for the descent the emergency descent mode (EDM) on the plane took over and began turning the plane 90 degrees from its present course, I deactivated the EMD and corrected the heading back to a safe heading (bad weather was all around us). I then notified ATC that we would need to begin an emergency descent due to pressure loss in the cabin.I requested 15,000 ft. altitude, and was cleared to descend (while I was already descending). Once we reached 15,000 ft. the pressurization system began to catch up and the cabin pressure had stabilized at 7,200 ft. MSL. We flew the remainder of the flight at 15,000 ft. and monitored the cabin pressure. We landed without incident. The 3 passengers reported to me to be fine. The passenger oxygen masks were deployed when the plane began the EDM.Once on the ground i contacted the FBO to determine maintenance and repair requirements. The problem had occurred before in very rare identical situation. Rain/ice conditions. Apparently, a slight amount of moisture in the door seal forms ice, and the seal breaks allowing for pressure from the inside to leak out. Once we reached a lower altitude the pressure reached normal, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful.After discussions with the FBO I was able to clean the seals and on the flight out, we monitored the cabin differential pressure closely up through 12,500 ft. Our plan was to return home at 12,500 ft. if there was any indication of an issue, but the cabin differential remained at 6.0 psi the entire flight. We have added to the preflight checklist, to wipe down door seals prior to each flight.
ASRS:1832210.s: The pilot experienced a cabin pressure loss at 31,000 ft caused by ice breaking a door seal, triggering an emergency descent to 15,000 ft. After stabilizing the cabin and landing safely, the crew cleaned the seals and added a preflight wipe-down step to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1832221.n: Aircraft X was level at 10,000 feet westbound to ZZZ. The pilot asked for a block 10,000 to 12,000 feet, which I issued. Lots of aircraft were taking that same block due to weather in the area. Shortly after the minimum safe altitude warning sounded, and when I looked, Aircraft X was at 7,100 feet in a 5,000 feet minimum IFR altitude. Confused, I continued to watch and realized it was sounding because the aircraft was dropping so rapidly. Knowing something was definitely wrong I reached out to the pilot, but no response. After the aircraft went from 7,100 feet to 6,400 feet to 2,400 feet, I reached out two more times with no response.Finally, the pilot responded and requested descent to 1,000 feet and I informed them they were in a 5,000 feet minimum IFR altitude. They then canceled IFR but never descended and actually climbed to 2,800 feet. Eventually they reached 5,900 feet and requested to return to ZZZ1. A clearance was issued direct and assigned 6,000 feet which they had requested but then climbed to 7,000 feet, so I just issued 7,000 feet. The pilot was very shaken up. It sounds like a software issue? I recommend fixing that or grounding the C208's until it is fixed.
ASRS:1832221.s: An air traffic controller observed a C208 pilot experience a rapid, unexplained descent from 10,000 to 2,400 feet, triggering minimum safe altitude warnings. The pilot, shaken and suspecting a software issue, eventually climbed back to 7,000 feet and requested a return to ZZZ1.

ASRS:1832225.n: I was relieving another controller. He was getting off position to take the CIC position. I listen to him brief. I turned up the overhead lights. Before I sat down, two aircraft were flashing. I sat down. Turned one 40 degrees right and the other 30 degrees left. My recommendations are, even though COVID is a factor of why I was distant from the sector to give both controllers room and space, I will have to get closer to see the scope to see what is going on.
ASRS:1832225.s: An air traffic controller relieving a colleague observed two aircraft flashing on the scope before taking the position. The controller issued turn instructions to separate the traffic and recommended sitting closer to the display to improve situational awareness despite social distancing measures.

ASRS:1832269.n: I have not taken the COVID vaccine. Because of this, I expect to lose my job in XX days or less. I flew a scheduled trip, ZZZ to ZZZZ, on Date 1 and returned Date 2. I am new to the [aircraft type] fleet and have XX total hours on type with XY hours towards my hours required for consolidation.In training, I was taught the importance of discussing threats before a trip with the other pilots. My dilemma was deciding whether to tell the other pilots that I am distracted because of my upcoming termination or not to tell them. I decided not to tell them because, having never met them before, I was concerned that this information might be perceived by them as anything from a minor annoyance with me to a possible outrage. Prior to both flights, I addressed all my concerns and considered myself fit for duty. Although I just recently completed training on the [aircraft type], I am proficient in my skills. I was convinced that should any non-normal situation occur I would be competent and able to properly perform my duties. What I did not expect to encounter was the anxiety and inner conflict I experienced once airborne.After the flight, I was unable to go to dinner with the other pilots on the overnight because I do not have a vaccine card which is required in Country. I felt uneasy about giving a vague reason for declining the invitation because I was uncertain about revealing the truth about my vaccination status. While in ZZZZ, I thought about the inner-conflict that I am experiencing, anxiety about losing my job, and concern over possible discrimination by other pilots and/or cabin crew members should they become aware of my vaccination status. I was pilot flying on the return leg to ZZZ and I found it more difficult to concentrate on simple tasks especially since I am new to the aircraft. I was also unable to sleep during my rest break and unable to eat very much due to the heightened anxiety I was experiencing. My landing at ZZZ airport was not as good as I had hoped. The inner tension was compounded by my uncertainty as to whether I should have confessed my vaccination status to the other pilots and what would happen to me if I made a mistake and they found out later that I did not tell them.The unexpected level of anxiety never reached a point that I would consider dangerous, but the possibility of increased errors was apparent to me. The conflict that I experienced because I did not reveal my vaccination status at the onset of the trip was an unnecessary distraction imposed on me by the company. In addition, I did not want to introduce an issue to the other pilots that could cause a hostile work environment. At the end of the flight, at the gate in ZZZ, I told the other pilots that I was unvaccinated and would be losing my job soon. I could sense their concern and as they are both true professionals, they seemed empathetic with my plight.I have not yet determined the best way to deal with my predicament and since there is no guidance from my union or the company, I will probably conceal my vaccination status on my next trip. I would hope that there would not be any hostility directed towards me if I revealed my status at the beginning of my next trip, but considering the contentiousness of the situation I am unsure. I believe that my training and prior experience make it easier for me to deal with these types of distractions than others. I am very concerned for those who may be unable to effectively manage their personal problems caused by the vaccine mandate.I believe that the company's vaccine mandate has created a potentially dangerous work environment that could impact safe operations. The divisiveness caused by the vaccine issue, the unknown side effects for those already vaccinated and the prospect of impending job terminations have culminated and become, in my opinion, an inherent risk to aviation safety.
ASRS:1832269.s: A pilot flying a scheduled trip on a new aircraft type reported experiencing anxiety and distraction due to an impending job termination caused by not receiving the COVID vaccine. The pilot attributed this mental conflict to the company's vaccine mandate, noting it degraded concentration and landing performance while creating a potentially dangerous work environment.

ASRS:1832277.n: Taxiing to Runway 8 at SJU, we were cleared to taxi and hold short at S1. I noticed the Captain wasn't going to make the turn at S1, so I prompted him, but it was too late and stopped just past the intersection. Tower called us and said that S intersection was closed, so there was no way for us to turn around and return to S1. Tower called a follow me ops vehicle and instructed us to follow him through S intersection, onto the runway and then taxi off at S2. We complied and returned for takeoff from S1. We missed complying with the taxi instructions, but there were no markings of the closed intersection, and the ATIS was unclear, stating only 'S intersection closed', which seemed ambiguous since it didn't mention S at Runway 8 closed.
ASRS:1832277.s: The flight crew at SJU inadvertently crossed the closed S1 intersection while taxiing to Runway 8 due to ambiguous ATIS information and lack of markings. Tower directed them to follow a vehicle through the intersection to return to S1 for takeoff.

ASRS:1832335.n: While being vectored on a base leg to final, approach requests us to call the field in sight. It was a night approach with good weather and we had the field at 10 miles but I initially declined to call the field because of our angle and unfamiliarity with the area. After the second (or third?) request from ATC we accepted the visual at around 6 mile dog leg. They had directed us to keep speed up so now I was gauging the energy state while working toward a straight in final. As we descended I scanned the radar altimeter and noticed it fluctuating between 1,300-900 feet. We were configured at flaps 25 and I verbalized this to my FO (First Officer) as I temporarily leveled our descent and checked our distance from the runway. DME was NOTAMed out of service so I put [the] runway on fix page during brief and it showed around 4-5 miles. Bar altimeter was 2,300 with 800 ft elevation so we determined that hilly terrain was causing the spike. By this time radar altimeter normalized above 1000 ft and we had selected flaps 30 so we continued approach to landing.Approach brief covered obstacles but I did not take into account hilly terrain in the area. Also, our desire to facilitate ATC requests to keep speed up and accept visual approach.At unfamiliar airports during night operations it is advisable to let ATC vector to the initial or final approach fix.
ASRS:1832335.s: During a night visual approach at an unfamiliar airport, the crew experienced radar altimeter fluctuations caused by hilly terrain while complying with ATC speed and visual acceptance requests. The pilots identified the terrain as the cause, leveled briefly to verify position, and continued safely to landing.

ASRS:1832343.n: After the Pilot Flying called for 'Slats retract, after takeoff checklist;' I promptly moved the flap/slat handle to RET and after slats retraction we received the Level 1 Alert HYD 1 OFF. After running the QRH and as a crew we elected to continue to ZZZZ. Once in cruise we discussed potential outcomes of our situation we planned that we may have a total HYD 1 Failure and discussed what we wanted to do if we did. After planning to configure early to see if our problem would manifest into a failure we did indeed have a total HYD 1 FAIL level 2. We [requested priority handling] with ZZZZ Approach asked to continue on our current heading for 5-10 minutes and we would get back with them after we accomplished our checklists. We were given Runway XXR as an option, given that this runway was the longest we elected to utilize this option. We ran the QRH procedure and discussed potential threats and issues. Given that our nose wheel steering would be limited to the left we elected to stop on the runway and request to be towed in via a tug. We informed ZZZZ Approach of this issue and let them know souls on board and approximately how much fuel we had remaining. After being handed off to ZZZZ Tower I once again reminded them we were not going to be able to clear the runway due to our failed condition. I thought this might be important because of the restricted visibility and poor runway conditions so no one would commence a takeoff or an approach with our airplane parked on an active runway. Tower understood clearly our intentions there was no miscommunication. Our approach was normal and normal procedures were utilized in the event. The airplane performed exactly as we anticipated. After engine cool down, assuring the brakes we not too hot and we started the APU we let Tower know our engines were shut down and the aircraft was safe to approach with our company tug. As Company Maintenance personnel entered through the FWD avionics compartment and communicated with Company ground personnel via his handheld radio and would sit in the CA (Captain)'s seat while in control of the aircraft's brakes. I continued to perform Pilot Monitoring duties to obtain a taxi clearance and monitored the aircraft until we set the parking brake at Gate XX. The event overall was a well orchestrated event, [the] Captain showed excellent leadership, CRM and cockpit management skills. [The] Captain reacted calmly and confidently as I backed him up during the process. I posed questions and [a] hypothetical to ensure we had all of our bases covered and [the] Captain was very respective the few I had to offer. [The] Captain demonstrated by example exactly how a captain should react and respond to a potential dangerous situation. I would also like to note that ZZZZ Approach and Tower performed above expectations despite a slight language barrier we all had an understanding of what we needed and they were able to provide that with ease. Lastly ZZZZ Company Operations performed flawlessly we couldn't have asked for anything more. After landing in ZZZZ, Maintenance personnel identified the issue right away it was stated it was an 'auto brake controller', that caused the #1 HYD system to leak all of its fluid and fail. I have not followed up to see if this indeed was the case after maintenance completed its final inspection and repair.
ASRS:1832343.s: The crew experienced a total HYD 1 failure after takeoff due to a faulty auto brake controller causing fluid loss. They landed safely at ZZZZ, stopped on the runway, and were towed to the gate with assistance from maintenance and ground personnel.

ASRS:1832360.n: As we were being vectored to get established on final, we received an IDG FAULT Caution message, I decided to run the QRH, while we were in a high [workload situation], lots of communication with ATC as we were being vectored, descended, and slowed, lots of radio chatter caused a breakdown in our communication within the flight deck and that resulted in turning the wrong IDG off, which caused a momentary loss of all AC and subsequent deployment of the RAT, at this point with emergency power only I decided to [request priority handling], accept the longer runway, and continue to an uneventful landing, after landing we continued to the gate, as normal power had been restored.The cause of this event can be contributed to the fact that we were rushed in completing the QRH in a very busy environment, while being vectored and slowed and while starting to configure for landing.Based on what I experienced, I would not run the QRH that close to the runway for a caution message, in a high [workload situation], rather I would wait and deal with it on the ground.
ASRS:1832360.s: During final approach vectoring, high workload and radio chatter caused the flight crew to turn off the wrong IDG while executing the QRH, resulting in a momentary AC loss and RAT deployment. The crew requested priority handling and landed uneventfully, attributing the error to rushing the checklist in a busy environment.

ASRS:1832364.n: I was doing touch and go's at ZZZ and Runway XX was in use. After my first touch and go, I remained in the pattern, and I was on left downwind for Runway XX when I heard another aircraft with the '[FBO]' call sign calling on a 3 mile straight in for Runway XX. I decided to extend my downwind to let him pass, and I said it on the frequency that I was still on the downwind for Runway XX and would extend my downwind for the traffic on the straight in Runway XX. Aircraft Y said that he was going to the left downwind for Runway XY. I was quite confused but continued to Runway XX as it was the best runway given the wind, and everyone else was using [Runway] XX. When I turn final, I asked 'Is there anybody on final for [Runway] XY?' And I also said that I was on final for [Runway] XX, the opposite runway. Aircraft Y answered me but he was unclear. After he finished talking I said once again that I was on short final for Runway XX. I touched down, and while I was braking, I finally spot Aircraft Y, right in front of me, on short final for Runway XY. I expected him to go around as I was still on the runway but he did not, so I expedited my turn to vacate the runway. Shortly after I crossed the hold short line, he touched down on the opposite runway I just landed on. Also, in the pattern was company flight. He was leaving the area during the event but heard the situation over the radio.After the investigation it was clear the other pilot violated right of way rule and landed in reduced safety standards.
ASRS:1832364.s: The pilot reported a runway incursion at ZZZ while landing on Runway XX, where Aircraft Y landed on the opposite Runway XY without yielding right of way. The investigation concluded the other pilot violated right-of-way rules and landed under reduced safety standards.

ASRS:1832375.n: Acceptance flight for new UAS was being conducted in the field with LAANC authorization. Since this was a first flight, the vehicle was placed in a hover approximately 15 feet for observation. After approximately 1 minute and with no control input from the RPIC (Remote Pilot in Command), the vehicle went into abrupt left graveyard spiral. This is the expected flight behavior for motor failure in a quad configuration. The failed motor was identified on postflight inspection and replaced with a spare motor. Subsequent flight exhibited the same motor failure after approximately 3 minutes, however there was no damage due to keeping the vehicle in a low hover. Operation Center was notified of the event. Tech support from the manufacturer revealed that the vehicle software was not properly matched to the controller software. A field software update was applied and subsequent fixed, low hover testing was successful for approximately 10 minutes. Build up testing was accomplished to demonstrate the vehicle to be fully mission capable.1) Future acceptance testing (first flights of a vehicle or new config) should follow the procedure used today. Fly in a fixed, low hover for several minutes to validate vehicle stability before conducting further checks. 2) This incident highlights the importance of ensuring proper software configuration on components of the system: flight controller, gimbal, ESCs (electronic speed controller), and controller. Although the manufacturer had been involved with a software update the previous day, even they missed verifying this configuration with us until it was revealed on the acceptance flight.
ASRS:1832375.s: During a UAS acceptance flight hover at 15 feet, the vehicle entered a graveyard spiral due to a motor failure caused by mismatched flight controller and controller software. A field software update resolved the issue, allowing successful subsequent testing and mission capability verification.

ASRS:1832389.n: Departed ZZZ on time. As we were approaching 10,000 ft. at XA:36, Flight Attendant (FA) received communication and instructions from Captain (CA) that the cabin was experiencing a decompression and would be diverting back to ZZZ promptly. Captain proceeded to brief passengers with the announcement of diversion due to safety. FA promptly made announcements to reaffirm CA announcements and proceeded to prepare the cabin for landing. Communication between FA and CA was timely and efficient x 4. The flight landed without incident, First Officer (FO) deplaned immediately to inspect the cargo door and vent door. Passengers then deplaned normally without incident.
ASRS:1832389.s: The crew diverted back to ZZZ after the Captain reported a cabin decompression at 10,000 ft. The flight landed safely, and the First Officer inspected the cargo and vent doors immediately after deplaning.

ASRS:1832401.n: On climbout, smelled musty smell. Was concerned how my mask hindered my ability to smell and clearly communicate with my coworker.
ASRS:1832401.s: During climbout, a pilot detected a musty odor and expressed concern that their mask impaired their ability to smell and communicate with a coworker. The report does not identify the specific cause or outcome of the odor.

ASRS:1832405.n: We started our preflight ETOPS Pre-Departure Check of Aircraft X. Woke plane up and noticed aircraft had a Fuel Auto Transfer fault and we noticed 5,000 pounds in center tank. Wings were approx. 10,000 pounds. Per Company Manual XX-XX-XX-XXX-XXXA needed to move fuel center tank to wing tanks. while transferring fuel from center tanks to wing tanks per AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) XX-XX-XX-XXX-XXXA paragraph X fault extinguished. Fuel transferred from 5,000 pounds to 800 pounds. At 800 pounds, fuel jumped to approximately 2,000 pounds and a fuel overflow message on the R/H wing.
