Shut off fuel pumps and stopped transferring operations. Fuel load on flight plan 36,000 pounds. Current fuel load on aircraft 30,000 pounds fuel density was 6.58 RH wing vent box fuel spill. Previous start up messages on fuel system. Fueler fueled during fuel transfer. Fuel door was open. Fuel indicators reflected fuel transfer. Fueler didn't notice fuel transfer approaching max wing tank capacity. Fueler didn't notice transfer in progress while setting fuel load prior to fueling A/C. Shut down fuel transferring procedures and cleaned up fuel spill.
ASRS:1832405.s: During preflight ETOPS checks on Aircraft X, a fuel auto transfer fault cleared while moving fuel from the center tank, but a fueler unaware of the transfer overfilled the right wing tank, causing a spill. The crew stopped the transfer and cleaned the spill after the fueler failed to notice the transfer approaching maximum wing capacity.

ASRS:1832413.n: Flying from ZZZ to ZZZ1 takes approximately four hours in this aircraft. Normal fuel management requires the takeoff and the first hour on the mains, then two hours on the auxiliary tanks, finishing the final hour on the main tanks. There was a tail wind that day so the distance traveled on each set of tanks increased. Just prior to ZZZ [VOR] the final fuel switch was made from the auxiliary tanks to the mains. Approximately twenty minute later, the left engine started to surge. Scanning all engine monitoring instruments showed normal temperatures, RPM, fuel flow, and manifold pressures being matched by each engine. The engine returned to normal cruise profile for about fifteen to twenty seconds, then surged violently. Thinking it may be a fuel contamination problem, I switched the left tank back to the auxiliary tank knowing that there was approximately fifteen minutes of fuel remaining. The left engine continued to surge and RPM of the left engine would not go above fifteen hundred RPM. I contacted Approach, apprised them of the situation and requested vectors to the closest airport, which happened to be ZZZ2. They vectored me towards ZZZ2 when the engine decided that it had had enough. The aircraft was handling erratically, so I decided to cage the engine and make the approach and landing on the remaining right engine, I had seven thousand feet to descend to airport elevation with only ten miles to accomplish it, so I circled the airport to the south to keep a right hand pattern into the airport. There was a successful landing and difficult taxi to tie down where I was met with the local [officials] and rescue squad. An inspection a couple days later with a certified A&P found that there was a leak around the filler cap on the left main tank which allowed the low pressure over the wing to suction out the entire tank. The main filler caps are hid from the pilot's view by the engine nacelle. I believe that after three and a half hours of flying through IMC up to the point of the incident weighed heavily on my initial decision not to cage the engine, but to try to troubleshoot problem and on this particular aircraft, the fuel gauges are obscured by the power levers and my initial scan failed to see the amount remaining in the left main tank.
ASRS:1832413.s: The pilot experienced a left engine surge and failure during cruise due to a fuel leak at the left main tank filler cap, which emptied the tank. After troubleshooting failed, the pilot caged the engine and executed a successful single-engine landing at ZZZ2.

ASRS:1832443.n: On Date about XA45 PM local time, during roll out after landing on Runway XX in ZZZ in Aircraft X, the plane veered to the right and exited the runway surface and came to rest in the soft mud just to the right of the runway. We departed ZZZ1 enroute to ZZZ, at XB25 local time on a part 135 passenger charter flight with passengers, their luggage, and groceries for ZZZ, and after a nice 2 hour and 20-minute VFR flight we arrived at ZZZ. We made a pass overhead of Runway XY to check the windsock, and then flew out about 3 miles and made a teardrop back to final to Runway XX. When we did our wind check I observed the windsock to be showing about 5 kts. or less of wind out of about 070 degrees. When we were on final to Runway XX, I again looked at the windsock and observed it to be showing about 10-15 kts. of wind at about a 30-degree right crosswind to the runway. After a normal approach and touchdown, during rollout while the tail was still in the air, I could feel the rudder starting to become less effective and the wind wanting to push the tail to the left, so as quickly as I could I got the tail wheel planted firmly on the ground to help with directional control. As the plane was slowing down through an estimated 35-40 kts. the plane started to veer to the right, I immediately applied full left rudder and pumped the left brake to make sure that we were getting maximum effectiveness out of the left brake. After rolling about another 100 ft., I realized that it was not likely that we were going to be able to get the plane straight again, so then I applied maximum right brake also and was just trying to get the plane stopped before it went off the side of the runway. When we were about 100-150 ft. from going off the runway the Copilot also applied maximum braking, but nothing we did was able to keep the plane on the runway, we went off the right side of the runway about 1,000-1,200 ft. from the end. The plane stopped quickly in the soft mud that was just off of the runway. We then did a quick assessment of the passengers and after none of them reported any injuries we evacuated the passengers and then secured the aircraft. There were no known pre-accident mechanical issues with the aircraft. Of the passengers and 2 crew members on board, there were no reported injuries. After the incident was over as I was back on the ramp, I was able to observe the windsock for a while. I noticed that the wind would be anywhere between 5 and 15-20 kts. and the direction would shift between approximately 060 and 150 degrees. At the time we landed I would estimate that the clouds were about 2,000-2,500 ft. broken-overcast and greater than 10 miles visibility. The ceilings and visibility did deteriorate throughout the day.
ASRS:1832443.s: During rollout after landing a Part 135 charter flight on Runway XX, the aircraft veered right and exited into soft mud due to a strong, shifting crosswind that reduced rudder effectiveness. Despite maximum braking and rudder inputs by both pilots, directional control was lost, resulting in an off-runway stop with no injuries to the two crew members or passengers.

ASRS:1832446.n: My copilot and I were doing a demonstration flight at 28,000 and then on heading back to ZZZ out of 28,000 to 18,000 I noticed smoke coming out of the right side of the flight deck we immediately put on our oxygen mask and ran the emergency checklist and [requested priority handling] and headed back to ZZZ Airport and landed without any incident.
ASRS:1832446.s: Two pilots experienced smoke in the right flight deck while descending from 28,000 to 18,000 feet during a demonstration flight. They donned oxygen masks, executed the emergency checklist, requested priority handling, and landed safely at ZZZ Airport without incident.

ASRS:1832449.n: During landing, overcorrected on the steering left, and went off the runway to the left, and R/H stabilator tip hit a runway light.
ASRS:1832449.s: During landing, the pilot overcorrected steering to the left, causing the aircraft to exit the runway. The right-hand stabilator tip subsequently struck a runway light.

ASRS:1832464.n: I used Airmap to look up the address of inspection location but did not type in physical address. I referenced the town of Tucker which was in Class G airspace but the actual location of the flight was a mile and a half west in Class D (PDK). No prior authorization was requested. Flight was completed and I was made aware of the flight error by management and we discussed the importance of looking up physical location.
ASRS:1832464.s: The pilot conducted a flight in Class D airspace at PDK without prior authorization after incorrectly referencing a Class G location in Tucker via Airmap. Management identified the error post-flight, leading to a discussion on the necessity of verifying physical addresses before flight.

ASRS:1832490.n: As weight left the wheels, my primary and secondary nav, heading, DG, compass failed. Along with the failures I had a PWS (Predictive Wind Shear) fail message and a TCAS fail message. My flight director failed as well. As we continued to climb, FO flying the aircraft, I began to troubleshoot the problems. I ran 2 checklist as they did not correct the issues. I opted to return to ZZZ. At that time I requested priority handling. I continued to communicate with company, FAs and passengers. The FO flew the ILS to [Runway] XXR. We landed and taxi to the terminal.
ASRS:1832490.s: The Captain reported that immediately after takeoff, the aircraft experienced simultaneous failures of navigation, heading, PWS, TCAS, and flight director systems. After troubleshooting failed, the crew returned to ZZZ for a priority ILS landing on Runway XXR.

ASRS:1832527.n: During cruise check PM noticed an Abnormal Cabin Pressurization indication at 16,000 feet based on Cabin Altitude versus differential pressure chart, MEL BOOK (Section X, Page X). At the moment Cabin Altitude was indicating 4,400 feet, Cabin Rate 700, Delta P 7.1 crew observed for about 1 minute and noticed that cabin altitude continued to rise up to 5,900 feet. Captain immediately requested lower (10,000 feet) and informed ATC about the situation. At 10,000 feet the cabin altitude remained steady 5,500 feet and Cabin Rate indicated 0. Crew followed QRH procedure (PRESSURIZATION AUTO SYSTEM FAILURE/CABIN DEPRESSURIZATION/CABIN RATE ABNORMAL FLUCTUATIONS). ACARS was INOP. Captain contacted Dispatcher through AIRINC notified about the issue. Crew and Dispatcher agreed to stay at 10,000 feet. Crew had terrain mode selected all time for situational awareness. Also, FA was notified about the problem. The entire flight we were VMC. Crew landed in ZZZ. At the gate Captain wrote up the problem, and contacted Maintenance.
ASRS:1832527.s: During cruise at 16,000 feet, the crew observed abnormal cabin pressurization with rising cabin altitude and descended to 10,000 feet following QRH procedures. The aircraft landed safely at ZZZ after the crew coordinated with dispatch and maintenance regarding the pressurization system failure.

ASRS:1832557.n: Approaching ZZZ (50 minutes into flight), Captain's airspeed tape went to zero and altimeter jumped to 250 ft. high at FL340. FD (Flight Director), AT (Autothrottles), and AP (Autopilot) went away accordingly. Captain's airspeed slowly recovered and failed multiple times. Priority handling was asked with no firetruck response needed. Diversion was coordinated with Dispatch to ZZZ. First Officer's data was always correct. Approach and landing were uneventful. ZZZ Approach and Tower were very helpful with groundspeed calls to verify airspeed. The courier compartment was wet when we arrived at the plane and an E&E Inspection was accomplished for water intrusion before departure. [This was probably caused by] ADC failure.
ASRS:1832557.s: The Captain experienced an Air Data Computer failure at FL340, causing airspeed and altitude indications to fail and disconnecting the autopilot and autothrottles. The crew diverted to ZZZ, where Approach provided groundspeed calls to verify airspeed, resulting in an uneventful landing and subsequent water intrusion inspection.

ASRS:1832562.n: On a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 while in icing conditions we received an HSDI FAIL CAS message. We started reviewing the QRH for HSDI FAIL when the HSDI FAIL ON appeared and the HSDI FAIL went out. We ran the HSDI FAIL ON QRH procedure twice with no results. We had exited icing at that point so we continued to ZZZ1. The HSDI FAIL ON CAS stayed on until shutdown in ZZZ1. We powered the plane up in ZZZ1 via a GPU and then started the right engine, we did not receive any HSDI CAS messages, we did cycle the HDSI system on and off and the valve seems to work normally on the ground. We departed ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 and climbing out we entered icing conditions, the IPS (Ice Penetration System) turned on automatically. We received both an HSDI FAIL and a HSDI FAIL ON CAS while in icing conditions. We exited icing conditions and diverted to ZZZ3, the HSDI FAIL ON CAS stayed on until shutdown in ZZZ3.
ASRS:1832562.s: The flight crew experienced recurring HSDI FAIL and HSDI FAIL ON CAS messages during icing conditions on flights from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and ZZZ1 to ZZZ2. The crew diverted to ZZZ3 after the faults reappeared in icing, though the system functioned normally on the ground.

ASRS:1832646.n: On Date, my student and I departed ZZZ1 in Aircraft X at approximately XA40 local time. While maneuvering over the ZZZ practice area at 4,000 feet MSL, our engine quit. We began turning towards my chosen landing site on [an] island as I was troubleshooting. I had my student run the 'Power loss in flight' checklist followed by the 'If no restart & time permits' checklist.We were unable to restart the engine so I continued setting up for a forced landing. During the rollout, we contacted a dirt berm which allowed us to decelerate and come to a complete stop in approximately 200 feet. We landed at approximately XB20 local time. Both my student and I sustained no injuries.
ASRS:1832646.s: The pilot and student experienced an engine failure in Aircraft X at 4,000 feet MSL over the ZZZ practice area. After unsuccessful restart attempts, they executed a forced landing on an island, contacting a dirt berm to stop safely with no injuries.

ASRS:1832657.n: While in cruise from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with my instructor on my instrument training long cross country, our plane began automatically lowering and raising the landing gear with the gear lever in the up position. When the gear would lowered automatically they would not lock into position and show three green lights indicating they were down and locked in place, rather they would just begin retracting after some time. After they continued to do this for several cycles of up and down we informed ZZZ Approach of the issue and said we needed to divert to ZZZ2. Approach informed us they were [giving us priority] and we asked if we could complete a low approach to over Runway XX to see if ZZZ2 tower could verify our gear was down when we moved the lever into the down position and if everything looked down then complete a landing on the second approach. On an extended final for our low approach we lowered the gear with the gear lever and they stayed down and indicated three green, the Tower verified they were all down. We completed a successful landing to a full stop on the 2nd approach and were able to taxi and exit the runway safely. After departing ZZZ to ZZZ1 on an IFR flight plan (a training flight with me as CFI) and climbing to our assigned altitude at 4,000 feet, the 'Gear In Transit' light illuminated and the gear extended without pilot operation. Upon checking aircraft systems (circuit breakers, warning lights, etc.) we advised ATC of the gear malfunction and advised we would be diverting to ZZZ2. [ATC was advised]. The gear a few minutes after extension then retracted on its own without pilot intervention. I placed the gear in the down position and got three 'Gear Down' annunciations. I did a low approach and ZZZ2 tower confirmed the gear 'appeared to be down.' With this and normal gear down annunciations we landed without incident to anyone on board or to the aircraft, and had maintenance investigate, to which they found a malfunctioning landing gear electric power pack.
ASRS:1832657.s: During an IFR training cruise, the aircraft's landing gear cycled automatically due to a malfunctioning electric power pack. The crew diverted, verified gear extension via a low approach, and landed safely after maintenance confirmed the fault.

ASRS:1832658.n: The airport management changed hands in 2007. Since then the current management has decided to not mow areas on airport which caused a dramatic increase in wildlife which has directly attributed to two bird strikes. Coyotes have started to wander on the airport runways hunting for food in the grossly over grown ditches next to taxiways and runways. Wind socks and flags have rotted and have fallen off poles. FARs have been proposed with no FAA approval. Ramps have been blocked off from GA pilots. Gates have had the combinations changed without notice to the pilots and placed high on the gate out of reach without the assistance of a ladder. Landing practice has been stopped due to noise. Grass landing areas designated by airport design have purposely been blocked by wrecked aircraft placement and at these same areas large vehicles were instructed to drive on the grass in order to cause rutting. Even bathrooms have over flowed and toilet paper not restocked is a normal occurrence. The pilots at 3J1 are asking for help.
ASRS:1832658.s: Pilots at airport 3J1 reported that poor management since 2007 caused overgrown vegetation, attracting wildlife and resulting in two bird strikes. Additionally, deteriorating infrastructure, blocked ramps, and inaccessible gates have degraded airport operations and safety.

ASRS:1832659.n: We recently purchased a new Piper P100i directly from the manufacturer. The aircraft was picked up and delivered by one of our staff members. We started conducting flight operations with the airplane last week. I conducted two days on flight training. Both days we conducted cross country flights. The aircraft has the latest advance avionics from Garmin ( G3X, GNX 375, G5). I verified that the POH was present prior to the flights. After reading the POH [Pilot's Operating Handbook] more carefully this morning I realized that the pilots guide for the Garmin G3X, G5 and GNX 375 were required documents, as listed in the limitations section. I have electronic copies of the manuals but no hard copies of the manuals were provided by the manufacturer of the airplane when it was received by our staff member at their plant. We have grounded the airplane and initiated an investigation. We are contacting Piper Aircraft and Garmin to determine if the part numbers listed in the POH require hard copies or if the electronic versions of the documents are adequate to meet all regulatory requirements. Our safety team will conduct a safety audit of the aircraft, its records, and all its documents today. I recently started training in this new aircraft PA28. Today I was informed by the Chief Pilot that there were documents missing from the aircraft. The plane is missing the physical copy of the pilot's guide for the Garmin G3X, G5 and GNX 375. All three of these documents are listed as required documents in limitations section of the POH [Pilot's Operating Handbook]. We have electronic copies, but do not have the hard copies of the manuals. The manuals were not provided by the manufacturer when the plane was released to one of our instructors. We have grounded the plane and are not flying until we receive these documents. The school is looking into verifying all the required manuals, and moving forward I will verify that I acknowledge all limitations prior to my flights.
ASRS:1832659.s: A pilot and instructor grounded a new Piper PA28 after discovering missing hard copies of required Garmin G3X, G5, and GNX 375 pilot guides listed in the POH limitations. The manufacturer failed to provide these physical manuals upon delivery, prompting an investigation into regulatory compliance before flight operations resume.

ASRS:1832670.n: Started our flight in ZZZ2 to ZZZ1, ZZZ, ZZZ2 for our commercial cross country requirement. Had flight planned around XA:00am with the student for our departure at XH:30 pm. Flight up to ZZZ1 was uneventful, burned we burned 21 gallons going up, leaving us with 29 gallons to get to ZZZ. The flight planned showed we required 19 gallons to land at ZZZ where we planned to refuel before returning to ZZZ2. This left us with 10 gallons reserve, meaning over 1 hour of flight time at cruise. Roughly 50 miles out from ZZZ we had engine roughness and realized we had pulled the tank dry, so we swapped tanks again with no issue. We knew we had a reserve left and headed directly for ZZZ. Upon entering the pattern and turning base (2 miles) the engine sputtered again and we knew we had run out of gas. Knowing we would not make the runway we notified ATC and landed uneventfully on highway. Fire responded with no injuries or damage. ZZZ ground crew towed the airplane to the airport we had an A&P check everything over, added fuel, did a ground run, everything checked out good and we continued the flight to ZZZ2. Coincidentally when we fueled at ZZZ knowing the airplane has a 50 gallon capacity and the POH says all 50 gallons usable, from dead empty the plane only took 48.2 gallons. In conclusion, during the flight back from ZZZ1 to ZZZ we knew the head wind was more than we had factored for so we recalculated midair and that is where our mathematical error came into play. A simple addition mistake caused us to land just short of the runway that night.
ASRS:1832670.s: A pilot and student flying a commercial cross-country flight ran out of fuel due to a mathematical error in fuel planning while approaching ZZZ. They executed an uneventful off-airport landing on a highway with no injuries or damage after the engine sputtered on base leg.

ASRS:1832706.n: While at cruise en route to ZZZ, we received a TO Data Available message via ACARS. Shortly after, Dispatch notified us that the HAZMAT we had onboard (we had proper paperwork for the HAZMAT) was not included in the Zero Fuel Weight (ZFW) calculations. We reviewed the new Takeoff Data for the correct ZFW and made the adjustment to the FMC, and calculated new landing data for that weight. The rest of the flight proceeded as normal.
ASRS:1832706.s: The flight crew received an ACARS alert during cruise that hazardous materials were excluded from the Zero Fuel Weight calculation. They updated the FMC with corrected takeoff and landing data, and the flight continued normally.

ASRS:1832716.n: While parked at spot XX on the ramp at ZZZ we were cleared to start the engines. After starting the left engine we noticed a strange smell. There were 4 crew members on the flight deck so we discussed the situation. After asking the Lead Flight Attendant if they could smell anything strange, to which they could not, we thought it could be something from the outside being sucked into the ventilation system. We decided to start the right engine and see if things cleared up. After a normal start we heard a grinding/thumping sound (hard to tell exactly, but definitely not normal). We immediately shut both engines down only to find out that the APU had also shut down. The plane was now dark. I tried to restart the APU only to find out that nothing worked. One of the Relief pilots went down into the amp bay to see if he could find the source of the smell and now smoke. The smoke was not very thick so we had no reason to think there was a threat of fire. The FO found that a box had shorted out and burned several wire bundles. There was no further evidence of a fire so the Captain decided to have the plane towed back to the gate and the passengers removed. I included 2 threats for Flight Attendant and crew communication because after the incident we had no PA system to communicate with the flight attendants in case an evacuation was needed. This would have slowed down the process. After push back and disconnect from the tug, the left (#1) engine was started. Upon commencement of the right (#2) engine start a very faint electrical odor was sensed. We deemed it prudent to call door 1 to inquire if the flight attendants also noticed any smell or smoke, to which they responded negative. as the right engine became stabilized after start the smell became worse and a shuddering or thumping sound was heard. No flight deck warnings occurred but there appeared to be some electrical malfunctions on the overhead panel (window heat lights flicking on and off). We decided as a crew that shutting down both engines promptly was the best move, to remediate the situation as quickly as possible. After both engines shut down, the APU failed leaving us with battery power only. At this time we noticed a small amount of smoke in the cockpit, but decided it was not dangerous enough to issue an emergency evacuation of the aircraft. The second Relief Pilot went into the cabin and stated there was smoke there as well, and he could see what appeared to be a burn mark in the amp compartment. With only one operable radio we had to switch between communication with Ramp Tower and Operations. This caused some confusion as to who we should be talking to, in order to get an expeditious return to the gate. The Ramp Tower controller did not seem to think the situation was urgent and this may have led to a delay in having a tug and ground crew called to return us to the gate. Flight attendants and passengers were briefed and there were no adverse events in the cabin. We returned to the departure gate uneventfully. Fire and police were called to be on hand and inspect the aircraft. Upon parking an exterior walk around was performed and no exterior damage noted.
ASRS:1832716.s: The flight crew experienced an electrical short in the amp bay causing smoke and engine shutdowns while parked at the ramp. The aircraft was towed back to the gate for inspection after the APU failed and communication systems were compromised, with no fire or injuries reported.

ASRS:1832749.n: While flying the Stadium Visual Approach to Runway 29 at Newark Liberty Airport as Pilot Flying, I saw a white squarish object pass off the lower right side of the aircraft in my peripheral vision. I asked the co-pilot what that had been and he replied it had been a drone. We were at approximately 1000 feet in a descending right turn between the fixes SLIMR and CHUMR. I would estimate the drone had passed underneath the right wing at less than 100 feet separation but far enough away to feel reasonably confident that it had not struck the airplane. The co-pilot agreed and then alerted Newark Tower of the presence of the drone on final approach so that they could pass this information on to the succeeding aircraft on approach. They requested that after landing we provide them with any additional description we could, which we did with Ground Control after clearing the runway and beginning our initial taxi to the gate.
ASRS:1832749.s: The Pilot Flying and co-pilot encountered a drone while descending on a visual approach to Newark Runway 29 between 1000 feet and the runway. The drone passed under the right wing with less than 100 feet separation, prompting the crew to alert Tower and Ground Control to warn succeeding aircraft.

ASRS:1832831.n: Had electrical issues on climbout of ZZZ. Diverted to ZZZ1 and advised ATC.
ASRS:1832831.s: The pilot experienced electrical issues during climbout from ZZZ. The aircraft was diverted to ZZZ1, and ATC was advised.

ASRS:1832869.n: We were loaded up on a brand new Max headed to ZZZ1. Shortly after initial speed up but before rotation we hear this loud pop sound from the #1 engine area. Then the plane fish tailed slightly to the left, we then hear braking and the reverse engine thrust and come to fast stop and an aborted take off. Sat on runway for about 10 seconds in silence. Aircraft stopped very quickly, no injuries reported from cabin that we could hear from passengers. Unknown damage at full stop.Parked on runway we then within a minute hear pilot on PA say to stay seated with seat belt on, as we will return to the gate to get it all checked. Pilot then calls flight attendant's (FA) on phone to alert us that everything is okay that we had a malfunction and we aborted takeoff.
ASRS:1832869.s: Cabin crew on a new Boeing 737 MAX reported a loud pop from engine #1 and left yaw shortly after takeoff roll, causing an aborted departure. The aircraft stopped quickly with no injuries, and the crew returned to the gate for inspection due to an unspecified engine malfunction.

ASRS:1832870.n: It was a very early show time XA:30. Once we landed in ZZZ, we had over 2.5 hr wait time for next flight. We had experienced a maintenance issue on the first aircraft after we had already boarded passengers. We had to deplane. Do plane swap, board and taxi out for departure. Just before takeoff another issue with the second aircraft. Return to gate, wait for maintenance decision and deplane. Waiting for another aircraft, that's a third one. Waited in open hot air at the gate area for next crew. Felt nauseous and lightheaded. Impossible to continue. We had been dealing with extreme heat, upset passengers and stress due to maintenance issues. I have long haul COVID symptoms. Get tired faster than before. Coming back to full health is taking time. All together had put me in the mental and physical condition of being unable to continue my work duties at 100%.
ASRS:1832870.s: A flight crew member reported being unable to continue duties after two consecutive aircraft maintenance issues caused delays and deplaning in extreme heat. The crew member attributed their physical and mental condition to the stress, heat exposure, and lingering long-haul COVID symptoms.

ASRS:1832881.n: Passenger X, boarded with a backpack in ZZZ and inflight FA B, noticed he was on oxygen and there was no note of this in our special notes on our manuals. We asked him if he'd had it approved or made CSA aware of it and he said no. It was a [model name] and FA B and I talked with his travel companion, Name and explained that when they get to ZZZ1 they need to see an agent and get approval for the unit to be able to use it on their flight ZZZ1-ZZZ2. We did not switch him over to a Portable Oxygen Bottle (POB) because we were not sure of what flow he needed and did not want to interrupt his oxygen supply that was working for him. They both confirmed they will see an agent in ZZZ1 upon deplaning. No way to have been aware of this until we saw him using it mid flight. None of us could find a list of approved units anywhere on our manuals.Not sure...the backpack was just a normal generic backpack and was stowed for takeoff so until mid flight when we saw him using it we had no knowledge of it. We all tried to search 'approved O2 Concentrator' to see if it was approved but could not find a list on our manuals.
ASRS:1832881.s: Flight attendants discovered a passenger using an unapproved oxygen concentrator mid-flight on a [model name] aircraft because no special notes existed and no approved unit list was found in manuals. The crew did not switch the passenger to a portable oxygen bottle to avoid interrupting his supply and instructed him to seek agent approval upon arrival.

ASRS:1832887.n: Aircraft X called while in flight. He had a momentary fire warning light for the aft cargo pit. I advised him to follow the QRH and he subsequently diverted to ZZZ. NOTE: The B fire protection system was currently on MEL so the current fault was on the A side. He also told me that the discharge light was on which seemed odd to me because he didn't activate. Once the aircraft landed in ZZZ, I had contract maintenance pull and reset CB per maintenance notes in MEL XX-XX-C, which is what I used to get the airplane out of ZZZ. I missed step D of the MEL which should have had me INOP BOTH the forward and aft pits because one of the bottles is used. I thought because we still had a good bottle, I could dispatch with the aft pit empty. It appears that I should have used MEL XX-XX-B and deferred BOTH forward and aft pits. I found this MEL to be very confusing. XX-XX-C. The system has two fire bottles.
ASRS:1832887.s: An air traffic controller advised a pilot to divert after a momentary aft cargo fire warning on an aircraft with the B fire system on MEL. The controller later realized they incorrectly applied MEL XX-XX-C instead of XX-XX-B, failing to defer both cargo pits despite one bottle being used.

ASRS:1832923.n: A student that I signed off to solo ran off the runway during pattern work, took out a PAPI light and had a prop strike. The weather conditions were fantastic with calm winds and unlimited visibility. The student had completed 7 previous touch and go's with no issues but on the 8th lost directional control after touchdown and ran off the runway. The student in question had 51 hours of total time and approximately 3 hours of solo time before the occurrence. The lack of ADM (Aeronautical Decision Making) and physical motor skills to keep the plane on the runway led him to have an excursion. Corrective action is to make sure that he is not challenged with directional control and talk about decision making if something just doesn't seem right.
ASRS:1832923.s: A student pilot with 51 total hours lost directional control after touchdown during the eighth touch-and-go, causing a runway excursion, PAPI light damage, and prop strike. The instructor attributed the incident to the student's lack of aeronautical decision-making and physical motor skills.

ASRS:1832926.n: Running practice approach for Runway XX at ZZZ. Hand flying, drifted high on glide path at about 2 miles out. Pitched to return to glide path and failed to pull throttle enough and airspeed increased. I didn't notice it until I crossed the threshold and was still doing 118kts. Normal approach with 10% flaps is 100. There was also a gusty crosswind and I was focused on maintaining alignment and centerline. Ended up landing almost 2,000 feet down the 5,000 feet runway. Continuing to maintain centerline, I saw the end of the runway coming up quickly and braked hard, speed then was 49 kts. Crossed the end of the runway into the grass at approximately 20 kts, continued to slow, executed a hard left turn and rejoined taxiway. Subsequent inspection showed no taxi light damage and no damage to gear. I need to maintain a closer watch on airspeed even when dealing with gusty crosswind, don't get fixated.
ASRS:1832926.s: The pilot hand-flew a practice approach in gusty crosswinds, drifting high and failing to reduce throttle, resulting in a 118-knot threshold crossing. The aircraft landed 2,000 feet down the runway, overran into grass at 20 knots, and rejoined the taxiway with no damage.

ASRS:1832928.n: Engine failure on take off at ZZZ in a CSA SportCruiser. After a successful run-up, my student applied full power for our take off roll and engine indications were green with 5,000 RPM. At about 200 feet AGL, engine RPM decreased from 5,000 to 2,000 with a very rough engine. 2,000 RPM is not sustainable for flight in the SportCruiser. I took flight controls and landed on the remaining runway and taxied back to parking with out incident. At maintenance, it was determined that the connection for the outside air filter for the carburetor and the carburetor itself was loose and became completely detached on take off which lead to the large RPM drop.
ASRS:1832928.s: A pilot and student experienced an engine failure in a CSA SportCruiser at 200 feet AGL during takeoff at ZZZ due to a loose carburetor air filter connection that detached. The pilot landed safely on the remaining runway after RPM dropped to an unsustainable 2,000.

ASRS:1832934.n: Student and instructor were on a night cross-country. Traffic pattern was entered and to verify wind direction we did not descend on downwind but continued on an upwind leg to ensure we would be ready for the landing. We turned crosswind and downwind and did our before landing procedure. Student was slow to configure the aircraft which extended the downwind leg further than desired and upon turning base we noted we were low on the VASI. The student made a correction to get back on/above the glide path which was too little. I as the instructor was too late and too slow to inspire a more aggressive correction until the top of the tree came into view. I took control of the airplane and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. There was no indication of flight control malfunction nor any indication of a loss of engine RPM. Subsequent inspection revealed slight damage to the right main landing gear fairing and damage to the left horizontal stabilizer fairing. I suspect that the propeller may have been impacted but there was no sudden stoppage of the prop. Of note, when the runway lights were activated by the CTAF, the lights on the north side of the runway from midfield to the departure end did not illuminate. What did come on was all of the lights on the south side of the runway and half the lights on the north side from the approach end to midfield. Also, I'm aware that the VASI glide slope angle is set higher than a three degree glide slope because of obstructions (trees) and the angle used to be published in the Chart Supplement, but that information is no longer available.
ASRS:1832934.s: A student and instructor on a night cross-country entered a traffic pattern but became low on the VASI due to delayed configuration. The instructor took control to avoid trees, landing safely with minor fairing damage, while noting partial runway light failure and an unpublished steep glide slope.

ASRS:1832940.n: Glider landing Area is not properly maintained by Airport management. Grass is overgrown and small bushes are [growing]. In the case of a crosswind, a slight wing drop could generate a dangerous Ground-loop both during Aero-Tow and landing phases.
ASRS:1832940.s: The pilot reported that the airport management failed to maintain the glider landing area, leaving it overgrown with grass and bushes. This condition creates a risk of a dangerous ground-loop during aero-tow and landing phases if a crosswind causes a slight wing drop.

ASRS:1832946.n: The following is my best recall of the events between approximately XA:00 and XB:30 Zulu on Date which resulted in damage to the aircraft.Student: Private Pilot seeking a Multi Engine add on ratingThe day's lesson was an introduction to engine failure procedures in the aircraft. We had previously covered these procedures in our simulator, most recently on date [two days prior]. Before the flight we reviewed the lesson plan, which was to include:1. I would conduct all communication with ATC during the flight so that he could focus on procedures.2. A simulated engine failure on takeoff to be verbalized by me as 'engine failure' with the student responding by retarding both throttles to idle and declaring an aborted takeoff. He did not respond to my first call, but on the second call of 'engine failure' he followed the procedure correctly.3. Simulated engine failure on climb out by retarding one throttle to idle and with the student following the appropriate response flow, then resetting the throttle for climb to the practice area. This went according to plan.4. Upon reaching maneuvering altitude in the practice area (4,000 feet) a simulated engine failure with fuel selector set to Off and the student following the response flow and troubleshooting checklist. This was followed by securing the engine per the checklist, then restarting per the checklist. This all went according to plan.5. Demonstration and practice of the VMC maneuver with engine failure simulated by throttle setting. This went according to plan.6. Return for landing, with simulated engine failure by throttle setting. This went according to plan.After landing, I requested a taxi back to the ramp as I thought the student was maxed out for the day based on previous flights and how much we had covered. However, as we had about 40 minutes left in our lesson block he asked if we could do some pattern work. Per his request I requested taxi instructions to Runway XXR. Once reaching the hold short line for [Runway] XXR I failed to recognize that the remaining flight was no as longer planned, and failed to develop and verbalize a brief specific to it. I was still operating under the assumption that we were practicing simulated engine failures per the original flight plan. In hindsight I believe that the student was operating under the assumption that we were setting up for pattern work with no planned (simulated) failures. We received clearance to take off and the student entered the runway following all normal procedures. He advanced the throttles for takeoff, and once we were rolling, but before positive airspeed indication, I retarded the right mixture control to idle cutoff (which we had done in the simulator on the previous lesson). The student did not respond to the engine failure, keeping both throttles full for take off. We immediately started veering south toward the right side of the runway. I called for the student to retard the throttles, but he did not respond. I moved the right mixture control full forward to restart the engine in an effort to eliminate the asymmetric thrust and regain directional control, but by then we were crossing the runway edge and about to run into a taxiway location sign (Taxiway 1). At this point the student did retard both throttles to idle. The nose wheel struck the location sign and the left propeller struck either a runway edge light or a taxiway light. We stopped on Taxiway 1, but in the process made a looping turn and ended up facing east on the taxiway. The Tower controller called to ask if we were alright and I responded that we were. I requested and received taxi instructions to our maintenance hangar. After clearing Runway XXL on the east side I provided more detail to the Tower controller and informed them that I would call with additional detail once I was back at the office, which I did. Additionally, Operations and Security personnel came to the office and took a statement from me. At this point the student had already left the school.Contributing factors:1. My failure to properly brief the unplanned scenario with the student and anticipate the potential failure.2. The student's failure to follow established procedure.3. No brakes on the right side limited my options for regaining control.
ASRS:1832946.s: A flight instructor and student pilot damaged a multi-engine aircraft during a takeoff when the instructor simulated an engine failure without briefing the unplanned scenario. The student failed to respond to the simulated failure, causing the aircraft to veer off the runway and strike a taxiway sign and light.

ASRS:1832948.n: New operator of sUAS asked for tips from an acquaintance who is a private pilot and commercial remote operator. With a small group of onlookers the new operator demonstrated the drones capability looking intently at display and launching it within 2 ft of an onlookers face. The new operator immediately launched the drone over a ridge of trees and out of sight head down on the display. I commented that he needed to have the drone in sight at all times to which he laughed and replied 'No. That can't be, what would be the fun in that' he proceeded to inform me that because the UAS was below 0.55 lbs that it was exempt from FAA regulation. As the new operator blew past 400 feet AGL he asked what was the max altitude again? To which I responded accordingly. A round of laughter commenced as the operator received a notification on his display that he may be violating the law. The new operator reached a maximum horizontal distance of 1,600 feet which he complained was too little and was sure the software was preventing him from going farther as he had gone 6,000 feet without issue before.From takeoff to landing this operator never had visual contact with the drone.The new operator flew recklessly in a corridor popular with manned commercial scenic tours, GA aircraft sight seeing, and GA aircraft coming in to BHB.When informed of the regulations the operator laughed, indicated that it did not apply to him, and if he were to get in trouble he would blame it on a blog post he read. Blatant disregard for FAA regulations, the safety of others, and no expectation of consequences.FAA should make something similar to the commercial remote operator course for recreational operators and make it mandatory for any UAS that has the capability of exceeding 400 feet vertical or horizontal.FAA should also crack down on manufacturers who are clearly advertising their products and encouraging use in disagreement with law.
ASRS:1832948.s: A new recreational sUAS operator flew a sub-0.55 lb drone recklessly in a corridor used by manned aircraft, exceeding 400 feet AGL and 1,600 feet horizontal distance without visual contact. The operator ignored FAA regulations, claiming exemption, and refused to maintain line-of-sight despite warnings.

ASRS:1832950.n: I had just taken over as [Sector] Controller 2 minutes prior to this event. Aircraft X was talking to ZZZ Approach on the ZZZZZ arrival. The previous [Sector] Controller had coordinated this aircraft stopped at 14,000 due to another emergency aircraft he had worked earlier. ZZZZZ aircraft, by procedure are already issued an OPD (Optimal Profile Descent) except maintain 14,000. Aircraft Y was descending via the ZZZZZ1 arrival. The aircraft neared the ZZZ approach boundary and I had to call Approach for a hand off. The Controller asked if Aircraft Y was descending OPD to which I replied yes and asked if the aircraft was radar contact. She replied no because the aircraft was not separated from Aircraft X. These aircraft are procedurally separated. I was forced to turn Aircraft Y but as I issued the turn away from approach, the Controller accepted the hand off. As a result of this I violated ZZZ approaches airspace without a hand off. I expedited Aircraft Y to 11,000 and shipped the aircraft to ZZZ Approach. The CIC spoke to the ZZZ Approach Supervisor who stated the Controller was new to the procedures. I don't believe this alleviates the need to know basic procedures of separation before plugging in and controlling traffic. The ZZZ Controller created an unsafe situation for no reason by forcing me to turn out Aircraft Y.The procedures work fine as long as the Controller knows how to use them.
ASRS:1832950.s: The Sector Controller reported that a new ZZZ Approach Controller refused handoff of Aircraft Y due to perceived separation issues with Aircraft X, forcing an airspace violation. The Controller expedited Aircraft Y to 11,000 feet, attributing the unsafe situation to the Approach Controller's lack of procedural knowledge.

ASRS:1832965.n: Aircraft X was departing on the ZZZ1 Obstacle Departure Procedure which climbs on a heading to intercept a VORTAC radial. The aircraft was NW bound, as expected, when the pilot advised that they were not receiving the VORTAC and requested a radar vector. The aircraft was at 3,200 in a 4,000 ft. MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). I explained that I was unable to vector and issued a low altitude alert. I advised the pilot to remain on the DP (Departure Procedure) if able.Aircraft was above EOVM (Emergency Obstruction Video Map) altitude, very near the airport, and on a general heading that mirrored the departure procedure and would clear the 4,000 foot MVA in a timely manner. The aircraft then turned towards the east and higher terrain. I re-issued a low altitude alert, instructed the aircraft to expedite the climb and upon reaching 4,000 ft., turn to a heading of 270. The aircraft reached 4,000 ft. and turned westbound. I put the aircraft on course and notified management. Reports from other aircraft indicated the VORTAC was functioning.I was instructed by management that I should have issued a vector to the aircraft below the MVA because it was an emergency. I was talked to and warned to be more cautious and issue headings when a pilot asks for them when they are below the MVA. I did the wrong thing by issuing a low altitude alert. A vector below the MVA would have been more appropriate in this situation. I will learn from this situation. I consider myself fortunate for not being disciplined officially and am grateful I was only 'talked to' about this egregious lapse of control judgment.
ASRS:1832965.s: An ATC controller issued a low altitude alert to a departing aircraft at 3,200 feet that lost VORTAC reception and turned toward higher terrain. Management later criticized the controller for not issuing a radar vector below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude, resulting in a verbal warning for poor judgment.

ASRS:1833018.n: After taking high speed runway turnoff NN off 8R at IAH, Tower instructed us to join SF. There was a line of aircraft on NA eastbound and both my First Officer and I missed that NN becomes SF. I followed the aircraft thinking they were going to join SF. We had originally planned to exit at NK and I turned eastbound on NA thinking SF was next right turn taxiway ahead. We informed ground control of our mistake and doubled back on NB and then joined SF southbound by their instruction. There was no conflict with other aircraft. The signage for NN turning into SF is nonexistent and in my runway turnoff I mistook and assumed SF would be ahead off NA. It was my mistake.
ASRS:1833018.s: The pilot and First Officer mistakenly turned eastbound on taxiway NA instead of joining SF after exiting runway 8R at IAH due to nonexistent signage. They corrected the error by doubling back on NB and joining SF southbound under ground control instructions with no aircraft conflict.

ASRS:1833026.n: During climb out through 14,000 ft. we noticed an amber oil pressure low indication on #2 engine. I was the PF(Pilot Flying) so I took the radios while the Captain ran the Engine Low Oil Pressure checklist which then directed him to the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist. The oil pressure dropped rapidly to approximately 3 PSI and the oil quantity dropped to 0. The checklist directed us to shutdown the #2 engine. We [requested priority handling] and coordinated with ATC for vectors to air return via the ILS XXL to ZZZ. We completed all appropriate checklists and coordinated with Dispatch, the flight attendants, and gave a reassuring PA to the passengers. The approach and landing were uneventful. After exiting the runway we were met by emergency vehicles and inspected. No damage or abnormalities were noted so we returned to gate X. We elected to shutdown and get towed to the gate. Two maintenance ELB (Electronic Log Book) entries were made and the Captain coordinated with Dispatch and the Chief Pilot via phone.
ASRS:1833026.s: During climb through 14,000 ft, the crew observed low oil pressure on engine #2, dropping to 3 PSI with zero quantity, prompting a shutdown per checklist. The aircraft returned safely via ILS XXL to ZZZ, landed without incident, and was towed to the gate for maintenance inspection.

ASRS:1833039.n: Received vector for initially an ILS to Runway 8R. Intercepted LOC just outside JELLI at 5,000 feet. Upon interception, glideslope captured aircraft autopilot began a 'substantial' descent (1,500 feet/min). At first I didn't think anything about it. Shortly after, we were cleared a visual approach. We were fully configured before MATON, and passing MATON I felt low on the approach, it was too shallow and looked wrong, and then I noticed our altitude was 1,200 feet MSL (1,100 feet AGL) when it should have been about 2,000 feet MSL. Flight Director still showed us on glide path. I immediately called out we were 800 feet low for some reason. Suspecting an instrument issue, I disconnected the autopilot, turned off the flight director, and began hand flying. We had been cleared a visual shortly after LOC capture and were visual, so I completed the final segment flying purely visually. I even took the precaution of having the First Officer deselect the ILS in the nav radio tuners. At approximately 1 mile from the runway threshold, I noticed 2 aircraft holding short on the north side of the approach end of 8R waiting clearance to cross. A B737 was holding short on Taxiway NE, and a E-170 was holding short at NR. It appeared those aircraft were causing interference of the glideslope signal resulting in the indications we were receiving on our instruments. Our manual recommends backing up a visual approach with the ILS, when available. However, good airmanship and situational awareness must always be maintained. An additional item: ATC gave us no call about our low altitude on the approach. I couldn't find it above anywhere on this form, but I could also consider this an incident which was successfully recognized and resolved in time with no incident. I have seen aircraft waiting to cross untold number of times, but never have I seen glideslope interference such as I saw during this approach.
ASRS:1833039.s: The pilot reported that during an ILS approach to Runway 8R, the autopilot descended excessively due to suspected glideslope interference from two aircraft holding short. The crew disconnected automation, hand-flew a visual approach, and landed safely without ATC altitude alerts.

ASRS:1833041.n: I was First Officer (FO) on Aircraft X operating to ZZZ. We were conducting the ILS XXR circle to XY approach when we received an abnormal landing gear indication. When I lowered the landing gear, the annunciator panel showed 3 red lights along with 3 green lights. The overhead panel showed 3 green as well. We briefly discussed continuing the landing as there was some confidence the gear was down. The discussion continued until around 500 ft. and I felt strongly that we shouldn't be making such consequential decisions that close to the ground without running a checklist. We performed a go-around, ran the checklist, got the gear down without the red lights, and landed successfully. ILS XXR circle XY at ZZZ. Lowered gear just prior to FAF (Final Approach Fix). 3 red, 3 green illuminated. After evaluating with First Officer (FO), executed go-around on XY due to gear disagree. Standard missed. Ran checklists. Vectored for longest runway... ILS XXR. Extended gear on 10-mile base. All indications normal. Executed normal landing. Taxi to gate to find puddle [of] hydraulic fluid at left main. Possibly unrelated.
ASRS:1833041.s: The First Officer on Aircraft X executed a go-around during the ILS XXR circle to XY approach at ZZZ due to conflicting landing gear indications (three red and three green lights). After running checklists and confirming normal gear extension, the crew landed successfully, later discovering a hydraulic fluid leak at the left main gear.

ASRS:1833051.n: Climbing out thru 14,000 ft. noticed engine #2 oil pressure in amber band. Oil pressure and quantity was dropping rapidly. Ran the 'Engine Low Oil Pressure' checklist followed by 'Engine Failure or Shutdown' checklist. No overweight landing. [Requested priority handling]. Normal approach and landing. Equipment met the aircraft after taxiing clear of runway. After getting the all clear from them we taxied to the gate and got tugged in. Called maintenance and dispatch. Spoke with Chief Pilot and maintenance. Made two maintenance entries. All went great.
ASRS:1833051.s: During climb through 14,000 ft, the pilot observed engine #2 oil pressure and quantity dropping rapidly. The crew executed relevant checklists, requested priority handling, and completed a normal landing before maintenance inspected the aircraft.

ASRS:1833066.n: Cargo Aircraft Only (CAO) label discovered during the loading process.
ASRS:1833066.s: Ground personnel discovered a Cargo Aircraft Only (CAO) label during the loading process. The narrative does not specify the aircraft type, phase of flight, or the outcome of this discovery.

ASRS:1833101.n: On visual approach to Runway 01L Tower Controller called an 'altitude alert'. We were cleared for the visual to Runway 01L to Tampa. The glideslope to the ILS 01L was NOTAM'd Out of Service. Tower instructed us to maintain 2,600 feet until north of Macdill AFB. I had briefed that this would cause us to be high and that I would configure the aircraft for landing at 2,600 feet and prior to Macdill. I had also briefed that we would need a high rate of descent to get us on glide path. Once north of Macdill, and runway in sight, I disconnected the autopilot, and started to hand fly the visual approach. At approximately 1,000 feet the First Officer stated we were approaching the (visual 3:1) glidepath. At that time, I had started to reduce the rate of descent. At about the same time the Tower called an altitude alert for Aircraft X. I started to pick up the PAPI and saw we were below glidepath. I continued reducing descent rate to intercept the PAPI glidepath. Aircraft was on glidepath and stable at 500 feet. Landed normally. [Suggest] Brief the visual in more detail on 3:1 glidepath and required rate of descent to intercept from above.
ASRS:1833101.s: The pilot and First Officer flew a visual approach to Runway 01L with the ILS glideslope out of service. After receiving an altitude alert while descending from 2,600 feet, the pilot adjusted the descent rate to intercept the PAPI glidepath and landed normally.

ASRS:1833173.n: After pushback from Gate XXX and given our taxi instructions 'XX-XY-XZ etc...' to XXL for departure, we commenced our single-engine taxi. While I was taxiing at a slow speed, taxi light on, I noticed a truck that appeared to be stopping on the roadway across Taxiway X between XZ and XY to give way to our aircraft. However, the truck did not stop and they rolled right through Taxiway X without giving way to our aircraft. I applied brake pressure to prevent the plane from hitting the truck. Due to the slow taxi speed, we did not think the braking action to prevent the collision was too firm to knock anyone down or warrant a drastic brace from anyone if they were up. We notified ATC about this taxiway incursion and they asked if there was an Operations car on frequency to go after the truck. We took off, were in cruise, and were past the CP (Critical Point) - [middle of the flight] - when we set up for the first bathroom break. I went out first and I asked [the] First Class Flight Attendant (FA), 'If everything is all right back here.' They responded, 'Yes.' I went to the bathroom, came back up to the cockpit, and was talking to the Purser who also said everything was 'fine' as well. When the First Officer (FO) came back he then informed me that [the] FA informed him that when I had to brake to not hit the truck, she hit her right side against the forward galley wall with some of the quarter turn edging. I then called back and asked if she needed medical help in ZZZ1. She replied that she was icing it and took Tylenol and she would not need medical attention in ZZZ1." I asked the other FAs if they were all right, one stated that they didn't even feel the braking action and two others stated they felt it as they were standing but everyone else was fine. To be clear, the first time I was told something was wrong was past the CP. Before departure I briefed the FAs that if there is anything wrong or abnormal, even if we are in sterile cockpit, do not hesitate to call up and let us know. Also, during the flight, no calls to see if [there were] medical personnel on board to help with an injury were made by the FA crew.Prior to the top of descent when we set up for another bathroom break, the Purser came in and I asked him how [the] FA was doing. He said, 'She seems fine, she wants to go home, she's just a little sore.' When I went out, I asked how she was doing. She stated, 'She wanted to call in enroute injured, but then wanted to deadhead home.' I told her, 'I don't know that they will be able to deadhead her home, but if she is enroute injured please let me know and I will contact Dispatch.' She then said she was 'enroute injured.' I said, 'Do you want medical treatment in ZZZ1.' She said, 'No.'I then texted Dispatch that we had an FA who was enroute injured and would call them when we landed per the reporting requirements. I also requested priority handling and asked the paramedics to meet the aircraft to evaluate her, just to be safe. We landed without incident. When the paramedics came on board, [the] FA refused additional medical care from them and stated to the FO, 'Why did you call them out, you didn't need to do that.' Appropriate reports were made per the manual to the Dispatcher [and others]." During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, most of which was uneventful, we had a minor injury on taxi out of our galley Flight Attendant (FA), but we were not notified until after the CP (Critical Point), [middle of the flight]. On taxi out we had to stop taxi for a truck that did not stop as we were taxiing X XY XZ from Gate XXX. As we came to a stop at the XX XY intersection, we at the time were more concerned about the truck that did not stop, and believed that we did not stop too abruptly for the truck but just more startled that it did not stop. Hindsight, we did not hear any clunking or hitting - and although we stopped slightly faster than normal, we did not realize that [the] FA may have been knocked off balance a little bit. We did make a call to Ground to let them know that the truck did not stop but we quickly continued our taxi not thinking too much of the incident. While the initial incident where [the] FA hit her arm may not have been that bad, it sounded like it got worse as we flew with some aching and building pain, so she let the flight crew, us, know about her sore arm and sore neck.As the flight continued, we reached radio/ACARS reception into ZZZ1 when [the] FA decided that the pain was too much and she was in flight injured and would not be able to work the return flight leg from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. As I continued to fly, the Captain (CA) coordinated with Dispatch and attempted to call ZZZ1 Operations to let them know the situation. After the CA was given all the information and was notified that she was incapacitated and unable to work the return flight, the decision was made to request priority handling [and] have paramedics meet us at the gate when we arrived to check on [the] FA.At top of descent the decision was made by [the] FA that her arm was hurt too much and after coordination with [the] FA, Dispatch, and calling Operations, we were approximately over ZZZ2 and the CA decided to request priority handling as a precaution due to an incapacitated crew member and in the best interest of the crew member's health. Our flight landed and taxied uneventfully and [the] FA [was] checked out by the airport paramedics. As we left the flight, we wished FA a speedy recovery, she seemed in good spirits.
ASRS:1833173.s: During single-engine taxi from Gate XXX, the flight crew braked to avoid a truck that failed to yield at a taxiway intersection, causing a Flight Attendant to strike the galley wall. The crew was not notified of the injury until past the critical point, leading to a request for paramedics upon landing, though the Flight Attendant refused further medical care.

ASRS:1833310.n: While climbing through 18,000 ft., we noticed the #1 engine had an amber 'XX' for the EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) display.No ECAM or status messages accompanied the failure of the EGT.The lack of ECAM messages for loss of EGT, along with no guidance in the QRH, led the FO (First Officer) and I to agree that continuing another 3 hours to ZZZ1 with no indication of the internal engine temperature was not the safest course of action. I contacted Dispatch and advised of our intention to return to ZZZ.We obtained ATC clearance to ZZZ. Flight attendants were briefed of the precautionary landing status, and an announcement was made for the customers assuring them of their safety. [Priority handling with] ATC was requested due to overweight landing. Uneventful overweight landing was accomplished on XXR. AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) entries were made, Dispatch was notified, and Company and fatigue reports were filed.The FO was extremely helpful in accomplishing all tasks asked of him in a detail oriented, extremely efficient manner. Please thank him for his professionalism.[The cause was a] failure to fix repeat maintenance item, [there is] lots of history on the engine. During climb above 18,000 ft., I noticed that the EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) indication for the left engine was displaying amber XXs. I notified the Captain of it and we proceeded to follow SOP and found no guidance in our manuals. After contacting Dispatch and Maintenance, we decided to return to ZZZ and request priority handling due to being overweight for landing. We landed without any further incident.[Regarding a cause, there is] nothing I can think of at this time except the issue with the EGT indicator.
ASRS:1833310.s: During climb above 18,000 ft., the crew observed an amber 'XX' on the #1 engine EGT display with no ECAM messages or QRH guidance. They returned to ZZZ for an uneventful overweight landing, attributing the issue to a failure to fix a repeat maintenance item on the engine.

ASRS:1833314.n: We almost slid off a taxiway. After landing [Runway] 27R in rain, we were cleared on C1 and proceeded southbound on Z. At the first right turn, I heard the Captain say, 'Oh [no]' and looked up to see us slowly sliding straight for the edge lights as my CA heroically held full right tiller and popped the reverse. We also heard a loud, sustained grinding noise from the nose wheel as we slid across its tread. The taxiway was noticeably wet with relatively new (slick) paint markings, plus we were operating a MAX that carries extra energy while taxiing. We informed ATC of our issue as we were able to return the airplane to the centerline. We continued to the gate after checking with our FA and PAX (all were well). Upon parking, my CA went outside and was able to verify that no contact was made with any lights or grass, and the airplane was undamaged. Flight concluded uneventfully.We were vigilant regarding the weather and ready for unexpected things while flying, but our attention became divided on the ground and our senses softened. Plus, Runway 27R is not a typically assigned runway. Normally, a slow taxi in wet conditions, as ours was, is sufficient to keep things safe. But in this case even that was not enough. Additionally, we are relatively low time in the MAX (CA w X legs, FO w XXhrs), so while expecting things to be different it may also be true that our reflexes were simply not mature.We later learned from a local ORD based pilot that this corner is notorious for being very slick when wet, given the nature of the pavement, paint, and its downhill gradient. This was news to us and would make an EXCELLENT addition to the company pages!! After clearing the Runway 27R at C1 we proceeded on to taxiway Z. At the first right turn on taxiway Z, I proceeded to make the right turn to follow the taxiway centerline but the aircraft would not turn. The nose wheel began to slide. The taxiway was wet at the time. We were in a 737 MAX at idle thrust and riding the brakes. The taxi speed was between 8 and 10 knots. I managed to keep the aircraft on the taxiway with aggressive braking. The taxiway was wet and with the strong residual thrust the aircraft nose wheel could not get enough grip on the painted surface of the centerline. It also seemed like the aircraft was tail heavy and that might have reduced the weight on the nose wheel.Go even slower when taxiing the 737 MAX with wet surface conditions.
ASRS:1833314.s: A 737 MAX crew nearly slid off a wet taxiway at a right turn after landing on Runway 27R due to slick paint, downhill gradient, and reduced nose wheel grip. The First Officer corrected the slide with aggressive braking and reverse thrust, resulting in no damage or injuries.

ASRS:1833323.n: Captain (CA) & First Officer (FO) commented on a dirty sock smell on taxi out, no other abnormal indications. Upon adding takeoff power, left side of cockpit filled with a smokey/steamy mixture and acrid smell. Captain rejected. Maintenance (MX) advised there was an engine wash performed night prior and the aircraft engines were not run up properly after the procedure. We ended up having MX onboard for the runup who had us perform duties from a checklist that should have followed this engine wash including a run up of at least 5 min at 70% N1. The odors were still present during this time. If MX had been performed accurately the night prior, this could have been avoided. And, unfortunately, this routine wash is performed under a 'work card' making it invisible to pilots during a preflight in any MX accounting systems or via the aircraft logbook. At approximately 90 KIAS, smoke came out of cockpit floor, under Captain's side, and rejected takeoff. Uneventful. Cleared off runway stopped and had emergency equipment check for fire. All clear and taxied to gate. Maintenance said engine wash were performed overnight, probable cause of smoke/steam on takeoff roll. Maintenance did a high power engine run, delayed flight and re dispatched after maintenance cleared aircraft. Maintenance crew did an engine run, at gate, versus high power one the night prior. According to mechanic, a duct clamp was installed improperly in the E&E bay, residual water and duct clamp coming off on ducting might have contributed to what appeared to be smoke/fumes/vapor on takeoff roll after takeoff power was applied. [Reporter recommends Maintenance] perform high power engine run after every engine wash. If non-high power engine run, performed by maintenance overnight (info only entry to AML should be recorded so as to keep flight crews informed).
ASRS:1833323.s: Pilots rejected takeoff due to smoke and acrid fumes caused by an improperly installed duct clamp and residual water from an overnight engine wash. Maintenance performed a high-power runup at the gate, cleared the aircraft, and the flight was delayed but eventually dispatched.

ASRS:1833334.n: 5,500 pounds of fuel became trapped due to #1 float switch issue. They [requested priority handling] and landed in ZZZ. While trying to communicate with the aircraft the ACARS send function in FPS failed. I tried the backup in the services link and that also failed. I had to have a fellow dispatcher send the ACARS for me since time was of the essence. It was a brief outage but at a very critical moment. Advised [supervisor] and contacted ZZZ Tower.
ASRS:1833334.s: A dispatcher reported that 5,500 pounds of fuel became trapped due to a #1 float switch issue, requiring priority handling and landing in ZZZ. During this critical phase, both primary and backup ACARS send functions failed, forcing a fellow dispatcher to transmit the message while the supervisor and ZZZ Tower were notified.

ASRS:1833347.n: I was acting as Pilot Monitoring on Aircraft X enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. We were climbing through FL270 just west of ZZZ2 when [the] Captain selected the cowl anti-ice switches to on position in response to a layer of clouds we were about to climb through. Within a few seconds of him selecting the cowl anti-ice, I noticed immediately that there was a loss of information on the Captain's side PFD (Primary Flight Display). The Captain had lost his white FMS course needle, a red RA flag appeared below the altitude tape, and on both PFD's, FMS1 in the FMA (which at the time was the active mode) had a red line through it. I called out this issue to the Captain, and he analyzed the situation to attempt to identify what information he had lost, which functionalities he still had, and which QRH checklist could be run to solve the issue. I do not recall what the active lateral mode in the FMA turned to after the Captain's side navigation information disappeared, but in troubleshooting, the Captain decided to transfer control of the aircraft over to me, as my navigation instruments were still working. We managed to arm and capture FMS2 on my side and continue flying the assigned route. We were still climbing in VS mode, now through FL280. I noticed that several functions of the FCP (Flight Control Panel) were now unavailable, including the SPD knob, and VS wheel, rendering it impossible to use any vertical mode of the autopilot. I informed the Captain that these issues may affect our ability to enter RVSM airspace, to which he agreed and informed ATC as such. ATC assigned us to descend now to maintain FL270. Unable to use any vertical modes of the autopilot, I had to disconnect the autopilot and hand fly down to FL270. I was still able to set an altitude in the altitude selector, so upon reaching FL270 I was able to reconnect the autopilot, which held altitude without issue.Meanwhile, the Captain continued to troubleshoot, looking through the QRH for what the issue might have been, and what checklist to run. He also notified the company of what components we had lost and called the flight attendants to tell them not to start any new service. At this point, ATC was aware of the situation, and an emergency had not been declared as, at the time, safe operation of the aircraft was not in question. As we were unable to identify what was causing the many failures, the Captain began suggesting a diversion to ZZZ2, which at this point we were only 25 miles east of. He began talking with ZZZ2 Maintenance and Dispatch over the radio to attempt to identify the problem and find the appropriate QRH checklist. After consulting Maintenance and Dispatch, together they were unable to identify the appropriate QRH checklist to run. The Captain and I discussed the possibility of a diversion. Given the descent and approach would need to be hand-flown on raw data (since the autopilot and flight director were rendered unusable beyond flying straight and level), all navigation information as well as RA on the Captain's side was unavailable, and there was inclement weather at ZZZ1 due to the approaching hurricane, we made the decision to divert to ZZZ2 (which at the time was VFR). Dispatch was made aware of the decision and notified ZZZ2 Ops, and told us they were prepared for our arrival into ZZZ2. We notified ATC of the decision to divert, and ATC began giving us radar vectors to ZZZ2. An emergency was still not declared as the Captain and I were still able to safely operate the aircraft in VMC and good weather conditions, and priority handling was not necessary, and ZZZ2 was not busy.Given that navigation information was only available on my side, I hand flew the rest of the flight while the captain made appropriate announcements, collected required information for landing, and set up the aircraft. We conducted a visual approach backed up by the ILS to Runway XXL at ZZZ2. The entire descent and landing was hand flown, as vertical modes were unavailable;including the ability to capture a glideslope. I was able to receive vertical and lateral information from the ILS, but the Captain's side was not, so he had to revert to cross-side information for the approach. His RA was also unavailable, so he had to make his call outs based on the information on my PFD. A normal, stable approach was conducted to a safe landing. We parked at Gate X. Maintenance came on board, and after a quick diagnostic, determined that the airplane would need to be hangared for further investigation. The passengers were deplaned and moved to a different aircraft. The cause of this event was maintenance-related. An unidentified failure occurred that resulted in a loss of multiple sources of navigation information and autopilot functions. Events like these can't always be prevented. I believe my training well prepared me for the outcomes of this event, and allowed me to return the aircraft to the ground safely.
ASRS:1833347.s: The Pilot Monitoring and Captain on Aircraft X experienced multiple navigation and autopilot failures after activating cowl anti-ice while climbing through FL270. Unable to restore vertical modes or identify the maintenance-related cause, they hand-flew a diversion to ZZZ2 for a safe landing.

ASRS:1833349.n: It was my first time loading Hazmat other than dry ice. I received 4 boxes of category 3 flammable gas. I pulled out the Hazmat binder and filled out the form. I called the safety hotline to ensure I filled it out correctly but no one answered. I called Operations and Name answered. I sent him pictures of the form I completed and shipping papers. He verified that the paperwork was correct. I however did not realize I needed to attach copies of the red shipping papers to the form. It was been one year since training when I learned about Hazmat. Being a First Officer in the charter department, I never dealt with Hazmat. I should have reviewed the Hazmat process before I was released to the line as a Captain. I have reviewed the procedures and am aware of the proper procedures. I became aware when I was submitting the form on the pm side. I saw another Captain stapling the shipping papers to the form. I notified Dispatch of the situation. [The cause of the event was] my flight was an overflow from another aircraft so loading started last minute so there was a rush to get my airplane loaded. I should have slowed down to make sure I submitted the paperwork correctly. [I] communicated with Dispatch [regarding the event]. [I suggest] recurrent [training] of Hazmat.
ASRS:1833349.s: A First Officer loading Category 3 flammable gas on a charter flight failed to attach red shipping papers to the Hazmat form due to a last-minute rush and lack of recent experience. The Captain notified Dispatch after observing another pilot's correct procedure and recommended recurrent Hazmat training.

ASRS:1833423.n: Unable to loosen/tighten any Flight Attendant (FA) jump-seat harness on this aircraft. Extremely unsafe. We need 'one-click buckle' and 'one-twist release' like we have on almost every other plane, except this one, and I imagine other Airbuses as well. Potential for FAs to not be buckled in as per FARs and potential for FA's to not easily exit jump-seat during normal and emergency situations. Recommend inspection and replacement of all FA jump-seat harnesses that are like the one [on other aircraft] to prevent potential unfortunate events from happening. Informed downline FAs to notify Captain. Unsure if all harnesses replaced. Other aircraft affected as well.
ASRS:1833423.s: Cabin crew reported unable to operate flight attendant jump-seat harnesses on an Airbus, citing a lack of one-click and one-twist mechanisms. This defect creates safety risks for securing and exiting seats, prompting a recommendation to inspect and replace all similar harnesses across the fleet.

ASRS:1833425.n: While signing off work steps on the electronic device Maintenance application, electronic sign-off allows the technician to N/A the step even when not allowed per GMM. E/A XXXX-XXXXX does not allow for N/A to be used. therefore the option shouldn't be allowed in the maintenance application.
ASRS:1833425.s: A technician reported that the electronic maintenance application incorrectly allowed marking work steps as N/A on aircraft XXXX-XXXXX, contrary to GMM requirements. The reporter stated this option should be disabled to match the restrictions found in the E/A system.

ASRS:1833443.n: Coming in on final approach on the ILS into MRY, we experienced wind shear over the water at about 6 miles from the airport. The rough air pushed us below glide path, receiving a low altitude alert from tower the decision was made to go missed. We continued missed approach and radar vectors to our filed alternate ZZZ.
