ASRS:1833443.s: The flight crew encountered wind shear and rough air at 6 miles from MRY during ILS final approach, pushing the aircraft below glide path and triggering a low altitude alert. They executed a missed approach and were radar vectored to their filed alternate, ZZZ.

ASRS:1833471.n: Bounced on landing, the plane started to porpoise, attempted to add power to go around, but the front landing gear collapsed. I was on Runway XXR at ZZZ.
ASRS:1833471.s: The pilot reported a bounced landing on Runway XXR at ZZZ that caused the aircraft to porpoise. An attempted go-around resulted in the collapse of the front landing gear.

ASRS:1833479.n: Descended 1,000 ft. then climb to 1,600 ft. to cross final approach fix.
ASRS:1833479.s: The pilot descended 1,000 feet and then climbed to 1,600 feet to cross the final approach fix. The narrative describes this maneuver but does not specify the aircraft type, phase of flight, or the cause and outcome of the event.

ASRS:1833492.n: I received a phone call from a student saying that he had gone flying solo (which I was not informed on until after the flight. I tell all my students to text me before going to fly and once they are on the ground) and when he came in for a landing with a light crosswind coming from the right, he recognized he was slightly left of the centerline so he attempted to correct. After touchdown, due to the right crosswind, my student had left rudder in due to the sideslip situation for the crosswind, and the plane then pulled to the left. The plane then veered to the left and my student overcorrected with the right rudder resulting in him ending up in the grass. While the aircraft was moving in the grass off the right of the runway, my student attempts to stop in the grass and reports 'the aircraft pulled hard to the left causing me to cross back over the runway and coming to a rest on the left side of the runway'.This report is all [the] words from my student, as I was not at the airport due to me not knowing that the solo was happening. My student has submitted his own NASA report as well. I'm student pilot and I was doing a student solo. I started my flight with a take off on Runway XX and did some practice ground reference maneuvers south of ZZZ. After working ground reference maneuvers at about XA:50, I headed back to the airport to land for the day. I was on final for Runway XY and had a right crosswind, and was correcting with left rudder and right aileron. When about 10-15 feet off the runway, I was slightly left of center line and as soon as I touched down, my wheel was turned left because of the rudder so my plane was jerked slightly to the left, I attempted to use right rudder to straighten the aircraft and lost control and went off the right side of the runway. I then attempted to slow down my aircraft in the grass off the runway, but the aircraft pulled hard left causing me to cross the runway, coming to a rest on the left side of the runway. During the time that I was off the runway my engine had shut down. I then turned the keys off and pulled mixture all the way out and exited out of the aircraft.
ASRS:1833492.s: A student pilot soloing a light aircraft veered off the right side of the runway during landing in a right crosswind after overcorrecting rudder inputs. The aircraft crossed back over the runway and stopped on the left side after the engine shut down while moving through the grass.

ASRS:1833511.n: [Received Priority].Crew was at cruise flight at Flight Level 410 from ZZZ to ZZZ1, both pilots were at controls when EMER BUS FAIL CAS message came up followed by a list of CAS (Crew Alerting System) messages. Autopilot was kicked off and Captain had to hand fly the aircraft. Depressurization of aircraft began, crew put on quick donning masks. Crew [advised ATC] and began running the appropriate QRH called for by Captain, EMER BUS FAIL. FO (First Officer) was able to complete the checklist for EMER BUS FAIL. Following QRH, by pressing the override EMER BUS switch to the right position EMER BUS regained power. All CAS messages went away except for CAS message override ALT EMER BUS. At that time Captain was able to get to a lower altitude to take oxygen masks off. FO continue working communications and Captain flew the aircraft. Crew diverted to the nearest suitable airport with no other incidents.
ASRS:1833511.s: During cruise at FL410, the crew experienced an EMER BUS FAIL causing autopilot disengagement and depressurization. After donning masks and completing the QRH, they restored power via the override switch, descended to remove masks, and diverted safely.

ASRS:1833540.n: Myself and an Instructor flight planned to do a commercial long cross country going ZZZ1-ZZZ2-ZZZ-ZZZ3. The flight plan read that we would have used up less than half our fuel (50 useable per POH) going to ZZZ2. We departed ZZZ1 having a ground speed much higher than expected of 125-131 using up less fuel than expected. Other than deviating around clouds and cells it was an uneventful flight. I have done this flight before and last time made the smart decision of fueling up in ZZZ2 to go back to ZZZ1. When we landed this time in ZZZ2 during day light, It was shown that we had used about 21 gallons. Leaving 29 gallons remaining. Then once our preflight was done in ZZZ2 we jumped in the plane and started it up. At this point it was night time. The plan was still to go to ZZZ. So we departed and start to head in that direction. We found ourselves deviating around storms and making sure we are of course not running into airspace. We found that we had a greater headwind than expected and our ground speed ending up being around 90. When we were en route to ZZZ the engine began sputtering south of ZZZ4. I thought we were having an engine failure because throughout the flight I had constantly been checking the fuel gauges to show we had fuel. I turn the fuel pump on and switch the tanks from left to right. Once I was complete the engine ran normally. It was after this that I said to the Instructor that I wanted to get on the ground as soon as possible. He reassured me that we had plenty of fuel based on the aircraft fuel gauges and the secondary JPI. The left fuel gauge read a quarter of a tank of fuel when we ran out. We were still going toward ZZZ and continued. We contacted ZZZ Tower and they instructed us to enter left base and report a 3 mile final for Runway XX. We enter the base to final and report a 3 mile final. Followed by the Tower's instruction that we were number two and cleared to land on Runway XX. On about a 1 mile final we had the engine sputter again. I turn the fuel pump on and switched tanks from right to left hoping there was a possibility we have a little bit more fuel in there to keep the propeller going. Unfortunately, there was no more fuel even though the gauges read there was and the JPI indicated we had 8.8 gallons remaining when the engine died. The Instructor [advised] Tower and we then landing on [the] highway.
ASRS:1833540.s: A student pilot and instructor experienced an engine failure due to fuel exhaustion while en route to ZZZ, despite fuel gauges and a JPI indicating 8.8 gallons remained. The aircraft subsequently made an emergency landing on a highway after the engine died on final approach to Runway XX.

ASRS:1833583.n: New METROPLEX procedures in effect. Aircraft X out the BNGOS DTA level at 140. Aircraft Y on the BNGOS1 SID level at 130 filed for 400. Climbed via the SID to FL230. Aircraft are laterally separated, radar picture appears like the old procedure of WINCO/THNDR DTA, aircraft exit Miami Approach laterally separated and remain separated. Aircraft Y turns into the flight path of Aircraft X due to the SID, Aircraft Y is instructed to expedite descent to 130 and given a heading of 020 to diverge. Aircraft X checks on, reports Aircraft Y in sight, and is given a westerly heading to diverge.The aggressive cross-outs of the Metroplex SIDS cause multiple conflicts during high traffic volume or NORDO scenarios. Recommend true parallels out DTAs to ensure lateral separation, and allow controllers to use headings/speeds/altitude to expedite traffic flow.
ASRS:1833583.s: Aircraft X and Y experienced a conflict during departure under new METROPLEX procedures due to aggressive SID cross-outs. Controllers resolved the situation by instructing Aircraft Y to descend and turn, while Aircraft X was given a diverging heading after visual contact.

ASRS:1833624.n: I was the Pilot Flying. The weather in ZZZ was deteriorating quickly. Thunderstorms, heavy rain and wind were moving towards the airport. On downwind we could see the airport through the spotty rain showers and were number 3 for the RNAV XX approach. The previous two aircraft reported light turbulence, heavy rain, negative windshear, and they broke out right at minimums. The weather radar depicted a large cell just to the south of the airport moving in quickly and one at the very end of the runway moving towards the airport. Lightning was also depicted on the weather radar. We broke out right at minimums with heavy rain on short final however the runway was visible and I continued with the remainder of the approach visually. At about 300 ft. I encountered a wind gust that caused the aircraft to go above the VASI glidepath slightly. I recovered by lowering the nose of the aircraft and also being cognizant of the increase descent rate that would occur. Even though there was heavy rain, the runway was still visible. With the heavy rain and wipers on max rate, it was difficult to hear anything else. My First Officer informed me that he heard an alert through the aircraft speakers that sounded like 'Don't Sink' but it could have been 'Sink Rate.' He wasn't sure. I glanced at the VSI and it was indicating about a 1,200 fpm descent rate. Speed was about 10 kts. Fast. I arrested our descent rate and got back on the VASI glidepath. I removed my headset from my ear to hear any further aural warnings. At about 100 ft. with a VSI of 850 FPM I also heard 'Don't Sink' in conjunction with the 100 ft. aural call. The descent rate had been stabilized and it was evident that a safe landing could be made within the Touchdown Zone. We were both quite certain there was no question that a safe landing could be made and also, if we initiated a go-around we would have gone directly into the thunderstorm at the end of the runway. I decided that the safest course of action at that given time was to land. I elected to land the aircraft rather than follow the Company requirement of initiating a go-around when a 'Don't Sink' Alert was received. The landing was uneventful. We touched down in the Landing Zone as briefed. Deceleration was smooth and as we were taxiing towards the gate the ensuing thunderstorms enveloped the field but the wait for our gate was not that long. We arrived at the gate a bit behind schedule. Company policy is quite clear on what is expected and required when encountering this, or any other EGPWS Alerts. I think our situation was a little precarious due to the weather, heavy rain, wipers and also a lack of direct communication as to what was heard. A prevention in this situation would be to not be in this situation. Hold, wait out the storm. Divert as necessary. Company aircraft send Aural Warnings through the speakers. There are some aircraft where the speaker volume is not that loud. Better planning and briefing would also be a factor in preventing this from happening. I was Pilot Monitoring during RNAV XX Approach to ZZZ. Last weather report from tower was 10 miles visibility and winds 150 degrees at 23 kts. gusting to 28 kts. with no reported wind shear however it was evident visually as well as on radar that a thunderstorm was rapidly approaching the field from the south. Because of this we were vectored north of the field and cleared the approach. We discussed the published missed approach would take us toward the incoming storm and how to mitigate the risk if we had to go missed approach. At the DA, the runway was in sight (despite a quick to develop rain shower between the FAF and DA) and would remain so throughout the landing, thus we continued the approach. However, on the descent from the DA, the gusty conditions resulted in the aircraft being above glideslope and in an effort to correct glidepath, the aural 'Sink Rate' sounded on short final, followed by a sink rate call from me. The PF (Pilot Flying) made appropriate corrections, maintaining a stable airspeed despite the gusty conditions, and landed in the Touchdown Zone without incident. The post flight report noted a max sink rate of 1,215 fpm. Although the sink rate aural caution sounded, I feel the safest action was to continue the landing considering the runway remained in sight from the DA to touchdown, airspeed remained stable and a go-around would result in flying the aircraft toward the fast moving thunderstorm enveloping the airfield.
ASRS:1833624.s: Two pilots flying an RNAV XX approach to ZZZ in deteriorating thunderstorm weather encountered a 'Don't Sink' alert due to a high descent rate caused by wind gusts. They elected to land safely rather than execute a go-around into the storm, acknowledging this violated company policy but was the safest option given the conditions.

ASRS:1833662.n: While cruising at FL410 west of DEN [airport], the Captain and I were analyzing a severe thunderstorm complex on our route of flight over NE. Our route of flight was DBL-HCT (Hayes Center)-OVR-BDF. I referenced my JeppPro app and suggested a route to the south, via HYS (Hays)-BDF. The Captain verified the routing with the dispatcher who agreed with the plan. The Captain then radioed Denver Center and requested the weather reroute by asking for 'direct Hayes Center direct Bradford'. I saw that on my JeppPro chart the VOR we wanted to fly to was 'Hayes', but I knew I often heard 'Hayes Center' referred to on the radio so I thought to myself it was a colloquial reference to the same fix. When the Controller asked for us to repeat the request, I reminded the Captain 'Hays' but he repeated 'Hayes Center', and I didn't speak up more forcefully again thinking it wasn't quite correct but it was colloquial reference to the same fix. I entered HYS into the FMS, verified it with the Captain and executed the turn, approximately 10 degrees right. A few minutes later we were issued a frequency change to a new Denver Center Controller who answered our check-in with, 'it looks like you're on a shortcut.' The Captain explained that we had received a new clearance due to weather from the previous Controller and said that we were 'direct hotel-yankee-sierra direct bravo-delta-foxtrot.' The Controller said something like 'I'll make sure that's updated for you' and that was the end of the discussion. At that point the Captain and I went back and reconstructed why the Controller seemed unaware of our routing and at that point I realized the Hayes vs. Hayes Center confusion - that there are two frequently-used NAVAIDs in close geographic proximity with extremely similar names.
ASRS:1833662.s: The flight crew requested a weather reroute to "Hayes Center" while cruising at FL410, but the First Officer entered the nearby "Hays" fix into the FMS. This confusion between two similarly named NAVAIDs caused a routing discrepancy that a subsequent controller noticed, though the crew resolved the situation without further incident.

ASRS:1833765.n: During the enroute climb at approximately FL270 on Aircraft X ZZZ1-ZZZ2 we encountered visible moisture below 10 deg c so I turned on the Cowl Anti ice. Immediately, my PFD red flagged the following, RA, FMS1, flight director and lost my bearing pointer, I took a second to evaluate the situation and quickly realized we were going into RVSM so I notified ATC that we had lost instruments and we needed to descend which we did. We transferred controls on the FCP to the FO (First Officer) side and quickly realized we had lost all pitch modes and the vertical speed wheel. We also noticed the speed knob and heading bug wasn't working. We decided to hand fly and I started communicating with ATC and Dispatch/Maintenance through the ZZZ3 operations. I started to look for possible failures in the QRH that may help explain what we lost and a solution with no success. I decided ZZZ3 was a good diversion airport but still was trying to figure out the problem so we slowed down. After some time looking through the QRH and trouble shooting the FCP I decided it wouldn't be safe to continue to ZZZ2 and into hurricane conditions with the instrument failures we had so I called for the diversion to ZZZ3. We were VMC the whole time so I didn't feel the need to declare an emergency. I notified the FAs (Flight Attendants) about our situation and assured them they were safe and this wasn't an emergency. I made a brief announcement to the passengers that we were diverting for loss of some of our instrumentation. We successfully landed in ZZZ3 called maintenance and did an aircraft swap. I made a passenger announcement both on the plane after landing and at the gate explaining what happened and what they could expect as well as made myself available at the new gate for questions in case anyone needed reassurance. After the plane swap we continued into ZZZ2 without incident.Unknown. Multiple equipment failures. Possible QRH for FCP failures.
ASRS:1833765.s: During enroute climb at FL270, the crew of Aircraft X ZZZ1-ZZZ2 activated cowl anti-ice, triggering multiple instrument failures including PFD red flags and loss of pitch modes. The captain diverted to ZZZ3 due to unsafe conditions and unknown equipment causes, landing safely before swapping aircraft to continue to ZZZ2.

ASRS:1833770.n: Two seats were deferred that could've potentially blocked the exact row. We picked the plane up in the AM starting with Aircraft X from ZZZ. When we arrived after three flights back in ZZZ1 maintenance said it shouldn't have been deferred for possibility of blocking the exit row.
ASRS:1833770.s: Maintenance deferred two seats on Aircraft X that could have blocked an exit row. After three flights, maintenance at ZZZ1 stated the deferral was incorrect because the seats should not have been deferred for potentially blocking the exit row.

ASRS:1833773.n: When we arrived at Aircraft X at spot XX, the APU was running and the other crew was deplaning. My crew, boarded the plane at gate and started to do our preflight inspections to get the flight ready. While I was doing my originating flow, the APU auto shutdown and only displayed a 'fail' light. I grabbed the E&A [Engine & APU] and ran the checklist, which only asked if there were any other lights illuminated. The answer was no so the checklist was complete. At this point it started to get warm on the plane, and we were just starting to board our specials. I allowed the APU to stay off for a few minutes, and then opted to turn the APU on again since there were no other indications of an issue. I started the APU again and it started fine, and the generator also came online fine. When I pressed the bleed air switch, the cabin and cockpit instantly started filling with heavy smoke. I instantly shut the APU down, and turned around to Flight Attendant A and told them to get the passengers off. By then, we only had about 5 passengers or so on the aircraft. After deplaning the passengers, I asked Ops to call the Fire Department to come and make sure there was nothing still burning on the airplane. They came and verified that there were no hot spots in the airplane. Maintenance was notified and the crew did a short debrief to insure we were still safe to fly. We continued our flight about an hour later. We had a plane swap, exiting crew said everything was fine, we got on. Captain was starting the APU then a [circuit] breaker blew and cabin lights went out... Captain did his checks... restarted APU... by this time we had our specials and people who needed extra time about 10 total on board. I was helping a women to her seat when I looked up and saw the end of cabin had smoke at that exact time Captain said to stop boarding. I immediately got on PA and instructed everyone to deplane. Captain called Fire Department and Maintenance they found no hot spots. We got our bags off then went to another plane to continue into ZZZ1. Captain was great and asked if we were both OK. Very thankful this happened while on the ground.
ASRS:1833773.s: During preflight at the gate, the APU failed and subsequently produced heavy smoke upon restart, forcing the evacuation of approximately five passengers. After a plane swap, the APU circuit breaker tripped and smoke reappeared during boarding, requiring a second evacuation before the flight continued on a replacement aircraft.

ASRS:1833778.n: While climbing out of ZZZ1 enroute to ZZZ I noticed that in RVSM we were close to having a 200 ft. discrepancy between mine and the FO's (First Officer) altimeter. We didn't go beyond 200 ft. difference and never got an ALT miscompare message.At cruise (FL350) the difference was roughly 130 ft.During descent in to ZZZ, I don't know when exactly it showed up, but I noticed at roughly FL330 during the descent we had a ALT message flashing on my altimeter. I thought maybe the BARO knob on my side or the FO side got bumped. I checked and saw that all three altimeters were showing STD. Then the message went away only to show up 100-200 ft. later. I looked at the altitudes and saw that we were either 200 or greater but not more than 220 ft. off. But then the next 100-200 ft. we were 200 ft. or less on the miscompare and the ALT message went away only for in the next 100-200 ft. for the ALT message to return and the discrepancy being 200 ft. or greater.It back and forth intermittently until roughly FL290, possibly lower, I do not recall when exactly the issue stopped.I sent an ACARS message to Dispatch to inform them and so that they could inform maintenance so that the issue could start getting worked on when we got to the gate.I also informed ZZZ Operations on the in range call what was going on and that we would need maintenance.I was looking through the QRH to see if there was a checklist for it just in case even though I was pretty sure there wasn't one.This being the first time that this has occurred to me, I unfortunately did not think to reference the standby altimeter to try to help isolate where the fault may lie, as the issue went away while I was diligently looking for a checklist and the issue was intermittent. Also because it was intermittent and went away on its own I also did not think to inform ATC since we were already in the process of exiting RVSM.No other messages on any display unit, including the EICAS, showed while this was happening nor throughout the remainder of the flight.We landed in ZZZ without incident.I should have known that there wasn't a checklist for this issue and I need to read back up on alt miscompare procedures and how it affects RVSM and what to do. I should have informed ATC and I should have referenced the standby altimeter to help isolate the problem. Otherwise I think we did everything else correctly.After working with Maintenance in ZZZ it turns out the number 4 probe had failed even though we didn't get any messages other than the ALT message on the altimeters. Maintenance said that there when they initially went through their task that there wasn't any active or logged faults with the system and that they had to do another task to isolate where to problem was, in this case the faulty probe. In ZZZ, during descent we had an ALT disagree message during descent.Upon arrival into ZZZ we had everyone deplane, had maintenance come on and do some checks.They were able to isolate the issue and ascertained it was going to be a lengthy delay.We got word that our new departure time was going to be XE:00 so we got a day room.We got back to the airport at XD:15 for the re-report time.Upon arriving at the aircraft I was informed that there was still work to do but that they just needed to tape a cover back onto the plane for one of the pitot tubes.After that they still needed to do some testing and that it would be about 30 more minutes.So, we went to the crew room to wait for the work to be done.I went back out several times to get updates and each time the return to service kept getting pushed back.Finally, once it became a return to service time of XG:00 I realized that we were going to be within an hour of our FDP (Flight Duty Period) time out in ZZZ1.So, I called scheduling and got a wheels up time of XG:55 before the pilots timed out and due to contractual issues that the main cabin door needed to be closed at XG:34. I was told that Maintenance would call ZZZ Operations who would then call me in the crew room when Maintenance was done in the flight deck and that we could go to the plane, preflight, board, and wait for the maintenance log to come back so we could hopefully get out in time.The call did not come in until roughly XG:10.We went out to the aircraft, I told the flight to not rush the preflight. I told them to take their time, not to slow down so that we didn't hit our times, but so that something wouldn't be missed, prevent mistakes, keep us legal and not on the wrong side of SOPs and Regs.We were able to accomplish our preflight in a timely matter, board in a timely matter, and we were able to get the MCD closed at XG:32. The AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) hadn't returned yet so I figured let's get the door closed so that we hit the Flight Attendant contract time and that hopefully the AML would arrive soon and could be handed to us through the flight deck window.I called Dispatch to make sure we were on the correct revision since we had a hard time getting our IFR clearance. I verified all the fuel and time values along with the correct revision. A few minutes after that a Ramp crew member came to the flight deck informing us that the fuel truck had arrived. There was apparently some confusion about fuel. I initially dismissed the fuel truck only to decide that I should make sure that wasn't any last second changes. So, I called Dispatch to re-verify our fuel numbers. There wasn't any changes and I moved on to the next step.Some time after this the AML arrived around XE:40-XE:45.After the cabin secured and we started our air start checklists due to the APU being INOP.At this point I knew that our timeline most likely wouldn't work but that it would close and that we needed to give our best effort.Right as we got to the part in the checklist to apply air to the aircraft for the air start, the FAs (Flight Attendants) called and informed us that a passenger had gotten up to use the lavatory. I told them to let me know when they had returned and were seated.I told the ground crew to apply air but that we were going to wait for the passenger to come out of the lavatory since the cabin was no longer secured. I do not know if this was the right call but I thought that it was the best call in regards to safety.After a minute or two we got a call from the FAs that there was a possible passenger removal situation going on. I asked what was going on and they informed me that the passenger was being non-compliant with the face mask and was being non-cooperative and nasty in the process.Knowing that we as a whole crew were feeling stressed, tired, and unhappy about all the delays I made sure to ask had we been on time, no maintenance, still XA:30, would this situation rise to the passenger beingremoved. They talked about for a few seconds and agreed that it wasn't. I then instructed them that since he was still being non-compliant, go back one more time and see if we can get him compliant and in line or that we would then look into removal and top report back.After a minute or two I was called back and the FAs informed that the passenger was apologetic and now being compliant and we were good to go.At this point, with the cabin re-secured, I turned back to do the air start. I glanced at the clock to check our time and it was XG:51. At this point I knew that there was no possible way to get the air start, taxi, second engine start, and wheels up at XG:55.I conferred with the FO (First Officer) if he was in agreement and if he was willing to do an extension. He gave valid reason for not doing an extension and agreed with me that there was no possible way that we could get wheels up by XG:55. The reason I asked him was just to get a second opinion and he reaffirmed everything that was already thinking. I had already decided once I saw it was XG:51 that we were done, that there was no point in starting the engines, wasting fuel, taxiing out and turning back. The most efficient and economical path was to admit defeat on there being no possible way to make it off by XG:55 for FDP limit reasons and throw in the towel.We had been fighting a losing battle, we did everything we could to safely get the plane going in time and we just had too many issues pop to delay us going out.I then informed the ramp that we had timed out and to pull the ramp back to the plane and that I would inform the Flight Attendants to do arrival procedures and that we were going to deplane.The FO and did after landing and parking flows and checklists.I then exited the flight deck to tell Flight Attendant A that we were done and to do arrival procedures and that I would inform the passengers.I wanted to be out in the cabin for the announcement to not only own the decision but to not leave our Flight Attendants hanging to deal with potentially irate passengers.I made the PA informing them what was going one, the regulations on duty limits, that we tried our best but unfortunately had timed out and that we need to deplane, that they would be taken care of inside the terminal and apologized profusely for the situation.The passengers got off, mostly understanding, some were understandably irritated, but left without incident.I called crew scheduling to let them know and it sounded like word had gotten around already.We waited with the plane until a hotel was assigned. We then shut down the aircraft, secured it, turned it over to the ramp crew, and left the airport.It was a comedy of setbacks. It was just one thing after another. If it wasn't for the passenger, or the maintenance, or the air start due to the APU being broken, take any one or two items out of the equation and we most likely would have made it. It was a losing battle from the get go, we just didn't know it until the time came were there was no possible way to get out in time.I believe we did everything safely, timely, accurately, with safety and service in mind. At no time did myself, the FO, or FAs intentionally slow down the operation for the goal of timing out. The times we slowdown was to make sure things were done safely and correctly, to catch our breaths, and move on the next step to be completed, all with safety in mind.I do not know what else we could have done. We were ready and on time until the passenger, air start, AML delay, fuel confusion came about. It just wasn't our day.That being said, in order to help speed up AML paperwork we should seriously look into getting electronic AMLs and maintenance. This has a huge potential to cut down the time it takes to get paperwork done. Plus, since we would have access to the AML on our iPads and that the AML lives in the cloud that anyone in the operation can access, we wouldn't have to wait for the AML to come back tothe aircraft. Just like in [program] we would get an alert that the AML is finished, review the changes, sign off on the review, and be on our way in a significantly shorter time.In addition to that, ZZZ is not only a base but also a place where maintenance takes place. There shouldn't be an excuse to not have parts and/or the tools necessary to get jobs done. We shouldn't be having to rely on parts and tools being flown in and we definitely shouldn't be relying on borrowing tools from [other airline] like our maintenance had to do today. I understand that it would be expensive to do all of that but is it more expensive than what we just paid for crew to stay in ZZZ in a more expensive hotel, giving 500-dollar voucher to the passenger in addition to getting them hotel rooms and food vouchers? More expensive than the domino effect that just occurred down the line. Vouchers and hotels were given to those passengers in ZZZ1 no doubt. It's more expensive to not give our Mechanics the resources to do their jobs in a timely fashion than it is to try to save money on parts and tools. Also, across all [aircraft type], things are failing at, to me, an alarming rate. Be it in the cabin or on the flight deck, these planes are not that old and should not be having things break this much, this fast. We need to stop kicking the can down the road and actually fix things rather than defer and hope for the best. Also, we need to figure out why things are breaking so much so often so soon. This is getting embarrassing and the 3rd major delay, break, cancellation in the past week for me and in talking with other crews and ramp crews, I'm not the only one experiencing these issues. We clearly have systemic issue that we are either unable or unwilling to address and sooner than later it is going to bite us real hard and cause a serious incident or accident.
ASRS:1833778.s: The flight crew experienced intermittent altimeter discrepancies during descent caused by a failed number 4 probe, resulting in a lengthy maintenance delay. Subsequent scheduling pressures and a non-compliant passenger incident prevented the crew from departing before their flight duty period expired, forcing a cancellation.

ASRS:1833821.n: Removed and reinstalled aft left emergency exit hatch per AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual). No fault of being open on ground on ECAM (Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitor). While climbing at 9,000 feet amber fault notification appeared on ECAM. Flight crew had a precautionary landing and it was troubleshot by day shift and released for service. Flown to ZZZ with no faults. The fault came back a second time and final repair appears to have been the inner seal of exit hatch. Lack of attention to detail of inner seal. Printed AMM did not have the photo figures to go with it. Inspected inner seal from interior with inspection mirror and noted ECAM had no amber faults. In my eyes and coworker being my monitor and challenge, this hatch was fully secure.More attention to minor details and printing photo figures with each and every aircraft manual. Learn from this experience moving forward and make sure something like this doesn't happen again in the future.
ASRS:1833821.s: A mechanic reinstalled an aft left emergency exit hatch, but an ECAM fault appeared at 9,000 feet, causing a precautionary landing. The issue was traced to a damaged inner seal and a lack of photo figures in the printed maintenance manual.

ASRS:1833840.n: During a morning approach, BJC was busier than usual. It took three calls to establish two-way communication with Tower, during which a right 360 was completed for spacing. On approach, ATC cleared us straight in for a left base on Runway 12L, then with about 2 miles to go, handed us off to Tower Frequency 2 and changed us to Runway 12R. After changing, we continued the southbound approach 'behind Aircraft Y'. about a half mile from the airfield, over US 36, we saw not one but two [aircraft], same altitude and 1/4 mile apart, heading for us west-to-east up US 36. I felt that this was loss of separation and far too close for comfort, and uncommanded (By ATC) evasive action was taken including a sharp right turn and an arrested descent, to allow the aircraft to pass under and behind us. No traffic advisory was given (possibly because the other two were on Tower 1 frequency), and it felt as though Tower had no idea where we were. After nearly missing, Tower cleared us No. 1 for Touch and Go on Runway 12R, and we completed our touch and go in front of Aircraft Y on right traffic behind us for the same runway. During the climb-out, the Controller gave us a traffic alert for a 'helicopter on your left' (he was on our right). It felt to me as though the Controller was over-saturated and had no idea where the aircraft he was in control of were located. I also believe there was a lack of communication between Controller staff in the tower during the hand offs from Tower 1 to Tower 2, as the receiving Controller seemed to have no idea where we were, what we were doing, or what we were previously cleared to do. To have the FAA breathing down ZZZ's throat for recent mid-airs (both of which were pilot error and had nothing to do with ATC), and then to be directed into a near-collision on base by BJC Tower, is unacceptable, and tells me that the FAA doesn't care until something makes the news.
ASRS:1833840.s: During a busy approach to BJC, the pilot reported a loss of separation with two aircraft while on a southbound approach to Runway 12R. The pilot attributed the near-collision to ATC oversaturation and poor handoff communication between Tower frequencies, necessitating uncommanded evasive action.

ASRS:1833852.n: After a recent training flight, maintenance personnel discovered an Avibank (screw) had come off an inspection panel and had hit the propeller. During flight no degradation of flight characteristics were noticed.Damage to prop blade is minimal and can be repaired in accordance with established procedures. No other damage noted.
ASRS:1833852.s: Maintenance personnel discovered a loose Avibank screw from an inspection panel had struck the propeller after a training flight. The pilot reported no flight characteristic degradation, and the minimal propeller blade damage is repairable per established procedures.

ASRS:1833887.n: We were cleared for takeoff by ATL Tower immediately behind a 757. As the 757 was not calling himself a heavy, I guess no wake turbulence separation was required. After takeoff, at about 1,000 feet AGL, we encountered a rolling motion to the left due to the 757 wake turbulence. I applied right aileron and the aircraft rolled wings level. I followed the magenta line on the NAV display, and we hit the 757 turbulence again. The aircraft rolled left, I applied right aileron but this time the aircraft continued to roll left. With full aileron input, the aircraft slowly came back to level flight. The 757 was climbing above us to our left. I checked the wind display on the NAV display (ND) and the winds were calm, so no help to move the wake turbulence out of the departure ground track. For safety of flight reasons, I decided to offset slightly to the right of track to get into clean air. At this point we were flying the 082 heading away from the south runway complex. It was a clear night and no aircraft were south of us. Once in clean air, I turned direct to RONII, but my ground track was slightly right of the magenta line on the NAV display. Now that we were safely flying, I was asking the First Officer (F/O) to let Departure Control know we were off track when Departure Control called us and asked if we knew we were south of course. We told him we had offset our track to avoid the wake turbulence we encountered, he replied that no deviation was allowed on the departure and gave us a phone number to call about a potential pilot deviation.If indeed the 757 was not a heavy, then no procedures were violated in having us take off immediately behind him. Had there been some wind in the climb out we probably never would have encountered the wake turbulence. As it was, I had the choice of fighting the wake turbulence and staying on the ground track or offsetting. Since I had one encounter that required full aileron input, and then was slow to recover, staying in the turbulence was not an option. The 757 was left of us. Had I attempted to offset to his left (north of track) I would have had to cross both turbulence vortices. Moving slightly to the right was the only option I could safely make. Climbing on the VARNM Departure off [Runway] 8R, we experienced moderate wake turbulence from the (other carrier) 757 ahead. Captain was Pilot Flying and decided it would be the safest course of action to deviate right of course, without notifying Departure. He deviated around two degrees right and we were immediately questioned by Departure. I responded to Departure, 'Yes, we are deviating right for wake turbulence.' He said we could not do that and to contact this phone number.
ASRS:1833887.s: The Captain deviated right of the VARNM departure track to avoid moderate wake turbulence from a preceding 757 that was not identified as heavy. Departure Control subsequently questioned the deviation, stating no deviation was allowed and provided a phone number for a potential pilot deviation report.

ASRS:1833902.n: Upon landing in LGA and taxi to gate instructions where, 'Taxi to gate via Sierra, Papa, Bravo, Lima, enter Ramp 9 Alpha to gate.' Making transition onto Lima and then towards 9 Alpha, the southeast corner of the unlit paved 'island' between Spots 20 and 23 can become a taxi hazard late at night, especially during inclement weather. The 'island' is unlit. LGA's islands have 1' diameter by 18' high, unlit, vertical poles painted blue on the top half. The blue color blends into black asphalt at night and is very difficult to see until one is right up on them. Unlit island between Spot 20 and Spot 23 can be a taxi hazard at night, especially [in] bad weather. Please coordinate with LGA Airport on either making the marker lit during night time operations, or removed for possible FOD hazard to taxi operations.
ASRS:1833902.s: A pilot reported a taxi hazard at LGA while transitioning to Ramp 9 Alpha at night. The unlit, blue-topped poles on the island between Spots 20 and 23 blend into the dark asphalt, creating visibility issues and potential FOD risks.

ASRS:1833911.n: Took off from TPA from Runway 19R on the ENDED Nine DP. There was a small TS cell south of the field and the Tower was calling approximately 20 kts. loss of airspeed on the climb from Runway 19L. Runway 19R looked clear to us so we didn't [think] much of it. As we were cleared to takeoff from Runway 19R, we used reduced thrust and Flaps 1. On the climb, we entered IMC and turbulent conditions as we penetrated the cell. I suddenly noticed that the vls was starting to climb up and overtake my airspeed, the vsi had a downward trend and suddenly changed to amber and the 'DON'T SINK' aural warning was triggered. I immediately pushed the thrust levers to TOGA and said 'TOGA Thrust, stow speed brakes' and executed the Windshear (WS) escape maneuver. We continued the maneuver to approximately 5,000 ft. and the Captain reported to Departure that the ENDED Nine DP is not feasible due to the presence of that TS. After 5,000 ft. MSL, we turned on course to the north en route back to ZZZ.
ASRS:1833911.s: The flight crew experienced windshear while climbing from TPA Runway 19R in reduced thrust after penetrating a thunderstorm cell. They executed a windshear escape maneuver to 5,000 feet and diverted north, reporting the ENDED Nine DP unfeasible due to the storm.

ASRS:1833921.n: We departed Tampa Runway 19R on ENDED9 STAR following 2 previous departures with no adverse reports. When cleared for takeoff, we observed heavy rain from a building storm about 3 to 4 miles South of field over I-275 bridge. On taxi out during the brief time when radar was pointed at weather, return displayed as a narrow band of red about 2 to 3 miles across from North to South spreading East to West well inland to East and ending over the bay to the West. We had been facing North with no view of storm for the past 10 or so minutes. Takeoff roll and climb was normal and we had penetrated the band of heavy rain by about 1000 ft MSL. Nearing S speed passing about 1,500 ft MSL, airspeed began to hesitate then decay and rate of climb turned to a descent of about 1,500 fpm down. GPWS sounded with 'DON'T SINK DON'T SINK' and First Officer (FO) reacted with TOGA and increase in pitch. The descent was arrested and climb continued. Lowest radar altitude was about 1,200 ft AGL. Total time was about 10-15 seconds and we never encountered any lateral course deviations nor any typical entry or exit parameters of windshear- just the vertical aspects. We reported the microburst encounter to Tampa Departure and advised that our flight path should be avoided by any subsequent departures.
ASRS:1833921.s: The crew departed Tampa Runway 19R and encountered a microburst at 1,500 ft MSL, causing airspeed decay and a 1,500 fpm descent that triggered GPWS warnings. The First Officer applied TOGA to arrest the descent at 1,200 ft AGL, after which the crew reported the event to Tampa Departure.

ASRS:1833970.n: At push-back time realized Captain headset transmit jack (not part of headset, but jack in sidewall) was INOP. Airplane had overnighted and previous crew had written up 'Captain headset microphone jack is loose and intermittent operation'. Upon arrival to aircraft, I noticed Maintenance was working on the flight deck in the headset jack area. I called Dispatch and Maintenance Control to report the INOP sidewall transmit jack. I expressed my concern that I thought Maintenance would attempt to MEL defective jack under MEL XX-XXX, and that I felt that that MEL was applicable to the headset not the jack, and that it would not be a legal MEL. Dispatcher agreed. Maintenance Control stated that line Maintenance would be coming out to plane to address the issue. I called Dispatch back when line Maintenance arrived and Dispatch stated that he (Dispatcher) and Maintenance Control agreed that it not being fixed was a no go item. I called Dispatcher and he conferenced in Duty Pilot. I explained that I thought line Maintenance would still try to MEL it under XX-XXX, and that I felt that was not a legal MEL and if they did do it that way I would not accept the airplane. In fact, Line Maintenance did MEL It under XX-XXX. I called Dispatch and Duty Pilot back, made mention of Line Maintenance applying that MEL, that I would not accept an illegal MEL (one that doesn't apply). Dispatcher agreed. Duty pilot said OK. Line Maintenance failure, especially on an overnight airplane, to properly fix [an] item. More disturbing is [the] Line Maintenance applying the MEL item, that I and Dispatcher and Maintenance Control, felt clearly was not an appropriate MEL. Unacceptable. Maintenance should have fixed the problem when initially reported and not stretch an MEL to get an airplane out. Unacceptable, illegal, unsafe.
ASRS:1833970.s: The pilot reported an inoperative Captain's sidewall transmit jack at push-back, noting Line Maintenance failed to repair it and instead applied an inappropriate MEL XX-XXX. The pilot refused to accept the aircraft, citing the maintenance failure and the illegal MEL application as unsafe and unacceptable.

ASRS:1833974.n: We were assigned Aircraft X. Upon reviewing the maintenance sheet I became confused regarding MEL #XX-XX. The original entry in the logbook and the description on the sheet were not easily understood so I elected to contact maintenance. After having a ten minute conversation with the technician about the complexities of the MEL, we both agreed that we were good to go. However, he stated that he was slightly concerned with the legality of the MEL, would look into it further and contact me before departure (we still had approximately 30 minutes before push) if he determined it was not legal. We did not hear back from him until we had pushed and had begun engine start. At this time, he informed us that it was indeed not a valid MEL. We then returned to the gate and the airplane was taken out of service. To the best of my knowledge, the airplane had flown for four days in this condition. Simplify the wording on the maintenance sheet and have a more direct description of this item in the MEL.
ASRS:1833974.s: The pilot contacted maintenance regarding a confusing MEL entry for Aircraft X, and both initially agreed to proceed. However, the technician later confirmed the MEL was invalid during engine start, forcing a return to the gate and taking the aircraft out of service.

ASRS:1833980.n: When we arrived at the plane the APU was already running. During our preflight we were notified that we would be transporting a large quantity of dry ice and would need to use the dry ice supplementary procedures. One of those procedures is to turn the temperature in the compartment with the dry ice to as low as it gets. We did this. Upon engine start we noticed that the right pack 'INOP' light was on with an associated EICAS message. As I was going through my after start flow (flap handle, APU off, engine heats, left pack, right pack) when we got to right pack we started troubleshooting the issue. We followed the QRH which required a 5 min wait time to see if the issue is fixed. We proceeded to taxi while we timed the 5 min. After the 5 min the pack reset and worked normally. We believe that the high OAT and humidity caused the pack to freeze up and fault due to the low selected temperature. On taxi we also had to balance some fuel due to the APU burn on the ramp. Operations were normal to the runway. Once we started our takeoff at 60 knots we got a right bleed off message. Captain executed a rejected takeoff and we exited the runway. After cleaning up the aircraft and completing the rejected takeoff QRH checklist we contacted Maintenance and trouble shot the problem. We soon discovered that the bleed air isolation valve was open. In troubleshooting the pack issue after start, I had not finished my flow and closed the isolation valve. So on takeoff the air from the left engine overpowered the right and closed the right bleed valve giving us the offending message. We re-ran our checklists and made sure our brake temp cooling was OK and departed uneventfully. Multiple non normal issues caused the flight crew to miss a flow item.
ASRS:1833980.s: The flight crew experienced a right pack fault and a subsequent right bleed off message during takeoff due to incomplete flow items while troubleshooting dry ice procedures. The captain rejected the takeoff, corrected the open isolation valve, and the aircraft departed uneventfully after maintenance checks.

ASRS:1833986.n: There is no Jeppsen Engine Out (E/O) departure [procedure] for Runway 27 BOS in current Jepps. There is an E/O SID for Runway 27 BOS in the current aircraft software. There has been an E/O SID for Runway 27 BOS for years and there's discrepancy between the current Jepps and APS software. The information doesn't match, probable cause lack of a reviewing process. Need to update the Jepps and aircraft software to match.
ASRS:1833986.s: The pilot reported a discrepancy between current Jeppesen charts and aircraft software regarding the Engine Out SID for Runway 27 at BOS. The probable cause was identified as a lack of a reviewing process, requiring updates to align both data sources.

ASRS:1834055.n: L2 door was making a noise that was louder than just the whistle you usually hear. More of a medium pitched hum. Called the pilots. They said cabin pressurization looked OK on their end. I looked at seals and put my ear up to an area that looked a little looser. It was definitely louder as we explored that seal. About a minute later I started to feel lightheaded and my ability to control my breathing/focus start to feel altered. I asked the Flight Attendant 'C' in the back of she was feeling different at all. She ended up feeling weird, too. Things started to feel like it was harder to focus and spin/euphoric feelings. Harder to breathe. She said, 'We need to get out of here.' And we immediately headed to the front. I felt that I immediately needed oxygen right away and to tell the pilots that something was wrong. I felt faint-like, was grey in color, and sweat on forehead. I felt like I was having a hard time with my ability to communicate as I was speaking with the pilots. The focus/cloudy feeling in my head was unusual and anything I've ever experienced. My breathing felt shallow and also rapid at times. I was able to tell the pilots and immediately went on oxygen. It took a while for my head and body to be able to focus and for the symptoms to lessen. Used almost a full bottle of oxygen.Sat in aircraft right, inboard jumpseat for landing, with the pilot's permission, in order to stay away from L2 door.Still was feeling lightheaded, cloudy, hard to focus feeling even after we landed throughout the night. And a little lightheaded the next day, too. Was checked out by the paramedics and went to the hospital to get checked out as well. FA 'C' felt better than I did more quickly but also mentioned she had never been through that before as well... and had never felt those feelings before, either.Maybe there was an air quality issue on my side that I was more exposed to? Or slight decompression/lack of oxygen by my L2 door. I did notice it smelled like dirty socks in the back galley later when I went to the back of the plane. Sat in L2 jumpseat, aircraft right, inboard for landing to avoid sitting by the L2 door for landing. With the captain's permission.I recommend having the door and cabin area on the particular tail number monitored.
ASRS:1834055.s: Cabin crew experienced lightheadedness, breathing difficulties, and euphoria near a noisy L2 door, suspecting a seal leak or air quality issue. They used oxygen and moved away from the door, with symptoms persisting post-landing and requiring hospital evaluation.

ASRS:1834068.n: While operating Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1, the flight crew noted a fuel imbalance message on the FQIS (Fuel Quantity Indicating System) display. A snapshot was recorded, and 0.0 readings were noted at L/H tank probes #14 and #16. Later, the R/H tank #10 position and L/H tank #12 position reported 0.0, as well. 777/787 Maintenance Control Technician then AOG'd probes to ZZZ1 to repair system prior to flight. Overnight, at some point, Engineering became involved and issued an EA (Engineering Authority) stating a specific MEL to use (which they do not have the authority to do) that was incorrect and bypassed the usage of the correct MEL, which limits the flight to 50 nm of land.Engineering must not be allowed to specify MEL usage in EAs. They do not have the authority nor knowledge to do so. Engineering must not be allowed to circumvent MEL usage causing a safety of flight or Out of Compliance issue.The correct MEL application is MEL 28-XX-Y, which limits the aircraft to within 50 nm of land. This created a major Non-Compliance and Safety of Flight issue.
ASRS:1834068.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X ZZZ-ZZZ1 reported fuel quantity probe failures, but Engineering issued an incorrect Engineering Authority bypassing the correct MEL. This error created a major non-compliance and safety of flight issue by ignoring the required 50 nm land limitation.

ASRS:1834092.n: Airport operations. While operating at this airport (Ridgeland SC) 3J1 the taxiway and runway markings are obscured by tall grass. Grass has grown to two to three feet and it is hard to see the markings and the airport now is being overrun with wild dogs and coyotes as well as deer. This airport was recently improved with new runway and grass areas however the airport management has chose to not maintain safe operations of the facility. My plane used to use the grass runway adjacent to the hard surface and now is unusable as the grass has grown too high making visibility restricted. My prop comes in contact with the taller grass. Please look into this for the safety of based aircraft and visiting aircraft as approaching the airport you can't tell the height of the grass from the air and we don't need wildlife entering the runway environment.
ASRS:1834092.s: A pilot reported that at Ridgeland SC (3J1), tall grass obscuring taxiway and runway markings caused propeller contact during airport operations. The pilot attributed this hazard to poor facility maintenance by airport management, which also allows wildlife to enter the runway environment.

ASRS:1834107.n: Aircraft took off from ZZZ enroute to ZZZ1 on a VFR Flight. When approximately 10NM west of ZZZ at an altitude of 1,400 ft. MSL, a slight inconsistency the operation of the engine was noted. When another brief change in engine sound and operation was heard and felt again, a climb was initiated to 2,500 ft. MSL. As the PIC (Pilot in Command) and sole occupant of the aircraft, when another brief change in engine sound and operation was heard and felt, a turn back to ZZZ was initiated. While returning to ZZZ the sporadic changes in engine operation become more frequent. At approximately 5NM from the airfield, priority landing status announced on CTAF to other aircraft operating in the pattern and practicing instrument approaches. At approximately 3NM west of the approach end of RWY (Runway) XX, the aircraft would no longer maintain level flight. A descending left 180* turn directly to a grassy field was executed. Configuring the aircraft for landing, an additional 90* turn to the south was made in order to land length-wise into the field. After maximum braking, the aircraft came to a stop in the southwest corner of the field, approximately 30 yards from the field perimeter. Landing rollout was approximately 960 ft. No injuries to the pilot, no damage to the aircraft, and no damage to property occurred. A number of local emergency personnel and vehicles responded within 5 minutes. Local media also arrived on scene as well as some witnesses. Word was passed to the property owners regarding the occurrence. Aircraft recovery efforts are forthcoming, and the plane will be disassembled and trucked home.
ASRS:1834107.s: The sole pilot of a VFR flight experienced frequent engine inconsistencies 10NM west of ZZZ, prompting a return and priority landing announcement. The aircraft could not maintain level flight 3NM from the runway, forcing an off-field landing in a grassy area with no injuries or damage.

ASRS:1834209.n: I was notified of an aircraft swap by a Captain who was dead heading into ZZZ1 to ferry Aircraft X to ZZZ. He was briefed by maintenance that because of a prior smoke/fumes event the aircraft wasn't suitable for a revenue flight and was to be a maintenance ferry flight to ZZZ. Our aircraft was delayed inbound so Aircraft X was swapped to our flight. My concern was: except for my inbound aircraft being late what maintenance was performed to change the plan from a no cargo/no passengers maintenance ferry to a revenue flight. Because there wasn't a good answer to that question I didn't feel it was safe or wise to take the aircraft, so I refused the aircraft. This event was a communication breakdown and pressure to operate on time. When unique circumstances happen related to previous maintenance a briefing prior to flight crew getting to the Jetway would help us make more informed decisions and avoid last minute disruptions to our operation.
ASRS:1834209.s: A deadheading Captain refused to operate Aircraft X for a revenue flight after maintenance swapped it from a ferry mission due to a prior smoke event. The pilot cited a communication breakdown regarding maintenance status and operational pressure as the cause for rejecting the aircraft.

ASRS:1834217.n: Gate changed to B1. Taxi lane paint stops before B1 and available concrete is dangerously close to aircraft parked on B2 - there is virtually no guidance from abeam B3 to the last gate, B1. Likelihood of contacting another aircraft is compounded at night. Inadequate airport taxi markings to assure separation from aircraft parked at the gate. Paint (continue) the taxi line. Or, provide tow-in, or require marshals from point of taxi line ending.
ASRS:1834217.s: The pilot reported that taxi lane paint ends before gate B1, leaving dangerously little concrete separation from aircraft parked at B2. This inadequate marking increases the risk of collision, especially at night, prompting a request to extend the paint, use tow-in, or provide marshals.

ASRS:1834238.n: After we landed in INL we had a runway excursion with a GA aircraft. While on approach we heard the GA traffic make radio calls about being inbound about 3-5 miles north of the field. We notified them of our location of about a 10-mile final for Runway 32 and they said they would wait for us to land before landing themselves. They also called us, 'In sight'. After we landed we advised on the radio we were back-taxiing, and as we were turning around we saw the GA traffic landing while we were still on the runway. They stayed well clear of us and were able to exit the runway so we could back-taxi with no issues, and no evasive maneuvering was required at any point.GA traffic apparently not being aware of the risk of landing on a runway we were still on. While he had us in sight I did not have him in sight or on TCAS, and therefore did not know exactly how close behind us he was. Construction in INL requiring back-taxiing and therefore a longer landing time than usual that the GA traffic was probably used to. Try to advise GA traffic earlier if a need to back-taxi is required. We were flying into an uncontrolled airport and made two-way radio contact with another aircraft north of the field coming into land on the same runway we were. He told us that he would let us go first since we were much faster than him and that he would follow us and be #2 to land. Normal radio calls occurred after that and we landed without incident. Because of construction there are no taxiway turn offs available on the runway and a180 degree turn and back taxi is required. After coming to almost a stop and just about to turn around I made a radio call stating that we would be back taxiing on the runway. Once we just about completed our 180 degree turn we saw the other aircraft about 50 feet off the ground at the other end of the runway in his landing flare. So we pulled as far to the side of the runway as we could just in case he made it down to us. We stayed still until he landed and pulled off on the taxiway about 2,000 feet down the runway where we needed to exit. Once the other aircraft was clear we continued our back taxi to the exit point without incident.The other aircraft stated he saw us on about a one mile final and would be number 2 to land. A contributing factor could be that he never actually saw us or he just disregarded us. Being that he was in aircraft type he might have just assumed he had plenty of runway to land and turn in before us without it being an issue on his end. Poor communication on his end as well, very few radio calls almost all of them were non standard, no tail number, no position reports at all outside of being north of the field, and simply stating 'I'll follow the jet'. A pilot with little regards to aviation safety more or less.The only thing I could think of is maybe more communication. We could have tried getting back on the radio real quick and attempting to have the other aircraft go around. By the time we saw it however, he was basically on the ground
ASRS:1834238.s: A jet pilot and a GA pilot at uncontrolled INL experienced a runway conflict when the GA aircraft landed while the jet was back-taxiing due to construction. The reporter attributed the incident to the GA pilot's poor communication, lack of situational awareness, and failure to recognize the jet's extended runway occupancy.

ASRS:1834291.n: I do not know how to report an incident witnessed around [a] federal prison at XA:45 am [on] DATE. [One] plane was actually chasing another plane a few hundred feet above the ground and literally a few yards apart over a residential neighborhood near Lakewood, Colorado. At the corner of Street and Street1. The tail plane was right on top of the other plane for a good 10 minutes before it veered off and let the 1st plane return to the BJC airport in Broomfield Area Colorado. Both planes were extremely low and this act was very scary to witness.
ASRS:1834291.s: A witness reported two aircraft flying extremely low, a few hundred feet above ground and yards apart, over a residential area near Lakewood, Colorado. One plane chased the other for ten minutes before separating, allowing the lead aircraft to return to BJC airport.

ASRS:1834297.n: I departed ZZZ at XA:10 with the intention of flying to nearby ZZZ1 for takeoff and landing practice. I made a normal takeoff and climb remaining under the ZZZ2 Class B airspace, but within the Class C veil, and ultimately climbed to 3000 feet MSL to clear the mountain ridge. After clearing the ridge, I decided to do some training maneuvers at altitude and began some clearing turns. At that time, I noticed my Garmin 430W, my primary nav/com and GPS receiver, had gone dark. Shortly after that, my second nav/com went dark. The ammeter showed a discharge. I tried to reset the alternator, but there was no effect. At that time, I elected to divert to ZZZ3, an uncontrolled airport nearby. My transponder was apparently still squawking on the ZZZ4 code, and I had ADS-B In traffic displayed on my iPad until I was within five miles of ZZZ3, and the transponder went dark as well. I lost my ADS-B traffic display on the iPad as a result, but was able to discern the runway in use from the traffic in the pattern. I entered a wide downwind leg for Runway XX, and made a normal approach and landing on Runway XX at approximately XA:35. There were no traffic conflicts at any time during the flight. Our maintenance shop at ZZZ3 confirmed the alternator had failed and it was replaced over the next few days.To the best of my knowledge, my transponder was squawking Modes A and C and ADS-B Out through the entire flight while in the Mode C veil. I lost power to the transponder just before entering the traffic pattern at ZZZ3.
ASRS:1834297.s: The pilot experienced a total electrical failure due to an alternator malfunction while conducting training maneuvers at 3,000 feet MSL. After losing all avionics and transponder power, the pilot diverted to an uncontrolled airport and completed a normal landing with no traffic conflicts.

ASRS:1834300.n: Reposition flight for new owner of Extra 300L. In route at 4,500 feet MSL, oil pressure dropped into the yellow. Asked Approach Control for vectors to nearest suitable airfield. Proceeded to gain more altitude in case an engine out approach was needed, it was not. No traffic at uncontrolled airport. Did a descending turn over field and an uneventful landing. Cleared the runway and shut down engine as oil pressure dropped below the yellow arc. Line boy and I pushed aircraft to FBO. Turned over to Maintenance to evaluate.Approach Control was extremely helpful. All the information provided by them allowed me to concentrate on the situation at hand. Asked to contact them after landing to insure I landed safely.
ASRS:1834300.s: The pilot of an Extra 300L experienced low oil pressure at 4,500 feet MSL during a reposition flight. After receiving helpful vectors from Approach Control, the pilot executed an uneventful landing at an uncontrolled airport and shut down the engine for maintenance evaluation.

ASRS:1834306.n: ZZZ was preparing for multiple taxiways being closed and aircraft back-taxiing to [Runway] X despite NOTAM prohibiting. Runway X was in use. It was the preferred calm wind runway and all aircraft were departing and landing 04. Taxi to X from the hangars requires crossing the approach end of [Runway] YY. I stopped at the hold-short line for YY, announced my intention to cross the runway, [and] turned on my strobes and checked for landing traffic in both directions. Not seeing any, I started to cross the runway and looked to my right, there was an aircraft on a takeoff roll on [Runway] Z. He did not announce he was taking off and did not have strobes or a landing light on. There was never any real chance of collision unless he aborted the takeoff and was going to run off the end of the runway, as the approach end of YY is at the very end of the runway.Several factors contributed to this chain of events. First, I scanned for landing traffic and did not consider an airplane taking off of Z as that runway is never used for takeoff. I've been at that airport for many years and never seen an aircraft take off on Z. Second, the pilot for some reason decided to use Z when all other aircraft and there were multiple aircraft flying, between coming and going for the airshow and high density of training on the field, were using X. Third, the pilot failed to broadcast he was departing Z, which he should have done multiple times just because all other aircraft were using X.I realize that a pilot is free to use any runway he chooses at an uncontrolled airport, but in this case with high density traffic and the favored runway being X, it was a poor choice. It does not excuse my failure to look both for landing and departing traffic. Perhaps the FAA should consider a rule change whereby airport management can actually designate an active runway at the field for given weather conditions.
ASRS:1834306.s: A pilot crossing Runway YY at an uncontrolled airport encountered an aircraft taking off from Runway Z without announcing or using lights. The reporter attributed the incident to the departing pilot's poor runway choice and lack of communication, combined with their own failure to scan for departing traffic.

ASRS:1834317.n: After taking off from ZZZ, the pilot in command was flying the plane. I was acting safety pilot for the flight. We were climbing to 5,500 ft. and heading northwest to clear ZZZ1 airspace. We had just contacted ZZZ1 Approach and requested flight following when the pilot in command noticed smoke coming out from underneath the bottom of the instrument panel on the pilot side of the aircraft. We contacted Wichita Approach and requested priority handling due to smoke in the cabin and requested to land back at ZZZ.Wichita Approach contacted us and asked if we wanted the fire department on standby at ZZZ. We told them yes and then told them we were going to switch to ZZZ CTAF and inform traffic we were going to be making a landing. We changed frequency and entered 7700 into the transponder. We then turned off the master control switch to the aircraft hopping it would stop the electrical fire. We landed at ZZZ, opened the door to the aircraft, and pulled the aircraft off the runway parking it on the taxiway. After taking off from ZZZ I climbed to 3,500 ft. MSL, heading northwest to clear the ZZZ1 Class C airspace with a VFR flight plan to ZZZ2. The incident happened 5 NM northwest of ZZZ airport. I noticed a little bit of smoke coming from under the yoke nearby the circuit breakers. I checked to see if we had any circuit breakers popped out and none of them were popped out. I then began a right turn towards ZZZ and got in contact with ZZZ1 Approach to [request priority handling] and I said that we are turning back to ZZZ. They asked if we needed a fire truck present, I said yes and squawked 7700 on the transponder. The smoke was no longer present at that time.We then got lined up for Runway XX and got in contact with the CTAF for ZZZ to let other traffic in the area know that we were an aircraft in distress that was on a 5-mile final for Runway XX. After making the contact, I did the checklist for an electrical fire and turned off the master switch and landed on Runway XX. We shut off the aircraft and evacuated the aircraft on the runway. Me and my safety pilot made sure that there was no fire and pushed the aircraft off the next taxiway. ZZZ Fire Department arrived to the scene 10 minutes after.
ASRS:1834317.s: The pilot and safety pilot experienced smoke from the instrument panel during climb to 5,500 ft after departing ZZZ. They squawked 7700, turned off the master switch, and landed at ZZZ where they evacuated and pushed the aircraft to a taxiway while awaiting fire services.

ASRS:1834328.n: While flying with a student in the left downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ, Aircraft X experienced an electrical systems failure. The transponder was lost first, prompting ATC to ask for an ident. Upon realizing the transponder had turned off, we tried to troubleshoot and further investigation revealed the ammeter was discharging. After notifying ATC we had a power issue and needed to land as soon as possible, we were vectored to make way for a fleet of inbound Aircraft Y's. After more troubleshooting I notified ATC that we were still losing power and requested priority handling. We were cleared for landing on Runway XX just before the radio died. After making a safe landing we exited the runway on Taxiway XX and came to a stop. Emergency vehicles responded so I shut down the engine and was eventually towed back to the flight school.
ASRS:1834328.s: A pilot and student in Aircraft X experienced an electrical failure and transponder loss while on downwind for Runway XX at ZZZ. After requesting priority due to discharging ammeter and radio failure, they were cleared to land safely, shut down, and were towed back by emergency services.

ASRS:1834356.n: Eglin Missions Coordinator had called the day before to try to approve Aircraft X and Aircraft Y, IFR at at 14,000 feet and 15,000 feet, to do holding north of R2915, just to the west of CEW, for a few hours. They were denied, correctly, by the Supervisor. That is right in the way of all departures and arrivals into PNS Approach and VPS Approach, as well as PNS N MOA (Military Operating Area), and some departures/arrivals into PAM Approach. You will be hard pressed to find a worse spot in the entire US airspace to have two aircraft hold for hours, during the middle of the day. They were planning on doing some sort of military targeting or work from that position south into R2915, repeatedly.After being denied on one day they launched anyway on the next day, and claimed to be VFR, at two IFR altitudes. When I took over the sector they had already been approved as pointouts by the previous controller, who had also voiced objections to the Supervisor, but VPS Approach or missions decided to launch them anyway, in spite of being denied the previous day. I worked for probably an hour and a half with Aircraft X and Aircraft Y in the way, moving perhaps three dozen civilian and military aircraft around these two 'VFR' aircraft at IFR altitudes. There was no loss of separation, but it greatly increased overall complexity and workload, with little communication or teamwork from VPS Missions. As far as I understand, VPS approach controllers were not exactly happy with these aircraft in the way either, nor was PNS Approach. If there had been more weather in the way, this could truly have been a colossal headache and possibly led to multiple separation errors.Note that the controller relieving me eventually, did not want to take the sector, and invoked Article 65 on the recorded briefing, as well as informing management that he was uncomfortable with the situation. At the time, PNS N MOA was active, just north of the Aircraft X and Aircraft Y holding area, as well as Rose Hill [MOA], along with the standard high level of inbound/outbound traffic, all directed at CEW, during this time of day. I cannot stress enough how poor of a spot that is to have aircraft holding, especially at those altitudes.Never allow this again. VFR or IFR, the FAA cannot allow the military to use up hundreds of square miles of airspace, and then take up even more airspace when they are unable to stay inside there already vast released airspace. They are literally putting civilian traffic in danger. If they must run some sort of targeting mission at R2915, come in from the south. Do not go north out of R2915. Missions coordinators at ZJX must deny these sort of insane requests by default, not approve them and then have the area supervisor try to be the voice of reason at the last second, let alone the controller at the sector. Readers unfamiliar with Crestview sector (R10) will not realize how crowded this airspace gets regularly, let alone with added aircraft holding right in the center, that are not in communication with ZJX, and have a poorly defined holding track/mission.
ASRS:1834356.s: Two military aircraft launched VFR at IFR altitudes into a denied holding area north of R2915, forcing a controller to maneuver dozens of civilian and military flights around them. This unauthorized operation significantly increased sector workload and complexity, prompting a relieving controller to invoke Article 65 due to safety concerns.

ASRS:1834396.n: Climbing through approximately 500 ft. AGL in a right turn to 360, the departure heading selected on the MCP by the FO (First Officer) prior to takeoff, the FO's flight director, FD2, failed, the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window indicated 50,000, not the pre-takeoff selected altitude of 3,000, and the FO's command bars biased out of view. The PF continued the climbing turn using PFD (Primary Flight Display) raw data in night-time VMC conditions. Cross-checking respective PFDs revealed no flags or indications as to the specific failure.In the busy initial climb segment, confusion as to the cause of current flight instrument condition gave way to confidence in the raw data. Directing the PF to continue to climb using raw data, I attempted to select 3000 ft. on the MCP, the altitude knob spun freely without any effect on the window. I then turned off the FD1 and FD2, reselected 3000 ft. in the MCP altitude window, confirmed the heading bug was at 360, selected heading, and turned the FD switches back on, FD2 first, in an attempt to restore FD2 guidance for the PF. Immediately upon switching on FD2, the MCP altitude returned to 50,000 and no command bars appeared on the FO's PFD.Switching to Departure Control, ATC gave us direct routing to the first fix, ZZZZZ, and continue climb to 11,000. I asked ATC for a heading, mentioning our concern that our navigation might be unreliable. They provided a 010 heading which when selected, had no effect on the FO's heading bug. Changing heading on the MCP failed to change the bugs on the FO's ND (Navigation Display) and PFD compass displays. I confirmed compass heading on the wet compass corresponded with both the Captain's and FO's compasses. They asked if we needed to declare an emergency, I declined as we had good raw data and were still diagnosing the malfunction.I attempted a second reset of FD2 with the same negative result. Leveling at 11,000, the PF reported the autothrottles were not holding commanded airspeed, we disengaged the autothrottles. Turning both FDs off again and selecting FD1 on provided accurate command bars on the Captain's PFD. We agreed that continuing using raw data was possible, and that full FD capability was available from FD1. I transferred aircraft control to myself and agreed with my FO's suggestion of going to the QRH for additional troubleshooting/procedural steps. A satisfactory QRH procedure to handle this malfunction was difficult to find and both FMS1 on the Captain's ND and FMS2 on the FO's confirmed FMC operation. We asked ATC for direct down range and confirmed FMS accuracy using FD1 guidance of MCDU1 entered direct routing. I engaged the autopilot and autothrottles and we continued on course using LNAV/VNAV.We discussed the status of the aircraft and the conditions at our destination, ZZZ. We elected to continue to ZZZ where we completed the trip without incident. I submitted an electronic logbook entry and called Maintenance Control after arrival.
