Approximately 35 minutes into our hour-long flight, I realized we had not requested [the] planned climb above our initial cruise altitude, FL310, and that contingency fuel had been burned during a slower climb than normal. Burn, alternate, ZZZ1, and 45-minute FAA fuel was still available, though a missed approach would have compelled diversion to ZZZ1. The FD2 diagnosis and distraction lead to the initial loss of SA regarding erosion to our fuel state. Beginning descent and approach planning brought for our new fuel and prepared us for contingencies. Communication throughout was key to understanding the status of the aircraft and mitigated the initial startle and confusion at such a low altitude early flight stage. We were cleared for takeoff by ZZZ3 Tower with instructions to turn to heading 360 and maintain 3,000 ft. The pilot flying which was me, the First Officer, put 360 in the MCP and deselected LNAV. We took off and as we were climbing through about 500 ft., the command bars disappeared and altitude went to 50,000 on both the PFD and MCP. We leveled at 3,000 on heading 360. ATC gave us climb to 11,000 and direct to a fix. The Captain told him we needed a heading we were having trouble with the flight director. ATC gave us a head of 010 and climb to 11,000 ft.The heading bug on the First Officer's PFD and MFD was stuck on heading 360 but was 010 on the MCP and on the Captain's displays. The Captain checked the PFD heading with the compass and it matched. We had no flags on the PFD or MFD. The Captain turned off both flight directors and then turned them both back on with the First Officer's being the master. When he turned it back on, the altitude went back to 50,000 and we could not change it. The command bars never came back. We saw that the Captain had a flight director and that his heading bug would turn with the MCP. The Captain then turned the FDs off and put his FD as the master. When he did that, the altitude went back to normal. On the FO's (First Officer) displays there was still no FD and the heading bug was stuck on 360 but now the altitude was correct. We continued the flight to ZZZ with the Captain flying.
ASRS:1834396.s: During the initial climb, the First Officer's flight director failed, causing the MCP altitude to display 50,000 feet and the heading bug to stick at 360. The crew managed the situation using raw data and the Captain's functional flight director, completing the flight without incident despite a temporary loss of situational awareness regarding fuel state.

ASRS:1834405.n: Outside the marker [Runway] XXR Captain received call from purser about chemical type smell moving forward from aft cabin. Noticed it on extreme short final but took measures to alleviate, if possible, the stated smell and monitored for reduction or increase. The landing in gusty conditions required focus there. On landing APU selected to start on final was on line and directed APU bleed air to packs and selected recirculate [fans] off immediately causing cessation of the smell and acknowledged alleviation in command. Smell was barely noticeable but a tad acrid then removed on taxi in. Recirculate [fans] back on blew it out completely. Never a need nor concern for use of cockpit oxygen. No persons affected nor did anyone use O2. No injuries. Event terminated at gate with a write up and briefing of mechanics plus filling out of required maintenance 4 page review by Captain. On approach in ZZZ the Captain received a call from the lead Flight Attendant about an acrid chemical smell moving forward from the aft cabin. By that time we could smell it in the cockpit as well. We turned off the recirculate fans to stop the spread of the smell, which helped, but then focused on the landing. We started the APU on short final and turned off the engine bleeds after exiting the runway, using the APU to power the packs. After turning off the engine bleeds the smell dissipated and we turned the recirculate fans back on. No oxygen was used or needed by the crew or passengers. We parked safely at the gate and briefed me and made a maintenance write up.
ASRS:1834405.s: The Captain and Flight Attendants detected an acrid chemical smell on approach to Runway XXR. They mitigated the odor by turning off recirculate fans and switching to APU bleed air after landing, resulting in no injuries or oxygen use.

ASRS:1834417.n: After landing on Runway 22R, we contacted Ground who advised us to taxi via Bravo, November. Since Bravo was directly off the nose of the aircraft, the Captain assumed, and I didn't disagree, that November was somewhere down Bravo closer to our arrival gate. Unfortunately, November was also directly across the nose and nobody noticed it until the Captain has commenced the same turn which resulted in a Boeing 787 taking out some taxi lights the week prior. As we were taxiing northbound on Bravo, Ground gave us a phone number to call which led to an intra-cockpit discussion of what we might have done wrong. Not finding any fault on our own, the Ground Controller advised us of the incorrect turn as we continued to taxi to the gate. This discussion never ceased until we were already into the gate area. No attempt was made to contact the ramp prior to entering the ramp area because ATIS stated (paraphrased) Company extended ramp procedures not in effect". When we read that during the approach briefing, we incorrectly thought it meant "Company ramp procedures effect". If the latter statement had been correct, we would have been correct to taxi to the gate with Ground...who had been talking to us the whole time. The expectation bias of believing that the ramp was closed, combined with the continuous chatter from EWR Ground led to us believing we were OK to taxi to the gate. When Ground finally let us go, I switched to Operations vs. Ramp for gate and we were told to contact Ramp...who was more than a little upset. Apparently the Captain hadn't followed the correct wide-body line but had followed the taxi line which met the one we were already on. The wide-body gate is not well marked as such at the intersection of all these lines to make it readily apparent to us, although a post-incident discussion and analysis showed us that the textual description of WB taxi lines is clearly something we could and should have seen. Despite having sufficient clearance, which was visually confirmed, Ramp was understandably angry with us for not contacting them and for following the eastern, rather than center taxi line." Landing 22R we exited highspeed B4. During arrival briefing we discussed that the normal ground flow was for arrival traffic to utilize A, as B is used for traffic taxiing out. Exiting B4 ATC said to join N and contact Ground. That intersection is a junction of B4, N, A & B. Obviously a dynamic situation as we are clearing the runway and changing controllers. We joined N and as we switched to Ground Control made the hard right turn onto A consistent with our arrival briefing and consistent with the need to clear the runway rather than stopping leaving the rear of the aircraft still on the runway. After switching to Ground, the controller inquired as to our turn onto A. The controller queried us wondering if the signage was not clear. He referenced a recent incident where taxiway lights had been damaged by a wide body making a similar (or same) turn recently. He suggested that we were not the first ones to make this turn. In a follow up phone call we suggested that the instructions be more specific, such as 'join N and a right turn on B' so that there is no guesswork on anybody's part. EWR ATIS indicated 'Company expanded ramp procedures not in effect'. We were still with Ground discussing our runway exit as we approached the alleyway. Ground control did not switch us to Ramp Control. On our 'late' switch to Ramp Control we discovered we were on the wrong frequency. Upon coming up on the correct Ramp Control, we were admonished for entering the alleyway before contacting them and for being on the wrong line". Contributing factors were 1) missing the note regarding using the center of 3 lines for wide-bodies, 2) the fact that the only graphic depiction of the lines is not on the ramp diagram, not on any of the 10-7's, not on the gate page. It only appears on the secondary JeppPro AMM display of 10-9, and 3) The lead in line from RK ties into the left alleyway taxi line rather than the center as in every other similar situation I have ever seen. 4) There is considerable anxiety and distraction caused by ongoing company responses to Covid. While Covid has knocked the wind out of the travel and airline industry, the company's actions to pile on additional unnecessary restrictions and requirements add a huge level of stress, anxiety and uncertainty, adding completely unnecessary and avoidable threats and distractions to the conduct of our duties across the board! I am making more mistakes and I am witnessing my crew members and others like ground staff, ramp agents and maintenance personnel doing the same."
ASRS:1834417.s: A Boeing 787 crew exited Runway 22R at EWR and incorrectly entered the ramp area without contacting Ramp Control due to misinterpreting ATIS and unclear wide-body taxi line markings. The crew was admonished for following the wrong taxi line and failing to switch frequencies, with the reporter citing poor signage, ambiguous instructions, and pandemic-related stress as contributing factors.

ASRS:1834433.n: About 15 miles west of ORD on arrival we were exposed to a laser beam from the left front of the aircraft. I was Pilot Monitoring, my First Officer (FO) was flying, and I reported the location to ATC. About 5 minutes later I experienced an intense nauseous feeling. I thought I was going to be sick. The intense nauseous lasted maybe 5 minutes and then I started feeling somewhat better. My FO [advised ATC], we landed and taxied in without incident. Medical personnel met our flight and checked my vitals, all being normal. The upset stomach was still present but not as bad as it was in the air. Side note...The flight was X hours and 10 minutes, about 90 minutes into the flight we ate a crew meal. I'm not sure whether the nauseous feeling could be food related or if it was because of the laser. Experience a laser event followed by a pilot incapacitation followed by an inflight [urgency situation] on approach into ORD. Arrived at the gate and was evaluated by EMS. Had to wait an hour for crew transportation to the hotel. Arrived at the hotel after midnight. Stayed up to record the details of the flight. Called [operations] around XA:00 to say I was not rested physically or emotionally to operate the flight tonight that had a hotel pickup time of XB:00 followed by a X hour flight.
ASRS:1834433.s: The Pilot Monitoring reported a laser exposure on approach to ORD, followed by intense nausea that required EMS evaluation upon landing. The pilot attributed the symptoms to either the laser or a crew meal and subsequently reported being unfit for duty due to physical and emotional exhaustion.

ASRS:1834448.n: After a cabin deferral item was listed in the maintenance logbook 'FA (Flight Attendant) Crew Panel', I attempted to locate the equipment in the operating manuals. After a thorough search, I realized that our operating manuals have no cabin safety items listed or major cabin components. We have water shutoff valves, IFE (Inflight Entertainment) equipment, ovens, and many more items that are crucial safety items for flight crews. This needs to be added to the operating manuals immediately. Cabin safety items and equipment need to be in the operating manuals immediately.
ASRS:1834448.s: A flight attendant reported that operating manuals lack listings for crucial cabin safety items, such as water shutoff valves and IFE equipment, despite a deferral being logged for the FA Crew Panel. The reporter states these items must be added to the manuals immediately to ensure flight crews can locate them.

ASRS:1834456.n: During the engine start we received an engine 3 start valve caution message. The Captain elected to start the engine 3 more times, finally starting it on the 4th attempt. During this time I suggested that we contact Dispatch to initiate a three-way call between the Captain, Dispatch, and Maintenance Control due to the fact that the engine was not starting. What actually ended up happening was the Captain used the DDG (Dispatch Deviations Guide) Procedure 80-XX-XX to start the engine, which is a maintenance procedure involving tools. He asked the pushback driver to do this procedure, I have no idea if this person was qualified to work on our aircraft or not?We had a Mechanic on board who elected not to go down and do the procedure but instead left someone else to do it. As it turned out, the tug driver outside said the valve moved by itself. However, what concerned me was if this person was qualified to work on our aircraft. I strongly suggested to the Captain before and after the event that we enter this item in the logbook as he'd been operating the engine start as though we were already deferred under DDG 80-XX-XX.After we continued out to the runway, we received a pack 1 caution message. The Captain had me run the checklist and eventually we ended up turning off the pack 1. Then, the Captain announced that the pack was just getting warm and turned the pack back on and turned to me and said, see it was just hot. I further insisted that we call Maintenance and Dispatch to report both of these items and was met with a tirade of sarcasm, trying to put me down. CRM at this time was at an all-time low. He finally agreed to do the 3-way call only as a further attempt to try and put me down. It turned out the items he didn't want to write up, Maintenance still wanted to him to write up in Miami. I think that further irritated him.Takeoff was normal, but as we reached 5000 ft. AGL the Captain turn round to me and expressed his further annoyance at me, saying we're going to have to talk about this. As we were in sterile cockpit, climbing out of mountainous terrain, I responded with let's talk about this on the ground, which I guess further irritated him and he yelled at me he'd take me to the Chief Pilot. I wanted him to concentrate on his flying duties and not lecturing me, that could come later, so I said nothing back. At approximately 17000 ft. we received another pack 1 message. This time, the Captain ended up turning off pack one and it remained off for the duration of the flight.
ASRS:1834456.s: During preflight and climb, the Captain used a maintenance procedure on Engine 3 via an unqualified tug driver and ignored Pack 1 cautions, leading to poor CRM and a verbal confrontation. The Captain eventually deferred Pack 1 after a second fault at 17,000 feet, though Maintenance later required logging both items.

ASRS:1834488.n: ATC notified us when we checked in, that GPS jamming was taking place. we received an ATC fail, and eventually GPS caution. We lost both the left and right GPS. They never came back, until we were on the ground and Maintenance reset the circuit breakers. I've seen GPS jamming before, but I've never seen that the GPS, and transponder didn't come back.
ASRS:1834488.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming and an ATC failure during flight, resulting in the loss of both GPS units and the transponder. These systems remained inoperative until maintenance reset the circuit breakers on the ground.

ASRS:1834493.n: Cruising at Mach .82/FL310, the aircraft entered an area of heavy precipitation. Engine ignition override was on. Crew observed N2 roll back to approximately 35% and received a Level 2 ENG 2 RPM LO. The throttle did not move and all other engine parameters were normal, EGT, oil pressure/temp. There was no yaw. The crew addressed the QRC, but the engine N2 RPM increased back to normal indications before they could run it. The rollback lasted less than 2 minutes. All indications were normal for remainder of the flight. Unknown cause.
ASRS:1834493.s: During cruise at FL310 in heavy precipitation, the crew observed Engine 2 N2 roll back to 35% with a Level 2 RPM LO warning. The engine recovered to normal indications within two minutes without crew intervention, and the cause remains unknown.

ASRS:1834556.n: I was PIC (Pilot in Command) and Pilot Flying. We were cleared to land and to expect to exit at Taxiway XX, approach and landing were normal, as I was approaching the high speed left turn onto Taxiway XX, the wind, which was out of the south and gusty, caused the aircraft to veer left, I attempted to correct with full right rudder and right brake, which was ineffective. I realized we were committed to going through the lights, went through/around them, then just as quickly back thru them onto XX taxiway. We taxied to the ramp and parked.While not minimizing my full responsibility for this event, I believe it's important to consider how this happened in order to mitigate any future occurrence. Contributing factors: 1. The gusty crosswind2. My inexperience with Aircraft X3. Excessive speed for the conditionsMitigation Strategies:1. Slow down, get to taxi speed more quickly.2. Understand the only connection to the nose wheel is the tiller and to guard/utilize it appropriately.
ASRS:1834556.s: The Pilot in Command reported that gusty south winds and excessive speed caused Aircraft X to veer left during a high-speed turn onto Taxiway XX, resulting in an excursion through taxiway lights. The pilot attributed the incident to crosswinds, inexperience with the aircraft, and speed, noting that rudder and brake inputs were ineffective.

ASRS:1834570.n: I was approaching the ZZZ airport for landing on Runway XX and observing other arriving traffic. I entered the traffic pattern and started my prelanding checklist. I observed another aircraft ahead of me making a nonstandard approach. I adjusted my approach to sequence behind the other aircraft and ran the prelanding checklist a second time. On final, I was sure the gear was down and indicated by three lights, but perhaps the other aircraft's close proximity caused me to overlook the gear handle not being fully locked in the down position and the lights on. Also, the gear warning horn was not heard.To eliminate the possibility of this happening again, a go-around and better sequencing along with maintenance to double-check gear indicators will be practiced in the future.
ASRS:1834570.s: The pilot approaching ZZZ Airport for landing on Runway XX suspected that close proximity to another aircraft caused them to overlook an unsecured gear handle despite three green lights and no warning horn. The pilot plans to practice go-arounds, improve sequencing, and request maintenance checks on gear indicators to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1834574.n: I was conducting a routine cross-country flight to ZZZ1, then back to my departure location ZZZ. The flight to ZZZ1 went as planned. We landed on Runway XX and were asked to back-taxi on the runway by ATC in order for us to depart back to ZZZ. We departed from Runway XX and headed back southwest. We climbed to 4500 MSL enroute back to ZZZ. Approximately 20 miles out I began my initial descent. As I began this descent, I also tuned into the CTAF frequency as Tower was closed at this time. Approximately 10 miles out I made my first position report. I made a secondary one at 6 miles. Upon reporting at 6 miles, I was under the impression that I was the only one in the airspace as there was no other plane making reports. Upon this, I began to set up for a 6-mile final straight into Runway XX at ZZZ. I made another position report at 4 miles and then another 2 miles. Once I reached 1 mile out, I made the announcement that I was on short final. I continued my descent until I had reached the numbers and started my round out. Upon doing this, my ADS-B announced that there was traffic on short final at 6 o'clock. This traffic had not made any position reports and gave nobody in the airspace an indication for what he was doing. Upon hearing this, I made the decision to land in order to avoid a possible midair collision with this traffic.Continuing my flare, I was dealing with a 15 kt. headwind which I had flown with through my entire approach. Upon flaring, I decreased power and the wind shifted from a headwind to a crosswind that became in excess of 17 kt. As a result of this, I side-loaded my right main landing gear. As an attempt to keep the nose gear off for as long as possible, I increased power to aid in my attempt. After doing this the crosswind sheared to a tailwind, which as result forced my nose straight into the ground. With the increase in power and the direct nose impact, this resulted in the aircraft bouncing. As a result of the bounce, I initiated go-around procedures. As a I began to gain altitude, the aircraft who was not talking to anyone came to a stop on Runway XY. As a precautionary measure I flew 10 miles out and climbed up to 2500 ft. I soon turned towards the airfield and began making position reports every mile as an attempt to make contact with this aircraft. Unable to make any sort of communication with this aircraft, I overflew the field to try and see his exact position. I observed that he was off the active runway and on a taxiway. Upon noticing this, I made the decision to go in and land. This decision was based upon the fact that I was unaware of any possible damage to the aircraft and I had no exact way of telling what this other aircraft's intentions were. Upon making my base to final turn for Runway XX, this aircraft turned off the taxiway and departed Runway XY. I made a landing on XX and was able to taxi back to the hangar.As I taxied up to my hangar, this aircraft was finally able to make contact with me as he reported radio difficulties. Upon performing a normal shutdown, I got out and examined the aircraft and the only direct observation that could be made was that the tube of the front nose gear tire had gone flat. It was only once the cowling was removed that the damage to the firewall was observed. A learning experience that I will take away from this is to be more aware of potential traffic surrounding me and in my airspace. The most important one I believe is to be more aware of the possibility of windshear on final. This better preparation and awareness I believe, would help me to respond better if a situation like this were to occur again and I was called upon to take action. Having this type of experience will benefit me as before, I did not have the chance to be forced to react in a situation like this. Having gone through this will help me to learn from my mistakes and allow me to correct them and perform an appropriate response to these less-than-ideal landing conditions in the future. I also believe that I need to learn to be more hesitant about adding power in a situation like this and learn to make more accurate or precise adjustments that might be necessary.
ASRS:1834574.s: The pilot experienced a nose gear flat tire and firewall damage after a wind shear-induced bounce during landing at ZZZ, triggered by a sudden shift from headwind to tailwind while avoiding unreported traffic. The pilot subsequently executed a go-around, circled to verify the other aircraft's position, and landed safely after the other pilot reported radio difficulties.

ASRS:1834613.n: Aircraft X entered Sector 25 airspace without a hand off.Sector 64 was combined at sector 65, with myself as the D-side and Name, as the R-side. We had alerted the supervisor that things were getting out of control, about 15 minutes before it actually got busy. We were working southbound overflights who were routed into our airspace due to weather, southbound arrivals, and all 4 feeds normally as 1 feed northbound.This sector completely blew up and became unusable, with 20+ airplanes all deviating for weather, stacked on top of each other, and no course of action out of it. It was extremely surprising there were not more LoSSes (Lack of Separation Standards) or airspace deviations.The supervisor and TMU failed to recognize or take action, even after being told, that the sector was out of control. Sector complexity has changed due to the Metroplex project, and unfortunately the TMI's have not caught up with it.Erring on the side of caution, the supervisor, with the concurrence TMU should be slowing down and putting on in trail on the sector. Unfortunately, it ends up with the supervisor not taking any action, and the sector controllers caught having to clean up the mess.
ASRS:1834613.s: Sector 64/65 controllers reported that Sector 25 airspace became unusable due to weather deviations and increased complexity from the Metroplex project. Despite warnings, the supervisor and TMU failed to reduce traffic flow, forcing controllers to manage the resulting congestion without additional support.

ASRS:1834648.n: We were seven miles behind a 747 on approach to Runway 9 in Miami, flaps 5, 170 knots on glidepath, when the aircraft abruptly went into 30 degrees left bank. We commanded full right aileron and there was no response for an unknown amount of time (possibly three seconds). We regained wings level flight only to encounter another abrupt 30 degree roll to the left with lack of aircraft control. After much discussion, my First Officer and I were worried that after such a 'minor incident' (seven miles behind a 747) that the event should cause such a severe loss of aircraft control. We both agree that the incident should be investigated. We were 15 miles out on the localizer to Runway 9 at 5000 feet. We were seven miles in trail of a B747. We encountered wake turbulence and the aircraft yawed to the left 30+ degrees for 3-5 seconds. We inputted right aileron with no results. The aircraft returned to level flight on its own and immediately went into a 30+ degree left bank turn for 3-5 seconds.
ASRS:1834648.s: The crew encountered wake turbulence from a preceding B747 while on approach to Runway 9 at 5,000 feet. The aircraft experienced two uncommanded 30-degree left banks with no response to aileron input, leading the pilots to recommend an investigation.

ASRS:1834668.n: Assigned ZZZZZ Visual to Runway XX at ZZZ. Briefed use of VNAV in accordance with Approach Briefing Guide. Prior to ZZZ1 VOR, instructed to descend from 4,000 to 3,000 ft. MSL and FLCH was utilized. Upon crossing ZZZ1, pilot not flying, while also saturated with LCA (Line Check Airman) duties, set 1,500 ft. for ZZZZZ1 and then touchdown zone elevation while slowing and configuring aircraft. We did not notice FLCH was still engaged until ATC provided an altitude alert at 900 ft. MSL. Pilot not flying/LCA took command of aircraft and performed a momentary level-off before giving aircraft back to original pilot flying for a stabilized approach and landing. Pilot not flying is an LCA (Line Check Airman) conducting an Initial Operating Experience flight for pilot flying, who is a transition First Officer from the other aircraft builder.Assigned to fly the ZZZZZ Visual Approach to Runway XX at ZZZ. Installed the RNAV V XX procedure in FMC and briefed RNAV/visual approach procedures. ATC cleared us direct ZZZ1 and cross ZZZ1 at 3,000 ft. LNAV was engaged to fly direct ZZZ1 and FLCH was engaged to descend to 3,000 ft. Crossing ZZZ1, pilot not flying entered 1,500 ft. in MCP altitude window for ZZZZZ1 crossing altitude. While descending on profile, aircraft was slowing to 180 kt. and configuring for landing. PM was tracking the configuration changes and verifying on course with LNAV, and then selected TDZE after passing ZZZZZ2 intersection. Pilot flying was having difficulty finding the runway which was out his right window behind [of] his shoulder line. Pilot not flying looked outside to acquire runway to direct pilot flying to look in the right direction. At that moment, ZZZ Tower Controller called 'Altitude Alert' for our flight. Pilot not flying looked inside and noticed altitude was 900 ft. crossing ZZZZZ1, below the 1,500-ft. altitude that was programmed in the FMC. Pilot not flying then also noticed that VNAV was not engaged but the aircraft was descending in FLCH, so was therefore not on the VNAV descent path. Pilot not flying took control of the aircraft, leveled the descent, and continued to follow the LNAV course to line up with Runway XX. Once aligned and in proper position to land, pilot not flying gave control of aircraft back to pilot flying, who conducted a stable visual approach to a safe landing.
ASRS:1834668.s: During a visual approach, a transition First Officer and Line Check Airman descended below the 1,500 ft crossing altitude at ZZZZZ1 because FLCH remained engaged instead of VNAV. The crew leveled off after an ATC altitude alert at 900 ft and completed a stabilized landing.

ASRS:1834739.n: While crossing the threshold at Vref, a loss of speed and slight roll was encountered, similar to that of mild wake turbulence. Power was added in a timely fashion to arrest descent and neither horizontal, vertical, or speed stability was lost. The GPWS called 'don't sink, don't sink.' The approach remained stable so the landing was continued. We uneventfully touched down safely in the touchdown zone and exited on a high-speed taxiway short of B intersection.
ASRS:1834739.s: During landing threshold crossing at Vref, the crew encountered a speed loss and slight roll resembling mild wake turbulence, triggering a GPWS "don't sink" alert. Power was added to arrest descent, allowing a stable approach and safe touchdown in the zone.

ASRS:1834745.n: Pine Ridge airport (IEN) does not have any runway markings, including runway designation, center-line, touchdown or edge markings. The airport beacon rotates but does not illuminate. The windsock is in poor condition, preventing determination of direction or approximate velocity of wind. The runway appears to have been recently re-sealed. During night operations, it is very difficult to identify the touch down point and determine height above runway during flare.Ensure appropriate agencies are informed and needed corrections made.
ASRS:1834745.s: A pilot reported that night operations at Pine Ridge Airport (IEN) were hazardous due to missing runway markings, a non-illuminating beacon, and a poor-condition windsock. These deficiencies made identifying the touchdown point and judging height during the flare very difficult.

ASRS:1834791.n: 1 hour into flight we received an ACARS message from Dispatch Center. They were advised from ZZZ Ramp, we had 10 lithium batteries in position 11L per the Dangerous Goods (DG) paperwork. We actually had 19 lithium batteries in position 11L. Weight and Balance was correct because they were weighed in the container, just incorrect amount on the manifest. [The cause of the issue was the lack of] attention to detail. [Suggest] double checking paperwork.
ASRS:1834791.s: The flight crew received an ACARS message one hour into flight revealing 19 lithium batteries in position 11L instead of the 10 listed on the Dangerous Goods manifest. The reporter attributed this discrepancy to a lack of attention to detail, noting that weight and balance remained correct as the batteries were weighed in the container.

ASRS:1834792.n: Received intermittent ATC Fault and right GPS EICAS message when crossing the military range of New Mexico. Notified ATC and complied with QRH. After exiting the military airspace, both messages disappeared and system worked fine. Apparent GPS jamming near military airspace over New Mexico. Received ATC Fault and right GPS EICAS messages. Selected radio updating for FMS. Indications went away after clearing the airspace. System then worked as designed. No human performance issues present as causal.
ASRS:1834792.s: The pilot experienced intermittent ATC Fault and right GPS EICAS messages while crossing a military range in New Mexico, likely due to GPS jamming. After selecting radio updating for the FMS and exiting the airspace, the indications cleared and the system functioned normally.

ASRS:1834799.n: We received an ACARS message stating that unmanifested DG was on board. We calculated that no limitations were exceeded and continued to the destination without further incident. Loading crew/Hazmat Agent error.
ASRS:1834799.s: The crew received an ACARS message indicating unmanifested dangerous goods were on board. After confirming no limitations were exceeded, they continued to the destination without incident, attributing the error to the loading crew or Hazmat Agent.

ASRS:1834845.n: Landing XXR ZZZ during gusty conditions, received too low terrain while on short final. Low-level windshear reported on east side of field. Wind gust took airspeed up to 175. Neither pilot flying or pilot not flying saw airspeed go above flaps 30 speed of 175, or any movement in flap retraction due to airspeed. Original flap 30 speed was 147. Added 15 for gust. Reported stable at 500 ft. AGL with 1,000 FPM descent. Gusty conditions from above FAF to 100 ft. AGL, but under control. Largest gust after 500 ft. AGL stable call, approximately 150 ft. AGL. On short final, I thought 'too low terrain' was an erroneous warning. Visual conditions from FAF inbound. Touchdown uneventful. Wrote up maintenance discrepancy for possible overspeed due to unusual GPWS warning.
ASRS:1834845.s: The flight crew landed aircraft XXR ZZZ in gusty conditions after receiving a "too low terrain" warning on short final. They attributed the warning to a wind gust increasing airspeed to 175 knots and filed a maintenance discrepancy for possible overspeed.

ASRS:1834902.n: Cleared to taxi from FBO Ramp to Runway XX, follow proceeding Aircraft Y. After starting to turn left on ramp, noticed right brake was soft. Once straightened out, tried brakes again, right went down halfway and after pumping it was not quite back to normal. Transferred controls to FO (First Officer) to try his side. He stated his right brake was a little soft. Transferred controls back to CA (Captain) and I tried brakes again while taxiing to Runway XX. Brake went halfway down and after pumping 1-2 times, it was still soft. Got to hold-short line of Runway XX and right brake went more than halfway down.We were on Tower frequency and told Tower we needed to go back to FBO Ramp due to brake issue. We had two flights to airports with short runways, ZZZ1 and ZZZ2. I did not feel it was safe to proceed. We were cleared onto Runway XX and to taxi to Taxiway XX and then back to Ramp. Tower asked if we needed any other assistance. We passed negative. While on Runway XX, I tested brakes three more times. Each time it got progressively worse on right side. After exit on XX, I transferred controls to FO. His right brake went halfway down. We transferred controls back to CA and my right brake was still halfway to almost three quarters down to work. As I was making my final left turn into parking, my right brake went to the floor. I was at less than walking speed and was able to stop aircraft with left brake and beta. Subsequently shutdown without any other issue. FO escorted passenger into the FBO and I contacted maintenance, and operations. Additionally, I had noticed yesterday while picking up aircraft in ZZZ3 that [the] aircraft had [a] brake write-up [last month]. I went back through all the logs in [the] can and discovered that there were brake issues [a few months ago] as well. It appears that [the] brakes were having issues every 28-35 days from [a few months ago].
ASRS:1834902.s: The Captain and First Officer experienced progressively worsening right brake pressure while taxiing from the FBO to Runway XX, prompting a return to the ramp. The aircraft was stopped safely using the left brake and beta, revealing a recurring brake issue documented in maintenance logs every 28–35 days.

ASRS:1834906.n: We were given a late hand off by the previous controller to Salt Lake Approach control controlling the LEEHY arrival. On check in Approach Control contacted us first and it was apparent that he was task saturated and that the sector was extremely busy. He told us he needed to give us a 'box pattern for spacing' and gave us a heading westbound over Utah Lake. We complied with this heading and the instruction to descend to 14,000 ft. and reduce speed to 190 KIAS. We were then given another heading turning us to our left and back towards the approach course. It was at this time that we got a traffic advisory of an aircraft that was in the direction we were now turning towards with the latest vector from ATC. The aircraft was climbing towards us as we were descending and turning as per the ATC instructions. Almost simultaneously ATC realized the situation and gave us a traffic alert at the same time the aircraft gave us an RA to descend. The Captain immediately disconnected the autopilot and began to comply with the instruction to descend. At this time I was looking outside doing what I could to see and avoid the traffic. At this point we were in a layer of smoke and visibility was low. I was able to spot the traffic as the aircraft was passing above us. It was very close, only a few hundred feet. It is hard to judge distance without anything to base the measurement on. Just prior to me seeing the traffic the TCAS system made the annunciation to monitor vertical speed and as the aircraft was passing off our right we got clear of conflict. It took us a minute to get back with the controller and he gave us a new altitude and heading to join the final approach course into Salt Lake. We made an uneventful landing on Runway 35 in Salt Lake and once safely parked contacted Company to figure out next steps. I believe the cause of this event mostly had to do with improper instructions from ATC. I obviously did not have the big picture of the traffic environment in that sector like the controller did. However I could tell he was task saturated and had more aircraft to control than he could safely handle. We were not aware of any potential conflict until beginning the turn to the heading the controller gave us which put us in conflict with the other aircraft. In the future I will attempt to be even more vigilant at situational awareness. I believe this event has only renewed my sense of importance on this matter. Furthermore I would suggest that the controller of this sector not be controlling more than one sector as it seemed he was. I believe that the controllers task saturation was potentially the largest contributing factor in the event. I am glad that we responded so promptly to the resolution advisory and were able to resolve the conflict. The training we had at Company prepared us well for this situation and I am glad that I have practiced it many times in training.
ASRS:1834906.s: Pilots on a LEEHY arrival into Salt Lake received conflicting vectors from a task-saturated controller, resulting in a near-midair collision with a climbing aircraft. The crew executed a TCAS resolution advisory to descend, passing the traffic at a few hundred feet, and attributed the event to controller task saturation and improper instructions.

ASRS:1834936.n: Received report from PWM approach control while on vectors for Runway 11 that aircraft ahead reported a drone 3 miles from end of Runway 11 above their glide path. We sighted the drone above our fight path and continued approach. Drone was hovering around 1,500 feet close to final approach course a 3 miles from touchdown. Drone was black in color and at least 3 feet in length. We reported drone sighting to ATC, Dispatch, and Chief Pilot.
ASRS:1834936.s: The flight crew sighted a black drone hovering at 1,500 feet on the final approach course for Runway 11 while on vectors. They continued the approach after reporting the sighting to ATC, Dispatch, and the Chief Pilot.

ASRS:1834950.n: This trip is actually the continuation of Aircraft X, on date, the day following our weather divert to ZZZ.While beginning our descent on the ZZZZZ 4 arrival into ZZZ1 the FO (PF) deployed the speed brakes to approx 50% in order to comply with the altitude restriction. When the FO stowed the Speed Brakes the aircraft abruptly rolled 35 degrees to the left. The autopilot had difficulty controlling the aircraft so we disconnected and FO flew manually. The FO quickly and accurately corrected the left-roll tendency with right ailerons, leveled the wings and continued the arrival. Simultaneously to these events the SPOILERS EICAS illuminated. We slowed to 250 KIAS to minimize the left-roll tendency and informed ATC. We decided to have the FO continue to fly and handle radios while I ran the non-normal checklist, coordinated with Dispatch and Maintenance and ran the TEST with the Lead Flight Attendant. After finishing the SPOILERS EICAS checklist and the other coordination was complete it was determined that some of the spoilers on the left wing remained in the UP position and would not stow. I opted to request priority handling and requested the ILS to Runway XXC with a long, 20 mile final, which ATC coordinated. We then gradually slowed and configured the aircraft, determining the aircraft controllability with each configuration change. Once final landing configuration (Flaps 30) and target speed were established the aircraft continued the left-roll tendency but was manageable. The FO accurately noted that at target speed the speed tape showed little margin above stick shaker activation, so we opted to add 10 Knots to our target speed. I believe this was due to the spoilers still extended on the left wing. The remainder of the approach and landing being uneventful as the FO made an excellent landing. I took the aircraft on the rollout and we met the responding Emergency personnel. They checked us over and we taxied to the gate.
ASRS:1834950.s: During the ZZZZZ 4 arrival into ZZZ1, the First Officer deployed speed brakes, causing an abrupt 35-degree left roll and a SPOILERS EICAS warning when they failed to stow. The crew managed the left-wing spoiler malfunction by adjusting speed and configuration, executing a safe landing with emergency services standing by.

ASRS:1834961.n: We started our descent to cross ZZZZZ at 10,000 ft. and 250 kias intersection on the ZZZZZ4, we started our descent and brought power to idle as the aircraft sped up we noted the number 2 engine. We advised ATC we would be unable to make the crossing restriction. They were okay with that, we made throttle inputs but had no engine response. We ran IAC (Immediate Action Checklist) for uncommanded acceleration/ engine overspeed. The engine didn't shutdown, we then ran QRH leading to inflight engine shutdown which was unsuccessful in shutting down the engine. We advised ATC and then ran the severe engine damage QRH except for discharging bottles. After that we received extended vectors to a 35-40 mile final, made a call to the Flight Attendant and passengers. Ran out of time to complete and send a message to Dispatch as we were inbound and trying to stay ahead of the aircraft and execute a safe approach and landing. There should be a QRH for unresponsive throttle or a tree in the inflight engine shutdown procedure for 'did the engine shutdown' after the action for putting throttle to shutoff, leading to instructions for a procedural shutdown using the engine fire push switch. On descent, realized right engine was stuck at full power. Pulled thrust back with no response. Advised ATC unable to comply with descend via, and we were working a problem. Ran uncommanded acceleration IAC (Immediate Action Checklist) and QRH. Decision tree prompted engine shutdown and single engine procedures, of which didn't produce an engine shutdown. Advised ATC, and requested delay vectors. Discussed with FO (First Officer) no alternative but to shut down via severe engine damage IAC/QRH. We both noted probably a disconnect of sorts from thrust lever to engine. FO and I agreed with course of action. I kept FO Pilot Flying, felt PM (Pilot Monitoring) tasks were more complex. Checklists completed and prepped for landing single engine Runway XXR. Requested 35-40 mile final after delay vectors. Began to send Dispatch a message via ACARS but ATC made for a very busy cockpit, with many requests and turns. I did notify FA (Flight Attendant) of issue, that we were shutting down engine due to over speed, and expect a normal landing with Aircraft Fire/Rescue vehicles to meet plane. Explained announcement to make to passengers, and she complied. Advised FO at anytime he could transfer controls to me if he felt the need. Landed without incident, Aircraft Fire Rescue vehicles did inspection, and we taxi'd to gate.I'd suggest an IAC/QRH option taking into account a failed thrust lever, not just uncommanded acceleration. It's not a problem to 'be a pilot' and make the right decision, but this scenario should be addressed at the procedural level should it reoccur.
ASRS:1834961.s: During descent, the crew encountered an unresponsive right engine stuck at full power, likely due to a thrust lever disconnect. After standard shutdown checklists failed, they executed severe engine damage procedures to shut down the engine and landed safely single-engine, recommending procedural updates for unresponsive throttles.

ASRS:1835014.n: There was an unclaimed vape in the aft galley on the counter that we believed may have belonged to either one of the cleaners, one of the caterers, or one of the people who did the security checks on the plane. Originally, [other flight attendant] thought it was mine and I thought it was his but when we found out it was neither one of ours, we disposed of it in the trash bin. After realizing very soon (within a few minutes after putting in in the trash bin) that it was a bad idea to put it in there, we took it out. We noticed that the light on the vape was flashing so we tried looking through the Operations Manual to figure out what we should do with the device. After not finding any information on it, we contacted the purser who contacted the Captain who then advised us to put the device into the thermal containment bag. I was concerned with the vape flashing because I have seen it before where it would flash and start producing smoke. We were not comfortable with leaving it out and exposed.
ASRS:1835014.s: Cabin crew discovered an unclaimed, flashing vape in the aft galley and initially discarded it before retrieving it due to safety concerns. After consulting the Operations Manual and contacting the Captain, they secured the device in a thermal containment bag to prevent potential smoke or fire.

ASRS:1835092.n: Landing with crosswind corrected for crosswind landed centerline, it was not a bad landing.Used aero dynamic breaking and aircraft brakes.The aircraft continued right I kept left aileron and left rudder to keep the aircraft straight.Aircraft exited the run way to the right and came to a stop.No damage to aircraft and no injuries. I taxied the aircraft back and exited Runway XXL and contacted Ground then parked the aircraft with no further incident.I inspected the aircraft and no damage had occurred.
ASRS:1835092.s: The pilot landed with a crosswind correction but the aircraft drifted right despite applying left aileron and rudder, exiting the runway. The aircraft stopped with no damage or injuries, and the pilot taxied it back to park after inspecting for damage.

ASRS:1835114.n: Familiarization flight with the airspace around ZZZ and carbureted C172 model with another instructor onboard. Departed ZZZ at approximately XA:00 local, After landing at ZZZ1, we departed southwest bound at 2,500'. I was flying the aircraft when we experienced a sudden loss of engine power, followed by complete engine loss. I gave controls to the other instructor and began troubleshooting / running checklists - Checked fuel selector / gauges, mixture/throttle, carb heat, and were unable to get it restarted. We turned south for a cornfield and began preparing for an off field landing while I contacted ZZZ Tower to let them know of our situation. The other instructor onboard maneuvered for a safe landing on the cornfield. Once the aircraft was secured, we exited the plane and inspected everything. No injuries or damage to the aircraft / property. I called Clearance Delivery and asked them to let ZZZ Tower know that we were okay. I spoke with various agencies over the next 30 minutes. I let them know we were okay and the plane was undamaged. We shared our location with flight school management, who then drove out and brought extra fuel. We began straining fuel, which all came back clean. Then added approx 5 gallons to each fuel tanks and did a thorough run up on the engine - All gauges were green and no issues seen. After discussing we came to the conclusion of carburetor icing affecting engine performance. We were at a relatively low cruise setting with high humidity due to showers/storms in the area. When troubleshooting in the air earlier, pulling the carb heat had no affect on engine RPM. We commenced a soft/short field takeoff from the cornfield and landed safely back at ZZZ. Loss of RPM, suspected Carb icing. Insufficient power. Ran checklist, restart and shutdown checklist. No damage to aircraft or landing site. No injury.
ASRS:1835114.s: During a familiarization flight in a carbureted C172 at 2,500 feet, the pilot experienced a complete engine loss suspected to be caused by carburetor icing due to high humidity. The instructor executed a safe off-field landing in a cornfield with no injuries or damage, and the aircraft was later refueled and returned to ZZZ.

ASRS:1835126.n: Departing Runway XX at ZZZ. Had approaching Aircraft Y on ADS-B while they were executing a practice approach to Runway XY. Pattern traffic was using Runway YY. After rotation, I had a visual on the other aircraft and started an early turn to pass behind. At that point, my glare shield mount for my GPS moving map came loose and dropped into the control stick arc dangling by the data/power cord. I grabbed it with my right (stick) hand and began controlling the aircraft with my left hand. I was holding the stick below the grip and unable to reach the push-to-talk trigger. If I had turned left to runway heading, I would have gone wing up to the other aircraft and lost sight. I focused on flying the airplane first and after passing the aircraft was able to move my left hand into position on the grip to reach the push to talk trigger. By this time the pilot in Aircraft Y was calling me and expressed, understandably, his alarm. The early turn was an effort to clear the pattern quickly for the training aircraft that use this field. However, I believe continuing the upwind further would have minimized the conflict that is a part of practice approaches opposite to the traffic patterns in use. Opposite direction approaches are common at this airport and other uncontrolled fields in the area. Secondly, I am re-engineering the bracket for my GPS moving map to preclude a recurrence. I will also add a 'bracket secure' check to my pre-takeoff flow.
ASRS:1835126.s: The pilot departing Runway XX at ZZZ experienced a GPS mount failure that dropped into the control stick arc, forcing one-handed flight and delaying radio contact with an approaching aircraft. The pilot attributed the conflict to an early turn to clear pattern traffic and plans to re-engineer the bracket and add a secure check to prevent recurrence.

ASRS:1835128.n: I am a pilot who hasn't flown GA in XY+ years. I hired this pilot to re-familiarize me in the GA world. Instructor is very capable and in my opinion did nothing incorrectly. We had been doing touch and go's at ZZZ1 airport, and we were returning to ZZZ to land. The runway being used was XX. The instructor was flying back and made all the required calls on the Unicom frequency. I was in the left seat, watching instructor fly and listening to instructor speak on the radio. I saw a plane turn toward us as instructor started to make base turn and I told instructor to roll out and stay downwind. Instructor lifted wing and saw the traffic coming right at us. He had taken off on Runway YY. He never made any calls. He was turning upwind when we were turning base. He finally saw us and passed behind us. He made a comment on the radio, admitting to making 'a huge mistake' and apologized for it. The runway in use was definitely XX with a 10 kt head wind. I shudder to think what would have happened if I hadn't seen him.
ASRS:1835128.s: A pilot and instructor conducting touch-and-gos at ZZZ1 on Runway XX encountered a GA aircraft taking off from Runway YY without radio calls. The pilot spotted the intruder during the base turn and directed the instructor to roll out, preventing a collision as the other aircraft passed behind them.
